<meta>This page serves as the official shelfmark and identification page for a manuscript within the Ottoboniani Latini collection of the Vatican Apostolic Library. It establishes the formal provenance and cataloging location within the Papal archives.</meta>

->The Supreme Pontiff<- <note>original: "S.P.", likely abbreviating *Summus Pontifex* (The Supreme Pontiff) or *Sacri Palatii* (of the Sacred Palace).</note>

->Vatican Apostolic Library<- <note>Seal description: The official seal of the library depicts the Papal Tiara—the triple crown—positioned above the crossed keys of Saint Peter, which symbolize the keys to the Kingdom of Heaven. The circular border contains the name of the institution in Latin: BIBLIOTECA APOSTOLICA VATICANA.</note>

# OTTOBONI LATIN 2074

<term>Ottoboniani Latini</term> — The "Ottoboni Latin" collection. This is a famous group of manuscripts named after the family of Pope Alexander VIII (Pietro Ottoboni), who acquired a massive library in 1690, including many items formerly belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden.
<term>Vatican Apostolic Library</term> — Founded in 1475, this is the central research library of the Holy See and one of the most important repositories of historical texts in the world.
<term>Shelfmark</term> — A unique identification code (similar to a modern call number) used by librarians and scholars to locate a specific book or manuscript in the stacks.
<term>2074</term> — The specific volume number assigned to this manuscript within the Ottoboni Latin series.

<summary>This page acts as a modern archival cover for a Latin manuscript, identifying it as item number 2074 in the Vatican's Ottoboni collection. It carries the official seal of the Vatican Apostolic Library to denote its ownership and preservation by the Holy See.</summary>
<keywords>Vatican Apostolic Library, Ottoboniani Latini, shelfmark, Papal seal, manuscript, archives, Latin collection</keywords>

<meta>This page continues a technical analysis of Scholastic thought. While the previous page focused on the "universal man" and the perfection of the soul through grace, this section shifts abruptly into a legal and dialectical argument, likely from a commentary on Canon Law (specifically the Clementines). It employs a standard "objection and response" format, common in medieval university settings, to define how laws and sentences are delivered or applied.</meta>

In this way, he does not deny that this thing is done by the act itself, and unless it is in the same delivery <note>original: "latione"; in this legal context, it refers to the formal delivery of a sentence or the proposing of a law</note> as the judgment. <margin>It is opposed</margin> This is opposed especially in the matter of delivery, against **Clement**, in the <term>single chapter "on prebends and dignities" in the Sixth [Book of Decretals]</term> <note>original: "c. un. de prebend. et dign. in 6."; a standard reference to the Liber Sextus, a collection of Canon Law</note> where it is said that one acts toward the observation of such habits through the common delivery of many, and not through a condemning division. Furthermore, regarding this part—that it looks to this method—this is not established from the cause alone, but also from many other circumstances, as can be considered. Again, toward the same reasoning.

Indeed, certain things regarding this part seem to be certain in writings and other records, so that some reason is not lacking for them, as appears from the opinion of those which ought to be found no less in others. Therefore, it seems from other opinions, which the above-mentioned doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to established legal or theological authorities of the medieval period</note> collect here and there in their treatises. Thus, it is more proven that this part proceeds, because it is so stated in that chapter.

To the first, we respond that that distinction of delivery seems only to have a place in that matter of which was spoken above. But to the other part, it is answered that the doctors seem to hold this part no less rightly. From this, it is concluded from these reasons that this matter must be firmly held, especially since there are not others lacking who assert the same equally, as appears from the words of the preceding [author] regarding this matter, and as is also clear through several other doctors of the same opinion.

To the second, indeed, Aristotle <note>original: "Ar."; standard abbreviation for Aristotle, "The Philosopher"</note> responded that this does not have a place in this case, but only in another, where it is clearly a matter of another thing.

...participating, and by delivery, as if he wished for this finite consolation in his own act thereafter; and therefore, some whom the delivery itself regards will be able to be restored to themselves afterwards—namely, after they have been so <unclear>cleared</unclear>. To the second, indeed, which is brought forward, it is answered that this is not against the aforesaid. To the third, indeed, Aristotle responded that this does not have a place in this case, but only in another, where it is clearly a matter of another thing; therefore he concludes that no change should be made from this. Although some think otherwise, nevertheless that reason brought forward above seems to be more effective for proving this matter, just as it is proven by several reasons.

To the fourth, indeed, the same Aristotle responds that that distinction of delivery seems only to have a place in that matter of which was spoken above. But to the other part, it is answered that the doctors seem to hold this part no less rightly.

From this, it is concluded from these reasons that this matter must be firmly held.

The text is highly repetitive, following a structured dialectical method to conclude that a specific legal interpretation is the only one with a "firm foundation."</summary>

In this way also, it is guarded as much as it sees into the present. While it sees thus, it does not see. If, however, he makes our mind <note>original: "mentem"; in this context, the higher intellect</note> in such a way that it sees nothing other than the present thing, and mixes a temperament <note>original: "temperamentum"; a state of balance or a proper mixture of qualities</note> with all other things; thus therefore, while it captures the soul of that mind, it perceives the present thing through images... if indeed vice sees some similar immoderate thing in the temperament of the mind, it sees nothing except that kind, nor does it see that which it sees, or indeed it hinders the soul and entirely integrates the mind. And now, when the soul integrates that certain mind, and the mind itself [integrates] the temperament, it does not see that the tempered mind itself becomes what it sees as tempered, or indeed it hinders the soul and entirely integrates the mind. <meta>The previous page's text appeared to be a repetitive printer's proof from Marsilio Ficino's *Platonic Theology*. This current page, however, transitions into a structured Scholastic treatise on the nature of happiness (*beatitudo*). It follows the classical university style of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, heavily citing Aristotle's *Ethics* and Saint Augustine to explore whether human fulfillment is found in the mind, the will, or in God.</meta>

<margin>What happiness is in general</margin>
In regard to the aforementioned rule, I say that the essence of happiness <term>happiness: the Latin *beatitudo* refers to both earthly flourishing and eternal blessedness</term> seems to be that which satisfies a perfect appetite, and we call this ultimate satisfaction "happiness." It is found properly in a rational creature, who is called either happy or miserable because of the freedom of their will; and every single thing seeks this ultimate perfection according to its own manner, as it is said in the rule of God—

<margin>Happiness is one</margin>
Because happiness is the ultimate end, which is desired by man by reason of goodness; yet happiness is one, insofar as it is the ultimate end; but it is manifold subjectively, insofar as it is desirable by man, namely according to different powers. For the appetite is divided into the rational and the irrational: and the intellectual into the cognitive and the loving. If it is cognitive, then it is called speculative happiness; if it is loving, then it is called practical happiness. And thus it is called the ultimate perfection; because the whole universe of beings seeks its own good, but especially the rational being, who understands the end and directs himself toward it: and their appetite exists in either the cognitive or the appetitive power. Therefore, when "happiness" is spoken of, it is understood as the highest good, which is sought for its own sake, and toward which other things are ordered; and in this way the appetite of all things tends toward it: for the good is that which all things seek, as it is said in the first book of the *Ethics* <note>original: "primo ethicorum"; referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*</note>. Because happiness consists in the ultimate act, it appears to be a certain act which finally reaches the end: and this is an act of the intellect or of the will. For each thing has an order toward the ultimate end, through which each is perfected; when the appetite of a thing is stilled in the one thing toward which it tends, then it is called happy. Happiness is also found as created and uncreated: the uncreated is God himself; the created is the ultimate operation of the intellectual nature, by which it finally enjoys God himself, as will be said hereafter.

<column-break/>

Here it must be seen whether there is an ultimate act of the essence of the universe; and whether it can be asked what happiness is insofar as it is universal goodness. Because the ultimate end is one according to the rationale of goodness, although it is multiplied according to the diversity of desirable things. For just as it is said that the end is one to which all things are ordered, so also happiness is one by reason of the end; although it is manifold by reason of the agents, insofar as each person desires what they judge will be better for them, as is said in the first book of the *Ethics*.

<margin>It is asked whether the ultimate act is cognitive or affective</margin>
It is asked in the second place whether the ultimate act is cognitive <note>related to knowing/intellect</note> or affective <note>related to feeling/will</note>. To this it is said: That happiness consists in the ultimate act of the intellect; and Aristotle followed this opinion, saying that the ultimate happiness consists in the contemplation of the highest good: for knowledge is higher than action; for the happy person operates through it by itself: and therefore an act of this kind is called happiness. Others, however, say that happiness consists in an act of the will; because the act of the will is perfected and satisfied in the "good" as its object: for just as the intellect is perfected in truth, so the will is perfected in goodness: and since truth is a certain kind of goodness, it seems rather that the will reaches happiness through this manner: for the ultimate act of the will is fruition <term>fruition: from *fruitio*, the act of taking joy or delight in the possession of an object</term>; and fruition is the end, as is said by the learned; whence it follows that happiness consists in the ultimate act of the will. Others say that happiness is a single act of both powers, namely the intellect and the will: because just as both are found in the rational creature, so happiness seems to consist perfectly in both. And this is more true: for happiness does not consist in the act of the intellect alone, nor in the act of the will alone, but in both; so that it is one complete act made of both; which act is sought for its own sake: just as the vision of God through the intellect is sought first, and afterwards the fruition of God through the will: for one cannot perfectly exist without the other: whence by both acts a man is called happy, and tends toward this.

<column-break/>

<margin>Imperfect happiness in the world</margin>
Because on the part of this world, happiness seems to be imperfect and fragile; whence it is said: "All glory is like the flower of the grass" <note>original: "Omnis gloria quasi flos foeni"; a reference to 1 Peter 1:24 or Isaiah 40:6</note>. What happiness is in itself, however, and how it may be perfect, must be seen. Happiness, according to what it is in itself, is the perfect satisfaction of the rational power in the highest good: whence it is said: that just as the ultimate end of the universe is one, so happiness in itself is one. Here, however, it must be seen how a man can attain this happiness: for it is asked whether happiness can be had here in this world. To this it is said, according to the Philosopher <note>Standard scholastic title for Aristotle</note>, that happiness is the perfection of nature; and because this nature seems to remain here in a certain ultimate satisfaction, it seems that happiness can be had here: for just as a thing tends toward perfection, so also man desires to be at rest here; therefore it seems possible to take this mode of happiness. But regarding this, it must be known: that created happiness is properly the ultimate felicity, which cannot be perfectly had in this life; although it may be had in a certain hope and speculation: and this is called the "happiness of the way" <note>original: "beatitudo uia"; the partial happiness of a person still traveling through life toward heaven</note>; but the "happiness of the homeland" <note>original: "beatitudo patriae"; the perfect happiness of heaven</note> is perfect and final: and this is that by which the soul is stilled in God. Whence it is said in the Psalm:
> I shall be satisfied when your glory appears. <note>Psalm 17:15</note>
From this it follows that happiness is not only in a single act, but in a habit <note>a settled disposition or state of being</note> by which the soul is rendered perfect for this act. Indeed, everything is called blessed insofar as it is perfectly ordered toward its end: and because the soul of man is in the final order of the parts of the universe, therefore it cannot attain this end unless it has been ordered toward God. Toward this end, there is said to be a certain disposition in the soul, by which it is perfectly ordered to this end: whence it follows that happiness is the perfection of the soul following the perfection of the universe; and because happiness consists in the ultimate act, and that act is the most perfect, it follows that the soul is perfected through that act in its very ultimate end, insofar as it relates to God, where the rest of souls is said to be. But on the contrary, how can a man be called happy if he cannot attain happiness here, since a natural appetite is not in vain? For it seems that if man desires happiness, without which he cannot exist, nature could not be frustrated. To this it must be said: that although the soul desires it because of its ultimate good, and does so by a natural appetite, it is not required that it attain this in this world, except according to a certain participation.

<column-break/>

Where it must be seen briefly how it is the end of the whole world, because the good is absolute and infinite; and therefore it cannot be satisfied in any participation of a creature: because whatever is finite does not satisfy a finite appetite <note>The text likely means "does not satisfy even a finite appetite perfectly"</note>, except through the ultimate end, which is infinite. To this I say, that universal happiness consists in the final conversion of all things into God, who is the ultimate end. What then is happiness? I say that it is the delight which follows the ultimate act of the intellect: because just as natural delight follows the act of a natural power, so happiness, which is the supreme delight, follows the act of the highest intellect: for since the knowledge of the intellect is the highest operation of nature, the supreme delight follows it. And it seems that delight is happiness: since as it is said in the first book of the *Ethics*, happiness is the one most perfect thing: and delight is of this kind; whence it follows that happiness is delight. But on the contrary: happiness is in a single act, while delight is a certain passion <note>a "passion" in the scholastic sense is something acted upon the soul, rather than an action of the soul</note>; therefore happiness is not delight.

<margin>Happiness does not consist in a created good</margin>
It is asked in the third place: whether the happiness of man consists in any created good. And it seems so: because whatever finally satisfies the appetite is happiness: but the soul is satisfied in a created good; therefore, etc. But on the contrary: the soul is a certain spiritual thing and desires the highest good; but nothing created is the highest good; therefore happiness can consist in nothing created. To this it is said: that happiness consists in God alone, as in the ultimate end: for God is the object of happiness, which is finally reached through the intellect and the will of man: whence it is said: happiness is the vision of God, and the enjoyment of Him. For in God alone is the ultimate rest: and this is evident through Augustine, who says:
> You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. <note>original: "Fecisti nos domine ad te, et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te"; from the *Confessions*</note>
From these things it appears that happiness does not consist in a created good: because every created thing is finite; but the soul desires the infinite; therefore it can be stilled in nothing created: for the finite cannot be satisfied by the infinite <note>The author likely means the finite soul cannot be satisfied by finite things because it craves the infinite</note>; but the infinite is desired by the soul; therefore it is God alone who satisfies it, and in whom it is perfectly stilled: and this is the happiness of man considered in itself.

<summary>This page explores the Scholastic definition of happiness as the ultimate fulfillment of the human intellect and will, concluding that while partial happiness exists on earth, true satisfaction is only found in the infinite nature of God.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on Divine Love as the source of life, this page transitions into a philosophical commentary on the *Asclepius*, a famous Latin dialogue attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. It explores how the unity of God manifests in the beauty and structure of the physical world.</meta>

From the good of the world to this world? Of men—or is it better said of the other world? Being established in a single union, a single mastery, it contributes to the knowledge of God <note>original: "cognitionem dei"</note> by those things which are done in turn concerning the world, just as they speak according to God. And now, in a fragmentary way, it is called the creation of God and this soul <term>beyond the world</term> <note>original: "ultra mundum"; likely referring to the World Soul or a transcendent spiritual reality</note> at the exterior of this world. Just as through the brief substance of individual bodies and a healthy procession to all things, this world is spoken of universally. Insofar as the world provides the body of the world, it is called God; through what follows from these things, the world is a body by compaction. And just as the world is beautiful, it gives birth to the world; humanity is still the soul of the perfect human world, proceeding from the One. Then, the cause of this world is not alone in those things which it has in itself; the universe, which belongs to this world, through many days and through healthy public discourse, has been reached. It is obvious that what has been obtained is that the world should be—that is, in which all things are—and that the unique product should not be one in itself, but prepared by impressions. It says the world in which unity exists; from here, if it has not passed away, just as the world is called God through itself alone, so that in the conjunction of divine reason <note>original: "divine rationis"</note>, as for the rest, it finds it ungrateful to be through itself.

Then indeed, all things move through the world from the body of the world to divine men; and toward these things, it holds itself by chance to the world, having from itself all the antiquity of the divine world. # On Justice, Truth, and Natural Law

Custom especially, and in a case of vague reasoning, is not contrary to common law: because by natural law, to which this rule looks, the law is to belong to each person: it is the nature of things, and let justice prevail: it ought to be equal. <meta>This page continues the manuscript's theological exploration of the relationship between the Creator and the created world. While the previous fragment touched on the limitations of human power, this section dives into a sophisticated debate regarding the "World Soul" and how God can be "all in all" without being physically part of the universe.</meta>

But God will be all in all <note>original: "Deus vero erit omnia in omnibus." A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:28, a central text for medieval discussions on the final state of the universe.</note> since this world which is called the **Greater World** <note>The "Greater World" or *macrocosm* refers to the entire universe, as opposed to the "Lesser World" or *microcosm*, which refers to the individual human being.</note> is greater. However, it is not so in the **Lesser World** which is called man. What then is the meaning of that which is said by the apostle, that "God will be all in all"? For in each of his most holy servants, God will be all through all things. God himself will be the very being of that which is blessed for them. In all his saints, there will be wisdom and contemplation, which they say they enjoy for the sake of their own world. And then he will be everything to man just as he is in himself. For just as it is said by those same people that "all things are God," in God truly—through a certain ineffable condition of composition and dissolution—nothing is foreign. Hence it is also said by those same people, as they themselves assert, that the world is a certain kind of "god," as is evident in the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The *Timaeus* is a famous dialogue by the Greek philosopher Plato which describes the creation of the universe by a divine craftsman.</note>. From these people also comes the idea that the very order and ordained nobility preserved in this world is said to be in God himself through his essence. In this order, therefore, and this perfect ordination, God will be all in all and is to be in them just as he is in himself. In the world which is called "greater," however, he is not as he is in himself; just as the human soul is not in man according to its substance, but according to a certain participation of light and an image of light. It is participated in as light is in the air or as power is in things. The soul, truly, is in the world like fire in iron, or as the sun is in the world, and is said to be all in all. Because of this, Christ is not said to be "God" in the sense that he is the **World Soul** <note>original: "anima mundi." This was a controversial concept suggesting the universe has its own living soul, often associated with pantheism.</note>, as certain heretics have thought, but because in him all things were created. Whence it is said, "in him all things were created," and "he is before all things, and in him all things hold together" <note>A reference to Colossians 1:16-17.</note>. For in him, as in one who is a certain unity, is the universality of the whole world. For in this are certain powers where there is memory, and hope, and reason; where there is also will; where there is also wisdom, and restraint, and justice, and fortitude.

<column-break/>

This was not done solely through the man Christ, but through him all things exist; that is, the world was made through him insofar as he is the highest principle. Whence in the <term>Book of Causes</term> <note>The *Liber de Causis* (Book of Causes) was an influential medieval philosophical text, mistakenly attributed to Aristotle, which blended Neoplatonic thought with monotheism.</note> it is said that everything that exists is either God or a separation from one another; there is no separation except in those things which are not one through themselves, but through another. For everything that is one through itself is one in and through itself. In God, however, all things are through himself and are one with him through his essence. Whence in the <term>Book of Causes</term> it is said that God is **Pure and First Unity** <note>original: "unitas pura et prima." This describes God as a simple, indivisible source from which all complexity flows.</note>. And whatever is above unity itself is spoken of through it, and through it was made whatever was made. Whence in the <term>Book of Causes</term> it is said that everything that exists through itself is before everything that does not exist through itself. According to this manner, it is said by them that God will be all in all, but it is not true. Because Christ is not one with all things through his essence, except as a cause. Now, a cause is not in the thing it caused through its essence, but through a certain power; for it is not in this manner that Christ will be made "in all." For Christ is whatever God is. Certain heretics have thought that the soul of Christ is the World Soul, which is erroneous. For he is not in the world through his substance, but through his power, like light in the air, or like the sun in the world. Whence it is said the First has a certain unity, and has unity in itself for all things, in itself and through itself. Whence it is said in the <term>Book of Causes</term>: "Everything that is made is made through the First, and the first thing made was made through the First Being." But this is not proper to God. Whence also Christ is said to be all things and the one world to be God, just as Peter is [not] through essence in all things. For just as the soul is not the same as the body, nor is Christ the same as the world, even though Christ is united to the Godhead as the soul is united to the body. For as the soul is to the members of the world, so is Christ to himself in the good, beautiful, decent, and perfect members of the whole world. Whence also Christ is in each most holy person infused with grace, just as the soul is in each of the members; just as the soul is in the eyes, in which there is sight, so Christ is in his members, and in those same members Christ has merit. And in the same way, blessedness will be in all and in each one through itself. Just as the whole soul is in every part of the body and as it is whole in each individual part, so Christ will then be whole in all, and then God will be all in all. To which <unclear>manner</unclear>

<column-break/>

Lest we assign a specific place to this Christian doctrine, they say specifically that only the world which is called the "greater world" is God. For just as there are members in a man, so in the world they say the world serves God, and is ruled and governed by him. And in it are certain powers of the soul which rule it and are ruled by it. So too, what is in the world are certain powers that rule it and are ruled by him, just as it is in man. Whence it is said that through this order, God is the whole world just as he is the man. This is true: for just as the **World Soul** <note>original: "anima mundi."</note> made all things through its power and is in all things like light in the air, so a certain "god" is said to be the whole world. To which Christ is said to be the soul and the world the whole world.
Hence the heretics say that just as the "lesser world" is properly called "man," so the "greater world" is called "god." And some say that just as the soul is in man, so God is in the world, ruling every substance by his power. And again they say, just as they call man the "lesser world," so they call the world the "greater world." For they say the World Soul is God through essence and ruling the world through power. And this is true in the way it is properly said that the whole man is God in Christ; so they say the world is God. But this is false, because as it is said through this opinion, just as the wise men of the Greeks say—as <term>Plato</term> says—that God is the **World Soul**, and this is false. Because the world is the body of Christ, and Christ is its soul, as the heretics say. But then it is true how God will be all in all, as we said a little while ago: like light is in the air, and like the power of the soul in the body, and like Christ in his saints through grace. For this will then be in its fullness. For in this manner, God is the World Soul according to what the heretics <unclear>claim</unclear>.

<column-break/>

...ruling in himself. In this manner of ruling, God is not said to be all things in his essence, but through this: that all things are led back to him and are from him as if from a cause. Whence it is said "all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made." For that life which is in him is the light of men, just as it is in a vine, like a branch is in the root. Whence it is said, just as a branch is in the root, so is Christ in his saints through grace. And thus it is clear that this is true; Christ says: "I am the vine and you are the branches" <note>John 15:5.</note>. For just as life is in the vine, so it is in the branch, and so in the saints through the influence of grace, through the power by which he rules the whole world. Because just as man is called a world through a certain likeness of the whole world—for in the world of man there are certain members that are under God... <note>The text here is slightly repetitive: "sub deo deo invite."</note> like a holy servitude. And just as in man there are other members that are under the soul's governance, so in the world there are others that are under God's governance, such as the angels, and archangels, and the members of Christ, which is the whole Church. For hence it is said that the world is God, just as the man Christ is properly God through the essence of personal unity. For just as Christ is God, so the world—the greater world—is said to be God. For just as in man we properly speak of soul and body, so in the greater world there is God and the world. So that the world is properly called "the body of God." For just as the body of a man is properly ruled by the soul, so the whole world is ruled by God himself, just as he is the soul and the world is said to be his body. However, this is false and is not true, because then God would be, by his essence, some part of the world, just as the soul is a part of man. This is erroneous and heretical. For God is above everything that exists and outside every world through his essence. Because just as he is the beginning and the end of all things, so also all things were made through him and are ruled through him. As it is said in the <term>Book of Causes</term>: "Everything that is made is made through the First," and it is not as if a part of him was made through him, like a branch from a vine. Christ, however, is the First in whom all things are, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him.

<summary>This page explores the medieval cosmological concepts of the macrocosm and microcosm, specifically debating whether God can be considered the "World Soul." The author concludes that while God rules the world like a soul rules a body, he remains essentially distinct and superior to his creation.</summary>
<keywords>macrocosm, microcosm, World Soul, Timaeus, Book of Causes, Christology, panentheism, grace, vine and branches, Plato, divine essence</keywords>

<meta>The previous page established a framework of theological concepts such as faith, grace, and the Church. This page moves into a deeper exploration of these themes through the specific lens of the Camaldolese monastic tradition, focusing on the mystical union of the soul with God through the Holy Spirit and the virtue of "caritas" (divine love).</meta>

# Page 19

Through the state of perfection of the Camaldolese <note>original: "Camaldulensium"; a branch of the Benedictine order emphasizing solitary life</note> they profess that each person, living under a single voice, submits himself to the Rule <note>The Rule of St. Benedict or the specific Constitutions of the Camaldolese</note> under a single voice, and does nothing of himself unless under the direction of the single leading voice, through which the Holy Spirit directs and leads to the expiating and cleansing of the path of the hearts of men, in which He himself wishes to sit and dwell. It is through this mode of charity <note>original: "caritatis modum"; "caritas" refers to the highest form of Christian love or grace</note>, through which one goes to God, that all things held are perfected. This continues until He leads each one into the One <note>original: "in unum"; referring to the divine unity</note>, toward which they strive, into the One toward which they come through charity; so that for each one, in the One whom they love, all things are to be referred to the One through Him, to be loved and loved again. And just as the end is, so also the middle and the entire way consists through this union of charity; through this, it tends toward this. Hence, that which is not in unity can in no way consist in that perfection, because it must tend toward the highest form of truth and unity itself. For the divine Spirit is universally in all things, and is whole in each thing; yet He is not in each thing in the same way, but diversely according to the degree of each one's union and perfection. For He is in charity and through charity in unanimity, concord, and unity: He is in those who are one, and who tend toward the One. In these, He alone wishes to live, and He alone wishes to work, just as He also wishes their heart to be one, and their soul to be one. This is charity, which makes one out of many.

<column-break/>

The creature would not exist as a self-subsisting thing if it were not through participation in the divine being within itself; so too the divine will would not be in it, if not through the divine will within it, through which and toward which all things exist. This divine will is the Holy Spirit himself, who shares His will with each one, and through Himself recalls all things to the same self—both in will and in nature—so that He himself and He alone may be in all things. This happens unless individuals have submitted themselves by their will into unity and into that which He himself wills: and through these things and in this, the truth appears to all. In this, all perfection consists: that one might come to unity into this charity, and through it. And this is the highest and only will of God in the creature: that it be united to Himself through the will, just as it is through nature. And so that truth may be true in all things—that is, that it may come to unity through charity by the truth. For the just man is truth according to his measure: and justice is in unity, and in that which He himself is. Whence He also wishes us to be one, just as He is one: and that we are one in Him. And in this is our perfection, and highest happiness, and blessedness: that He may be in us, and we in Him, just as He wills: and that the will of all may be the same, and the heart of all one, and the soul one. And the Holy Spirit wishes to unite us in Himself, so that there may be one body and one spirit. And in this the charity of God is perfected, and lives, and reigns, so that we may be one in it: and through this we may come with the whole intention of the mind to Him, who is unity itself, and remain perpetually in Him, as in unity itself. This is the highest unity of perfection, and this is what we must strive toward.

---

# Page 20

Why does He want us? Why does He want us at all? Because He is charity alone, and the most loving lover of the good <note>original: "amantissimus amator boni"</note>: but not only for Himself, but also for us and all things which He wills for Himself, and He wishes to be loved. He wishes us to be loved by all those whom He wills and loves: and He does not wish that anything be taken away from this charity of His by anyone. And He wishes this charity of His toward us to be and to appear manifest to each of us: He wishes us to feel that He loves us: and He wishes to be loved by us, and He does not wish this charity of His to be empty in us, but operating and industrious. And this is what He says: 
> *and he who loves me will be loved by my Father: and I will love him, and manifest myself to him.* <note>John 14:21</note> 
Because He wishes to be manifest to us through love, and He himself wishes to be the only author of this our charity toward Him, and the one who works and perfects it in us. And since He himself is our whole good, and our only good: therefore He wishes to be loved uniquely by us, and He wishes nothing to be loved in us except Himself, unless for His sake, and in Him. And in this our charity is perfected: He also wishes this charity of His toward us to be one and indivisible, and just as it is in Him, so He wishes it to be in us: and He wishes this our charity toward Him to be that by which He loves Himself in Himself: and He wishes this charity to be in us, which is the Holy Spirit. And in this it is clear how He is in us, and we in Him: and how He loved us, who gave Himself to us, so that we might love Him in Him, just as He loves Himself in Himself: and so that the same charity which is in Him may be in us.

<column-break/>

The spirit breathes where it wills <note>A reference to John 3:8</note>, and let good be done as something has come to be done: Because the spirit is both the cause, and the beginning, and the power, and the perfection of all things: and without the spirit nothing exists: and all perfection consists in it: and whatever is in it, is the same spirit according to the measure of each one's union and perfection. And just as He is in the highest degree in Himself, so also in individual degrees He is perfect and whole: and according to this measure of each one's charity is the Holy Spirit. And therefore it is said, the spirit is given to each for their benefit, just as He wills: and in this He shares His whole self and to each according to their measure, and acts in individuals: so that all things may be referred to Him, as to the one and only end of all. And from this it appears how charity is the principle and cause and perfection of all things: and how the Holy Spirit is charity itself: and that each one has the spirit according to their charity, and charity according to their spirit. And He wishes this highest charity and this unitive charity toward God to be perfected in Him. And this is His highest will toward us: and from this is His happiness in us, and ours in Him. Because just as a lover wishes to be loved by the one whom he loves: so God wishes to be loved by us, so that in this there may be the highest unity of the lover and the beloved. And in this may be the perfect perfection of all creatures. This is that charity surpassing all knowledge <note>original: "caritas illa supereminens omni scientiae"; likely a reference to Ephesians 3:19</note>, which he who possesses, has come to fullness.

# On the Grace of Divine Adoption and the Sonship of Christ

Without the grace of God, one is neither a son nor one with Him. There is an abundance of grace and a glorying in works that are not superfluous or vain. Let one not consider it merely a personal worth, but rather that He chose His own Son to adopt from every race those men who would draw near. So now, that which belongs to the divine lovers is given also to the sons—creatures who are superior through the **restoration of divinity** <note>original: "reductionem divinitatis"; likely referring to the Neoplatonic or mystical idea of the soul returning to its divine source</note>. 

And let you not suffer the **unbegotten son** <note>original: "filius ingenitus"; a paradoxical term, as "Unbegotten" usually refers to the Father, while the Son is "Begotten." He has reminded and moved the unbegotten nature so that He alone might be conceived as born freely—in whom this is most fully revealed to the sons. In Him, a position is always established and confirmed through veneration. For how great is this faith, surpassing all else, the faith of **adoption**? 

In this adoption, gratitude can never be concluded or confined merely to the revealed sun, unless the benefit itself is revealed as being born from so many degrees through which God willed to confer upon His own—us, the adopted sons. This gift seems to have been <unclear>given</unclear> to us. And thus, has He not made Himself the heir, and us the **co-heirs of Christ**? It is for this reason, surely, that the Spirit is signed and sealed, lest it be unknown. The gift rules in this way so that one might study safely. To this end, one should especially consider after what a marvelous gratitude of **re-creation** <note>original: "recreationis"; refers to the spiritual rebirth or second creation of man through grace</note> and charity He will give to us to become sons through the Spirit.

# The Deeds and Virtues of the Prince

A vigorous battle was fought. Having been struck by two missiles <note>The Latin 'missilibus' refers to thrown weapons like javelins or arrows.</note>, one of which had impacted his chest and the other his face, he dragged out his life in great danger. Little hope would have remained for either wound had he not been snatched from imminent death and led away by the swift work of the physicians. This victory would have been small, had they not soon distracted the entire army into flight by a rapid approach to the camp. For the enemy who were in the city, having gained victory, placed all their hope in the confidence of a victorious hand, as if they were already conquerors. On the next day, when they had approached the city with the army, the enemy received the entire line of march with a city triumph.

Meanwhile, while the enemy fortified themselves with new reinforcements and brought in an abundant supply for every use, especially of grain, our men meanwhile heard of the deceit of the barbarians and their untrustworthy faith. When frequent messengers had been received, [stating] that they should depart from the cities in which all the garrisons of the armies had been; when those stationed for that work perceived that they must do nothing except what pertained to conquering and sustaining the enemy and escaping from these affairs in this manner: putting aside all fear, they came to blows; and on that day, they overcame those who were in the front rank with their retinue.

Moreover, in another part, the neighboring enemies, seeing that they were joined and would be just as many, began to strike at the war. For even if they were surpassed by the frequency of the enemy and the army by day, it nevertheless used to happen that they excelled the courage of any superiors. For the enemy's line had something disordered about it, and they soon terrified their courage—which did happen, and events proved it by the outcome. Finally, the battle having already begun, when the retinue of the Gauls were preparing themselves for surrender, and the state of the Belgians: for the Gauls [sought] nothing except for liberty, as I said above, and that all things which they reported should be restored. These things were also added: that for the love of the neighborhood they desired peace for them. For then, indeed, the enemy desired to have nothing but peace and quiet among themselves and to obey our men, who preferred to be bound rather than be drawn into the hands of the enemy. Therefore, the enemy rejected these efforts, by which the enemies, having been received, wished to add them into slavery themselves. Meanwhile, as the Gallic leaders rejoiced, the prefect of the enemy joined the others, who, as allies especially received into faith, [brought] war to him who then held this entire province. And these things were done meanwhile in the parts of Gaul and in their jurisdiction.

<column-break/>

...he may arrange. He bestowed upon the supreme commander a distinguished faculty for speaking in all matters; finally, the same supreme commander, who with the greatest virtue and benevolence desires peace: who shall be absent from victory? By whose wisdom, therefore, has friendship <term>amicitia: in a political context, this often refers to a formal alliance or diplomatic bond</term> been conciliated? In which [matters] he has come to this place: since if I wished to say a few things, in all the greatest and most frequent matters, both virtue and wisdom would shine forth, from which also in the greatest affairs, and those which are properly referred to as one? Do other things from these matters also look toward the memory of posterity? Since these things must be done not in oblivion but at all times. And certainly all these things pertain to the glory of the prince, if not only matters pertaining to the conduct of war, but those which pertained to the matter of peace: for both contribute equally to this end. Indeed, kings have done this thing, who after they obtained empire, strove for all these things. Since they have come to this point, will not those things which you do, from among the things that are seen, certainly look toward this end? Moreover, as to the things which leaders might have sometimes called peace of this kind, the matter pertains to peace, and to that thing which seems to be of peace? For nothing pertains more to glory than to preserve peace: for that is what is most accustomed to be done by the diligence of kings and Princes in the republic: so that they might give a reward through themselves to those who had done well, especially when it was given to the justice of things. To this prince, who is so outstanding in many virtues that he ought rightly to be loved, and that looks toward the effort of many men in both directions: for from this, those things which seem to pertain to that love will shine forth hereafter. Moreover, a glorious King and he who does these things perform justice, and through that justice they are loved for that reason. For that praise of justice, from which even those who love may shine forth? And to this end we arrange this matter of ours, and so that we may gird ourselves for this matter with our worthy virtues. But indeed, from these well-done things, our own modesty also seems to come to us. For we do not only attain the first things, but also those which will pertain to our matter, if anyone should look back at these things.

<column-break/>

...was there such great, such great humility in the Prince also? So that if you knew him thoroughly, you would see him excel well in all things, and that he joined himself even to the received leisure of peace: and to that justice of which we spoke. But not even virtue publicly, because they protected nothing that was not justice, so that he might rule himself instead, on account of you, Caesar, in this experience, since there was the grace of justice, in which such great indulgence arrived? If fame be not joined to virtue: but that one thing seems to arrive in this man—that they do not conduct any business except by justice: would not all things seem to obey you in this matter? And certainly they seemed then to be the greatest things. And that certainly is most closely joined to justice: for as it is a matter of justice to have [things] from friendship: so especially from here whoever wishes to be joined to friendship. For a matter of law of this kind pertains to friendship. Whence also wisdom seems to be present. For whatever is of justice, in whomsoever this matter is: that is, as one who wishes to act rightly, both in what regards God and what regards men. But if it cannot happen that this justice be reached in one man. By which things of affairs they also seemed to be. But he commanded us to join that certainly of justice also especially to friendship: because it is joined to both in this matter, he would rightly arrive at this justice: for wisdom also pertains to this king. Nor does justice seem in any way to be disjoined from friendship: since they are the princes by whom they protect justice. Truly that matter of justice properly looks toward friendship, since all who seem to be hoping for justice from him love the king. It behooves princes also to apply all faithfulness to justice. Since indeed the end appears to be <term>truth</term> <note>original: "ueritas"; the ultimate objective and goal of the intellectual process.</note> and
 the thing in its very self is in the end where the truth is,

but the truth of reasoning itself.

the truth of the soul, and reasoning in it.
Truth is the <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; the realization or operation of a potentiality.</note> of the soul and the reasoning,
since the end of the soul is the virtue of the soul, the truth;
since reasoning is in the soul, and thus
it is in itself, it is called the truth and the act.
For truth is the act and the power of reasoning;
the soul is called in itself the truth and the act,
and thus it is seen to be the end, and the end through itself.
The thing is said to be in itself as if in a vessel;
but it reasons the reasoning, and thus
truth is the reasoning and the soul is the truth.
For truth and the soul are said to reason,
which truth is the soul itself, and in itself
is the end of the soul and the virtue of the soul; and
it is said to reason the end of the soul, and this is
through itself and properly the end of the soul; and in itself
it is properly called the power of reasoning, the truth.
Indeed, this reasoning of the soul is the truth,
and reasoning is the end of the soul, and it
is the power of reasoning, and for that very reasoning
the truth of the soul's reasoning is in the soul.
This reasoning, however, is the reasoning, and thus
in itself it is the act of the soul and the virtue.
The truth of the soul is said to be the act in the soul.
For reasoning is the act of truth in the <unclear>thing</unclear>;
the end of the soul is said to reason, truth is [the end],
and truth is the virtue of the soul's reasoning;
for the reasoner reasons, and the soul is the truth.
Truth and virtue are said to reason, and
truth is said to be the end of reasoning, and thus—

<column-break/>

this is seen to speak of those things which are,
and thus it appears for what [reasons] they are in
the soul, which are the soul, the truth of reasoning;
and thus the virtue of reasoning is said to be in itself.
The soul, truly, is the truth and virtue of reasoning.
Here it is said to be the virtue which, since it is
in the soul, is the truth of the soul, which since it is
it is seen to become the virtue of the soul and the truth;
it is seen to become the virtue of reasoning and
the virtue of the soul, the act of the soul. It is the end so that
the virtue which is called truth is said through itself
to be the virtue of the soul, and thus it reasons, and
the soul is the truth of the reasoning and the very
end, which soul is the virtue of the reasoning;
which virtue, the truth of the soul, is said to reason.
But the truth of the soul in virtue, the truth,
is seen to be the truth of the reasoning,
and thus truth is the virtue of the soul; the soul
with truth, the truth of the soul, the truth of reasoning,
is the act of reasoning of the soul. For
truth is said to be by the act of reasoning;
it is the act of the reasoning of the soul, the truth,
and thus the virtue of reasoning is said to be in itself.
The truth in the soul is the virtue of reasoning,
and thus the act of reasoning.
The soul is the virtue of the soul, and the soul is the truth
which is called in the soul the end of the soul.
Reasoning is finished, and thus to reason;
and just as truth is said to reason in the soul,
and the end of reasoning is the virtue of the soul,
the end of the soul and <term>that which is placed</term> <note>original: "locatus"; referring to the object contained within a "place."</note>. Thus the truth
of the soul is in the soul just as the thing placed;
truth is in the soul just as reasoning.
Since the truth of the soul in the soul is the virtue,
the end of the soul is finished as truth, and the <term>place</term> <note>original: "locus"; the intellectual "space" or container where a faculty resides.</note>
is the place, and thus the place in the soul
is the truth of the reasoning of the soul, and
this is the truth of the soul's virtue and the place;
and the soul itself is the truth of the reasoning.
So also truth is called the place of the soul,
and the truth of reasoning, of reasoning.
The truth is the end of the soul, and the truth itself
is the very thing placed, the truth of the reasoning;
the thing placed of the soul and the end of the reasoning,
in which the truth is the soul, the reasoning.
Since the soul is the end of the reasoning
and the place of the reasoning, the truth of the soul;
and the end of the reasoning is the truth of the soul.
The soul is the virtue, the truth of the soul;
in the soul is the truth of the reasoning.
Reasoning is finished in the soul, and thus
the truth is the virtue of the soul and the act;
and in the soul is the act of reasoning.
For the truth, the virtue of the soul in the soul,
is finished [as] the truth of the soul, of the reasoning of the soul;
it is in its very self the virtue of reasoning.
The truth of the soul, the act of the soul, is to reason,
and the place of reasoning is the truth of the soul.

<summary>This page presents a complex scholastic argument defining the soul as the "place" of reasoning and "Truth" as the ultimate "end" or goal of that reasoning. Using the metaphor of a vessel, the author explores how intellectual faculties exist within the soul as "placed" objects within a container.</summary>

However, the consideration of this **end** <note>Original: "finis." <meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into natural philosophy, moving from the physical properties of elements like water to the cosmological governance of the "inferior" (earthly) world by "superior" bodies (planets and zodiac signs). It bridges Aristotelian physics with medieval astrology, focusing on how celestial "virtue" influences the "complexion" or constitutional balance of elemental bodies.</meta>

<summary>This page explores the medieval cosmological theory that the physical "complexion" (balance of qualities) of earthly bodies is governed by the movements of the sun, moon, and zodiac signs. It synthesizes Aristotelian physics with planetary influence, explaining how the four elements are ordered by celestial "virtues."</summary>
<keywords>celestial virtue, complexion, four elements, planetary influence, governance, sublunary world, Chalcidius, spirit, elemented body</keywords>

<summary>This page explores the physical properties and movement of water, arguing that its flow and distribution are determined by the "rarity" or density of its location. It concludes that water naturally tends toward a spheroid or spherical shape in relation to the earth's circumference.</summary>
<keywords>hydrostatics, rarity, density, spheroid, circumference, Aristotelian physics, medieval cosmology, fluid dynamics</keywords>

...they flow with floods through <unclear>which</unclear> they flow. 
The **second conclusion** is that in every sea there is **ebb and flow** <note>original: "fluxus et refluxus"</note>, but in some it is more and in others less. This is evident because in the **ocean** the greatest ebb and flow is seen, but in the **Mediterranean** sea it is very small or nonexistent; and this is because of its narrowness and because it is enclosed between lands, nor does it have a free exit, as is evident from various places.
Furthermore, note that at the [proper] time, the water is seen to rise more toward the shore and then it is "flow," and afterward to descend and then it is "ebb." And so it is seen to happen twice in a **natural day**, that is, in twenty-four hours; and this is because of the motion of the **moon** around the horizon, according to whether it is above or below the horizon. 
And thus it appears that the moon is the mistress of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids thought to control health; here, the author applies the concept to the earth's waters.</note> and the motions of the sea, as **astrologers** and also natural philosophers testify, such as **Aristotle** in his book ***Meteorology*** <note>original: "metheororum"</note> and other places in which he speaks of the nature of waters and the influences of the heavens upon the <term>elements</term> <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> and also upon lower bodies. 
Although some deny this, yet the truth is that the heaven influences these lower realms in various ways, as is seen in the changes of seasons and the air and of other natural things which we see every day in this world.

<column-break/>

[to] do, and then when it has reached the shore, the water itself recedes. This is because of the violence of the motion and also because the moon is already receding from that place, and then the "ebb" occurs and the water is seen to recede from the land. 
And so the moon causes the ebb and flow twice a day, and this is what seems most marvelous in nature. For this reason, many philosophers wanted to know the cause of this thing, and some said that this is because of the **winds** which are generated in the bowels of the earth under the sea, which lift the water, and afterward when they exit, the water descends and the ebb occurs. 
But this does not seem reasonable, because winds do not move as regularly as we see this ebb and flow occur. Therefore, it is better to say that the moon is the cause, because she herself moves regularly, and therefore she causes this motion regularly. 
And so it is evident that the moon has the greatest power <note>original: "virtutem"</note> over waters; and this is also seen in other moist bodies, such as in the human brain, which is also seen to increase or decrease according to the motion of the moon. This is testified by the **physicians**, who said that illnesses which arise from the humors follow the motion of the moon. And so the moon appears to be the cause of all humors and changes of waters; and let this suffice concerning the ebb and flow of the sea for now.

In the same way, one would hold that divine things are not indeed <term>said</term> <note>original: "dicitur"</note> to be ordered according to their location, but rather the opposite. Consequently, as others who wish to prove it in this way, the world—since by its <term>nature</term> <note>original: "ratione," meaning the logical structure or essence</note> it exists <term>essentially</term> <note>original: "secundum per se," meaning in its own right or by its very nature</note>—is the same <term>essentially</term> within the world. From this, it is not reduced unless it exists <term>essentially</term> in the world and is a <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantia," the underlying reality of a thing</note>. It is just as if among the divine beings of the world there is a "good," not <term>essentially</term>, but because of the goodness of the world. Just as they are not said to be divine toward one another by the nature of the world, but rather because of the divine qualities within the world, so he says the world is divine not <term>essentially</term>, but because of the divinity of the world. In the same way, the world would have one world against another according to a division that is not <term>essential</term>, but because of the opposites within the world. Then, however, because of the opposite <term>distinctions</term> <note>original: "differentias," the specific qualities that set one thing apart from another</note> in the world, the world is said to be divine because by its nature it exists <term>according to itself</term>. Then it would not be a <term>substance</term> as it is in the world, since the <term>substance</term> that is in the world is, by its nature, <term>essentially</term> distinct. In this manner, it is <term>essentially</term> a distinction of the world by the nature of the world, since they are <term>essentially</term> distinctions of the world within the world. <summary>This page contains a highly repetitive scholastic investigation into the relationship between the nutritive faculty of the soul and the faculty of reason. It concludes that while biological processes like nutrition are distinct from rational thought, they possess an inherent logical order (ratio) that allows them to be described as "reasoning" in their own mode.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical inquiry from the previous folio, moving from the specific role of grace and the will (citing Aquinas) into a broader Aristotelian framework. It focuses on the relationship between matter and form, specifically how matter "desires" form to achieve "actuality." The text references Averroes's "De Substantia Orbis" to explore whether physical bodies are derived from the substance of matter itself.</meta>

->From the communion of the first principles of things, the spirit.<-

Whether small bodies flow from matter, or are of the substance of matter itself, is a matter of doubt for Aristotle and many others generally. It is stated by Averroes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western scholasticism.</note> in his *Treatise on the Substance of the Orb*, that from these "flowings," it is of the substance of matter until it becomes an "actual being" <note>original: "ens in actu"; a thing that truly exists in reality rather than just potentially.</note>, that is, it is made according to the manner of a being in a specific degree. And it is said that those "flowings" have within themselves certain natural virtues directed toward some act; by reason of what is in them, it is said that substance is predicated of matter according to its state as an actual substance. Therefore, that which is an actual being does not come from substance in "potency" <note>original: "in potentia"; the capacity to become something else.</note>; rather, it is said that a being exists toward something according to the primary account of matter and not according to act. Furthermore, Aristotle says that a thing is not called a "being" except according to the act of possessing substance and form. Whence it follows from these points that an actual being is of the substance insofar as it is made an actual being through its form. Otherwise, it is said by others that an actual being is that which is composed of matter and form, and it is defined insofar as a being is that which exists in act. But this does not seem to be true, because form is not substance except by the fact that it is a part of substance. Others say instead that the actual being is both substance and form insofar as it is an actual being. Therefore, it is said that an actual being is that which is composed of matter and form, and it is defined insofar as a being is that which exists in act.

<column-break/>

<margin>the expulsion, however</margin>
The expulsion, however, causes a reversal for the generation <note>The process of coming into existence or "birth" of a thing.</note> itself. And it is said on the same leaf that just as motion appears to the rest of the things having been acted upon—in the manner that appears in "generation and corruption" <note>original: "generatione et corruptione"; the Aristotelian cycle of birth and decay.</note> and in speaking of nature—it occurs according to a certain mode and not according to a universal mode. Therefore, it is said that "being" is spoken of in many ways, as is clear in the first book of this work, and according to this mode we see that in each of these things there is a certain virtue of "natural appetite" <note>original: "naturalis appetitus"; not a conscious desire, but an inherent tendency of matter to seek its completion in form.</note>. Otherwise, it is said of matter insofar as it is matter desiring form. And it is said that matter, according to itself, is "substance in potency" <note>potential substance</note>, and it is said that matter desires form just as the "ugly" <note>or "base"</note> desires the "good." But this does not seem to be true, because matter according to itself is nothing except in potency. Therefore, it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires to be "in act." And it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires its own perfection. And therefore, it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires its own being.

<column-break/>

Whence first are the <term>sylo. baratri</term> <note>Likely a corruption or abbreviation for "syllogisms of the abyss" or "hyle" (matter). The OCR is unclear here.</note> <unclear>through</unclear> which, when those are moved... for here there are certain acts of heat and dryness in the matter... and it is said that matter and form are the principles of natural things... matter, however, according to itself is substance in potency, and form is substance in act... and it is said that from matter and form one thing is made according to act... and therefore it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires its own perfection... and it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires its own being... and this is evident in the generation and corruption of natural things... and it is said that matter according to itself is not an actual being... but is a being in potency only... and therefore it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires to be in act... and it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires its own perfection...

<column-break/>

And this is evident in honey, but much of philosophy says that nature exists only insofar as it is form, and it is said insofar as a being is that which is an actual being. But matter desires form just as matter desires its own being. And therefore, it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires its own perfection. And it is said that matter desires form just as matter desires to be in act. And this is evident in the generation and corruption of natural things. <summary>This page presents a dense scholastic analysis of the soul's nature and its relation to material things, utilizing a highly repetitive dialectical structure to test the definitions of sensory perception and rational existence. The text explores how terms like "nature" and "it is said" (dicitur) apply to the generation and function of the soul in animals and humans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of the human being, shifting from the metaphysical subsistence of the soul discussed on the previous page to a physiological and humoral analysis. It explores the "Microcosm" theory, where the human body reflects the composition of the universe through the four elements and the four humors.</meta>

### Column 1 (Verso, Left)

In another sense, it is said that there are three things from which a human being is generated: namely, **blood**, **body**, and **spirit**. **Blood** is that which naturally tempers the body, as it is from blood that human generation occurs. **Spirit** is like a certain tempered heat—a focus of warmth for the interior—and by its nature, the spirit enables the powers of the soul. The **body** is that which is of the earth; it provides the human with a place to exist and remain. From these three noble things, the individual generation of man is established.

Furthermore, man must be governed by the four materials, just as the world is: **water**, **earth**, **air**, and **fire**. The spirit through which a man walks proceeds from water <note>Medieval physiology often linked the "vital spirit" to the more fluid or vaporous elements.</note>, and through the spirit, the man is guided in his inner parts. It is ruled that blood is tempered like water, and within it are the four humors, just as water exists in the earth through which man rules. Inwardly, however, there is the body, which is earth. Likewise, the spirit of man is like a certain fire, which from the nature of things possesses within itself a spirit of nature and heat, providing sight to the man.

Man also has four humors that are his own: **blood**, **melancholy** (black bile), **choler** (yellow bile), and **phlegm**. At its natural time, blood possesses the power of sight <note>original: "visum habet," perhaps meaning "appearance" or "active force" in this context</note> because it proceeds through nature. See, for instance, how blood has within itself properties that are liquid and light, and its temperament is moist.

Below this, it is ruled that within the blood are the four humors which find one another. A man is tempered through his blood. Blood is "inferior" in that it proceeds from nature and comes from the lower parts. Blood in its density is natural blood and heat. Just as in these three humors which proceed from themselves: **Fire** is that which has within itself spirit and heat; **Choler** is red and is called **Air**; **Phlegm** is **Water**; and **Melancholy** is **Earth**. 

Whence, when these four run and flow in the body of a man, then the man is healthy. But when any one of them begins to intensify and exalt itself, then the man is sick. Therefore, from these four is man himself created, and each of the humors has a certain seat in the body. <margin>Note on the seats of the humors</margin> It is said that melancholy resides in the **spleen**, choler in the **gallbladder**, blood in the **heart**, and phlegm in the **lungs**.

Whence it should be known that the nature of man is so composed. As some wish to say, the soul consists of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire. Then it must be understood that just as the elements are in the world, so they are in man. For this reason, man is called a <term>minor mundus</term> <note>original: "minor mundus" — literally "small world" or **Microcosm**. This is the ancient and medieval idea that the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>. Because he has the four elements within himself and governs them. For it is said that **earth** in man is like the **bones**; **water** is like the **blood**; **air** is like the **breath**; and **fire** is like the **heat**. And just as the world cannot exist unless there is a flower within it, so too can neither man, nor flower, nor fruit exist without these elements.

<column-break/>

### Column 2 (Verso, Right)

As it is said, blood is the thing by which a man is ruled, and man is nature. Whence in the blood there are many elements. For blood in itself holds the form of a cross where the earth is. It is linked to labor, such as choler and melancholy. Likewise, it is nature and is almost like a spirit. In this way, physicians, by examining the blood, know what is happening within a man—discerning between red choler and black choler. Thus they may know the types and natures of any person's fluids. 

It is said that if there is a certain flowing within a man, and the blood does not have the quality of a melancholic nature, nor red choler, nor those other three, the man will be healthy. Whence it is said that there are many who are by nature moist, others melancholic, and others choleric. We see that some are "red" (ruddy) and are healthy men, and this is due to the heat of the blood. When we see such a red person, it is said that he is healthy. Indeed, it is said that the life of man is in the blood, because the blood, along with the spirit, runs through the whole body via fibers and veins. 

At various times, there will be one blood in man which is a "planet" <note>This likely refers to the astrological influence on bodily fluids</note>; others say there is a "fullness of blood." It must be known that if blood is too abundant in a man, he becomes sick because of this internal fullness. Thus, when someone is sick where the body abounds in blood, it is said that he must be "relaxed" (bled) through various methods and rules. We see that each humor has its property and its seat in the body, as was said above: choler in the gallbladder, which inflames its water. The gallbladder of a man is described as being like a blast of wind. Melancholy is in the spleen; red choler is in the lungs. Red choler inflames the blood. If there is an excess in the heart, then the man is sick. 

It should be known that if there is an issue in the heart, one should not perform bloodletting <note>original: "non debet sanguinare"</note>. Physicians say that if a man is healthy, the blood should not run except in service to the body. There is a time determined by the nature of the blood; it is said that one should "relax" (bleed) at other times, such as in **Springtime**, when there is much heat. Then one should draw from the middle of the blood. If one bleeds for too long, the body remains weak. 

Blood is the body. There are many melancholic things in the body, just as there are in every man. Then the body is called weak, and as stated above, nature rules the body.

<column-break/>

### Column 3 (Recto, Left)

The <term>complexio composita</term> <note>A "composed temperament" or "complexion," referring to the specific balance of humors that makes up an individual's physical and mental character.</note> flows through many membranes. Within these members, one specific property proceeds, which is noble. That which is called blood is a tempering force; it tempers the heat. In many men, there is nothing but an internal consistency of heat. The cause is the blood, and a man cannot exist unless it is always flowing through his veins. Thus a man is always cured in turns. 

We see that many men always find a place where there is heat; these are the things that constitute a man. Thus, color is resolved and carried away, for man was made from the earth in its likeness. At all times, toward the right side and the left side: the **right** is very pure and provides strength; the **left** provides many evils. It is said that the blood is on the right side where it is tempered, and there the man is said to be healthy. On the right, a man is strong and invigorated by the blood, which is like the loveliness of the spirit. 

If the vein is tempered, the matter is restored by the spirit which the man receives. Then nature imbues that which returns and hastens the heat; where the spirit is, there is nature. Then a man is said to be strong. Conversely, it is said that in the spirit a man is weak. There are four humors toward the right side. A humor is a tempering found within, which acts as a repellant. Thus there are four from the earth: **blood**, **red choler**, **black choler**, and **melancholy**, as is evident in men. 

The body has much of the property of the earth, where the man tempers his own property. Thus, in the body, a part of the earth in the many faces of the children <note>original: "facie fili is" - possibly a corruption or reference to "sons of men"</note> cannot flow through the purity of the organs. Whence the spirit is seen in men, providing sight and better condition. 

Besides these things, the "complexion" hastens the man. It is said that if one time does not come from the earth, it would resolve where the blood proceeds. Then it comes to those parts where the spirit is. The spirit of man is that which arrives through virtue. It is very compassionate where the spirit is in the weak part of the blood. By the virtue of the spirit, man returns, just as it is the virtue of the son. It is said that where the spirit is, man rules the body just as virtue and the spirit of the temperament temper it. Through the spirit, the blood tempers itself. Thus it is clear that through the spirit, man is a carrier of many properties. This is called the complexion...

<column-break/>

### Column 4 (Recto, Right)

...and of the humor. From this property, a superfluity <note>An excess of bodily fluids</note> proceeds. It is said to be a single property. For in the property of a man’s infirmity, there is much blood. Then it flows like the sea in the rivers that flow in the parts of the body, the veins, and the head. A man must have much tempering in his part. 

If a man has "manliness" in things, it is said that in that part is the virtue of his complexion which finds the man. In many men, they are not tempered by blood as was said; then the man is "poor" (depleted) and cannot hold himself up well. Whence rule comes to many men. In those men, through the realms of the earth, where the head of the man is, he is then said to be healthy. In those places where there is much blood, it tempers itself, and the man always proceeds toward his own property. 

It is said that in this, through these three things which are in man—namely, **blood**, **spirit**, and **body**—this is the nature where men are established. Likewise, it is ruled that in the blood is the life of every man, where the man is healthy as was said above. Likewise, man is one where, in the earth, it is said he must carry himself lower. Through these things, the man resolves himself. In sickness, it is said that one has that which ought to be relaxed (bled). The blood in the heart must be tempered. 

In that part, it is said that it tempers itself. It must rule the man in temperance. For every man is a man where the blood tempers itself. And it is said where something else comes from this. Likewise, it is stated and they find that man is equally body and temperance, which is said to be from two things. 

However, the physicians respond that they must be tempered where the blood must rule the body. Whence it is clear that if he tempers himself where he is one, he is said to be tempered. This is the spirit, where it is said he tempers himself through parts of the earth. Just as it is said of many men, they temper themselves through the blood; in that part, the blood must be carried. It must be from the property of the man's body and from the property where the man is resolved.

<summary>This page outlines medieval humoral theory and the "Microcosm" (minor mundus) concept, explaining how the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) correspond to the four humors and parts of the body. It discusses the diagnostic and therapeutic role of blood, including the importance of balance (temperance) and the practice of bloodletting.</summary>
