<meta>This page continues the physiological discussion from the previous page, moving from the definition of the four humors to the mechanical and elemental "ruling" of the body. It specifically focuses on the concept of "natural heat" and how the elemental properties of fire and earth interact with the human spirit and "nourishment" (digestion). The text heavily references Aristotle, likely his *On the Generation of Animals* or *On the Soul*.</meta>

Just as the power of the heat of the primary fire is distant, yet its nature is fire and its heat is like the heat within the elements, so too there is a **natural heat** in each of these four <note>The four elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note>. Or, from that which is in the place of fire—the universal mother of plants—this itself is "natural heat," just as **Aristotle** says. And because it overcomes by that same property pertaining to the **measured and ruling spirit**, it reaches the measure of the earth. In these things, there is an honor to the property pertaining to fire; thus is its nature. Wherefore, because there is heat from fire, it possesses the property and nature of fire, and thus **natural heat** is generated in humans and proceeds in the honor of nature.

Thus is heat balanced in animals; and because it overcomes in such a way that nourishment occurs, this will be from the "dry," so that the nourishment might attract that which overcomes. Whence the nature of fire makes a man **good and stout-hearted** <note>original: "cordatum"</note>; but for a man to be so made in nature, he must then be within the heat of fire. And then he belongs to the man, and just as fire attracts more than other things toward its own consumption—as it has that property in fire—so natural heat is able to hinder consumption. And then the earth consumes the nourishment, and they belong well to the man.

But if his heat overcomes that which the nourishment produced, but in the property that overcomes where the nourishment is then to be made, thus the nourishment will pass into itself from the earth to the fire. It is measured because it is nourishment; but then, if it happens through the property of the earth, it is called nature. The earth will be the balanced heat of the man, just as the earth is measured, and just as the earth is measured through heat (as was said above). Then they will fail in power in the earth, which is like the **cold and the dry**. And in animals, that which is less in nature is [found] in the balanced animal power.

And here, if the property and heat of the man are in the earth as above, so it is said that there will be moisture within the measure of the earth. So it is said there will be moisture within the measure of the moisture of the earth; thus the man will be **dry but warm**, just as the nature has been measured. In this measure and the aforementioned power that measures, the man will be **quiet** <note>In this context, "quietus" implies a state of physical stability or lack of agitation in the humors.</note> in himself by the power of the man, in the honor of the earth. Through the property, it proceeds in nature by the power that the man will be moist; the man will be in judgment within the man. Thus, by the power of moisture, it will be that he is quiet in the man by the property of moisture and <unclear>thus</unclear>

<column-break/>

Thus it is useful to understand regarding **generation**: another thing increases and preserves the whole body through the heat of the **spirit**, properly just as fire measures the earth in the elements. For just as the heat of fire transforms the earth through its hardness, so the heat of the man measures and transforms the nourishment. Just as the earth is measured through the hardness of fire, so too the man measures his own moisture of the earth. Thus, through the honor of the property of the man—but properly so—it is said through honor, and so in the property, thus through the **lordship of power** <note>original: "principatum virtutis"</note> in the body through the spirit.

It is so because the heat of the man (as above) will rule the moisture; and through the heat which will be thus in the ruler, it has heat and moisture. Just as the proper heat transforms something, such as through nourishment which is by power in the earth, so is the heat; so that it overcomes, so that the nourishment properly overcomes the **cold and the dry**.

And so in the body of a man, the nourishment of measured power will rule; the nourishment <unclear>comes</unclear> properly and transforms the man. Thus in the property through which the nourishment in the earth, cooling the moisture, wherefore it says the man measures the heat. And so in the property in the man, and the property of the man measures in the man that he will be **balanced in moisture**. Just as in the property of the earth (as was said above), if the man overcomes thus through moisture, it will be earth. Wherefore, just as it is said that the earth [is formed] through hard heat, so the man is spoken of: that the heat of the man will rule the nourishment which overcomes the man.

As **Aristotle** says of the dry: that it ought to be transformed through the heat of the man toward nourishment through fire, so that he rules the nourishment in the body by measure. And then the body will be a measure by the property; the property of the man is thus measured to the heat, because the power of the man, by the power of the man, thus through the property proceeds from the heat. And so then the man measures the moisture and overcomes by the property. So says **Aristotle**: that the man measures the heat thus in hardness and moisture and moisture and...

<column-break/>

The body runs just as in fire, so by the power of nature's heat; so that through heat it is measured. Thus fire measures the earth as in its property, so that in the heat of the man it measures moisture. Thus in the man, so that the heat will be in measure; through the heat of the man, the earth—so in the body of the man—that the man will be **quiet in himself** properly and will rule the whole body of the man. Thus by his own power, by the power of the man, he rules the power of the man in the body.

When **water** is lacking, he is thus **cold in nature**, transforming; and then the body of the man will be such that he is quiet and properly a measure by the ruling power properly in the man. And the heat will be in the moisture, so that the man will be thus in the property of power. If the heat of the man overcomes, then the man will be in the property by the power of fire, transforming the hardness. And then the man will be thus in measure through moisture, so that power will be failing in the body of the man, thus in hardness.

And **Aristotle** says, regarding the heat of the man and properly the man, so it is said that the heat of the man thus rules the hardness and the moisture in the body of the man. Just as through the heat of fire [one rules] the hardness and measure of the earth in its property, so will be the heat of the man in the body; it measures the hardness of the earth.

Just as **Aristotle** says: that the hardness of the earth will be thus in the heat of the man, and the heat measures the hardness of the man in the body, just as in the property. So the heat of the man will be the measure in the body, so that the hardness of the earth thus cools the nourishment of the man’s power. Thus in the property of the man's measure, and so the heat of the man will be in the property. ### [On the Passions of the Soul and the Nature of Christ]

The fourth point is how the passions <note>original: "passiones". In scholastic philosophy, this refers not just to emotions, but to the state of being acted upon or "suffering" an effect from an outside force.</note> which are united are more similar to these or differ more according to species and genera; and concerning the human soul and concerning Christ. Here, we ask what might be the essence of motion and the same respective thing from which there would already be a subject that is a motive cause <note>original: "causa motiva". The principle that initiates change or movement.</note> through itself. Here, however, it is first asked whether there is passion in the soul, and secondly concerning its property which regards passion. First, it must be seen what passion is; and first, what is the expression of passion or the act of regarding it. Second, concerning its quiddity <note>original: "quidditate". A philosophical term meaning the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note> and secondarily concerning the mode of the aforementioned experiments?

In the first chapter, there is this question: whether the soul is passible <note>original: "passibilis". Capable of undergoing an action, feeling, or suffering.</note>, and it seems not: for action and passion ought not be contraries. The opposite of this seems true, and on the contrary, it is said that by chance it makes [a thing] passible both in movable things and in the first causes. In movable things, however, <unclear>through</unclear> the second, and it seems there is passion in them: because that which is passion is passion for itself, not according to the thing itself, or it seems that it is nothing else but the work or the power, as is clear from the name whose principles are the same. And such things are contraries; therefore it seems that it is by accident and according to some order, and this is passion. Second is concerning its quiddity, which is motion properly in respect to the soul: as is also clear, nothing else is done: and it is also clear through what it is and what is the moving force? But on the contrary, this is an accidental motion of the soul; nothing is a passion of the soul according to its essence nor through itself: but only for a soul having it in itself. However, in such motion there is not properly passion; the passion of the soul would not be a single thing, nevertheless as it may now be according to itself in respect to the motion of the subjective movement. And in fact, it is clear from those things which are in the soul; they seem at times to regard the body and at other times? also on the contrary, so that the soul itself at times exists through itself and is not the soul according to itself. And this is the nature of the soul, and thus it seems that things existed according to spiritual motion.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the faculties of the soul, specifically moving from the general concept of "passion" to the specific relationship between the "appetite" (the faculty of desire) and "delight" (pleasure). The text continues to use Aristotelian frameworks to explain how the human soul processes goodness and truth.</meta>

<margin>
Appetite <note>original: "appetitus". In this context, it refers to the soul's natural pull toward a perceived good, encompassing both physical desire and intellectual will.</note> is a power of the soul which holds nothing except what it wants; otherwise, it would not be an appetite. For if it held what it does not want, it would already possess it and still be an appetite, but this is impossible. Therefore, appetite is the power of the soul by which it wants whatever it wants. Whatever it wants, it appetizes [desires]. Therefore, appetite is the power of the soul by which it desires whatever it wants. Because it wants for the sake of something—either for the sake of the honorable, the delightful, or the useful <note>These are the three classic types of "the Good" in Aristotelian ethics: *bonum honestum* (virtuous), *bonum delectabile* (pleasant), and *bonum utile* (functional).</note>—therefore, whatever it wants, it desires for the sake of this. Thus, appetite is the power of the soul by which whatever it wants, it wants for the sake of something. And it is a determined power; therefore, appetite is the power of the soul toward something, and it is a determined power.
</margin>

...properties regarding the distinction of delight: since delight, which is considered in itself, is twofold: namely, on the part of the one who is delighted, or on the part of that which follows. Then, concerning the property of the different types of delight, this delight—which is considered in itself—is said to be "outside itself" <note>original: "extra se". This likely refers to the soul's focus being directed toward the object that causes the pleasure.</note> because in that which delights, it intends itself. However, it is true that if such delight possesses the "reason of the honorable" <note>original: "rationem honesti". The quality of being morally good or worthy of honor.</note> and through this follows the reason of the appetite of the intellect, then there would not be a "species" [form] here in the appetite, just as there is not in the animal. In this way, delight is now acting in this manner as it is in itself. From this, it is clear that delight is spoken of from itself, just as it is spoken of regarding the appetite which is from nature. And here, concerning itself, as it is spoken of regarding the appetite which is from nature, it is thus clear that this delight is not of nature, nor is it about itself, but as it is in itself. 

Hence it is clear that delight, according to that which is in itself, is said to possess the reason of the good <note>original: "rationem boni". The aspect or quality of being "good."</note> just as it is said to possess the reason of the delightful. According to the reason of the appetite, it is said that the difference between appetite and delight is as it is in itself, and appetite is toward the good. Thus it is clear that this difference of delight and appetite is as it is in itself. Just as it is also clear that appetite is toward something as it is in itself. Therefore, it is clear that this appetite is called appetite as it is in itself, and this delight is called delight as it is in itself.

<column-break/>

Truly, however, even evil is desired under the proper reason of appetite, just as the thing desires the good under its proper reason. For the good and the evil are the proper objects of the appetite, just as the true and the false are the proper objects of the intellect. <note>This is a fundamental scholastic principle: the Mind seeks Truth, while the Will/Appetite seeks the Good.</note> This is clear through the difference between the appetite and the intellect: for the intellect is carried toward a thing under the aspect of the true, so that the thing exists in the intellect according to the reason of truth. But the appetite is carried toward a thing under the aspect of the good, so that the thing exists in the appetite according to the reason of the good. 

And just as the intellect is not said to *be* true, but is said to *possess the reason* of truth, so the appetite is not said to *be* good, but is said to *possess the reason* of the good. And just as the true and the false are in the mind, so the good and the evil are in things. This is stated in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*, Book III, a core text for medieval psychology.</note>, where it is said that the appetite is toward something as toward an end-point, and it is said that the intellect is toward something as toward a beginning principle. Thus it is clear that the appetite is carried toward the thing under the aspect of the good. And as it says in the third book of *On the Soul*, the appetite is toward the good. Thus it is clear that the appetite is carried toward the thing under the aspect of the good, just as the intellect is carried toward the thing under the aspect of the true. And just as the good and the evil are in things, so the true and the false are in the mind.

---

Now, concerning the first point, as in the preceding section, it must be examined: first, concerning its reason and essence. Then it is said that delight is, according to itself and properly, delight. This is stated in the second book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book II.</note>, where it is said that delight is according to itself, and it is that which follows upon something. It is said that delight is something perfect and whole. It is said that delight is a certain thing that "perfects the action" just as beauty [perfects] youth. <note>original: "sicut pulchritudo juventutem". A famous Aristotelian analogy: pleasure isn't the action itself, but a "bloom" that completes the activity, like the glow of health on a young person.</note> It is said that delight is something that terminates the appetite, like peace and tranquility. It is said that delight is something that contributes to the perfection of the work, like rest and peace. It is said that delight is something that contributes to the continuation of the work, like perseverance. It is said that delight is something that contributes to the enjoyment of the work, like love and desire. Thus it is clear that delight is something according to itself, and it is that which follows upon something.

<column-break/>

<margin>
virtues and honors which first...
In addition...
</margin>

...virtues and honors: where it should be noted that it is according to the presence of the object itself, just as there is delight in virtue and delight in science [knowledge]. Thus it is clear that delight is something according to itself, and it is that which follows upon something. And it is said that delight is something perfect; thus it is clear that delight is something according to itself.

Furthermore, it should be known that delight is twofold: namely, delight in act <note>original: "in actu". Pleasure experienced during the performance of an action.</note> and delight in habit <note>original: "in habitu". A state of readiness or a lasting disposition to find pleasure in certain things.</note>. Delight in act is that which follows upon the operation; delight in habit is that which follows upon the disposition. Thus it is clear that delight is something according to itself.

And it should be known that delight is something perfect, and it is that which follows upon something. It is said that delight is something that perfects the action, just as beauty [perfects] youth. And it is said that delight is something that terminates the appetite, like peace and tranquility.

It describes "delight" (pleasure) as a perfecting force that completes an action, famously comparing it to the bloom of beauty upon a youth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the appetite, focusing on how different internal states (like temperament or passion) alter a person's perception of "the Good" and the "End" (goal) of their actions. It draws heavily on Aristotle's Ethics and Physics.</meta>

...more frequently. It should be noted, however, that it only seems this way because the following object is present. The reason for this is that the appetite is directed toward only one thing; however, that which follows the law of nature changes it in reality and **in itself** <note>original: "per se"</note> through the connected object. But where it is ordered toward many things, it acts through something else. We see this in the case of water: water desires its own place, which is downward, and this is **in itself**; but when it is in fire, it does not desire to go downward, but desires to ascend. However, this is not **in itself**, but **by accident** <note>original: "per accidens"; essentially, a secondary or circumstantial quality rather than an essential one.</note> according to its presence in the fire.

And the soul behaves in the same way: it naturally desires one thing, which is the Good according to the truth in a general sense, toward which it is ordered by nature. But **by accident**, according to its particular state, it seems to itself to desire something else. For instance, concupiscence <note>The physical faculty of desire or "lust" for sensory pleasure.</note> desires what is delightful according to the senses, and this is a "good" insofar as it is perceived by the senses. Even Reason, when it is in such a state, desires that which is delightful. We see many rational beings who, out of habit or out of passion, desire that which is evil; but this is because the appetitive power desires a thing exactly as it relates to it. Therefore, when the appetite has been changed by some passion, such as anger, then it seems to the person that vengeance is a good, and this is what he wants, desires, and judges to be right. It seems to him to be a good because his perception matches his emotional state. This is why **The Philosopher** <note>The standard medieval title for Aristotle.</note> says: "As a man is, so the end appears to him."

Therefore, when one is in the grip of such a passion, he does not judge according to right reason, but according to passion, and then he desires that which is not good **in itself**, but only according to that specific state in which he finds himself. Just as a sick man desires that which harms him—not for its own sake, but because of the illness which has changed him. Therefore, when anyone wants or desires something, even if he wants what is evil, he does not want it insofar as it is evil, but **under the aspect of the good** <note>original: "sub ratione boni"; a fundamental Scholastic principle that the will only moves toward things it perceives as having some benefit.</note>. It is said that he wants nothing except the good, or under the aspect of the good; and thus it is said that nothing is desired except the good, or under the aspect of the good. Delight is also the end <note>The "end" (*finis*) refers to the goal or purpose.</note> of the movement of the appetite, and therefore it is seen as a good. As is said in the first book of the *Ethics*: the Good has the character of being pleasing, and the "desirable" is that which is pleasing. And because there is rest in the "end," it is said that "grace" <note>original: "gratia"; here used in the sense of a pleasing favor or for the sake of something.</note> is the end.

<column-break/>

...is consoled. The third point is that, just as we see in the effects of the soul, one end is more pleasing to some and another to others. For example, because of a person's **complexion** <note>original: "complexione"; the biological temperament or balance of humors in the body.</note>, a certain end seems right to him. From this, it is clear that although the soul has one ultimate goal, it is nevertheless "one" under the aspect of the individual. Thus we see among people that one finds his end in glory, while another, through his passions, desires it less. 

The cause of this is stated in the second book of the *Ethics*: a person desires what is similar to his own complexion. As Aristotle says: the spirit is raised toward the external according to the complexion. It is said that the "end" follows the complexion; for example, if one is "phlegmatic" <note>One of the four temperaments, traditionally associated with being calm or sluggish.</note>, he desires those things which pertain to phlegmatic people. Thus it is said that the end is "complexioned." As Aristotle says in the third book of the *Ethics*: "as each person is, such does the end appear to him."

The third factor is **custom** <note>or habit.</note>. From custom, we see that one thing seems good to a man and another evil. This is because custom is "a second nature," as is said in *On Memory and Recollection*. Therefore, just as nature inclines toward something **in itself**, so does custom. We see Aristotle saying this in the second book of the *Ethics*: from many acts, a **habit** <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition of the soul.</note> is generated, and from that habit, we see that someone chooses one thing and not another.

The fifth factor is **passion**, because we see that passion changes a man and makes something appear a certain way to him that does not appear so to another. In all these causes, we see that everyone has a specific end. Since the "end" is that which is desired, when it is desired, it acts like a principle <note>A starting point or foundational truth.</note>. Just as principles function in theoretical matters, so do "ends" function in practical matters, as is said in the seventh book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, we see that as a man is, such does the end appear to him; and thus, as the soul is disposed, so it desires.

The sixth factor is **reason**, because reason also changes things. Thus it is clear that according to the soul’s complexion, custom, passion, and reason, so it desires. 

The seventh mode is according to the **end** itself: because everyone, according to the end they seek, wants the things that lead to that end. From this, we have the idea that as a man is, such does the end appear to him, and he desires accordingly. 

The eighth mode is according to the **will**, since the will also changes a man. From the will, one thing seems good to him and another not. Thus we see a man either desire or not desire according to his will. 

The ninth is according to the **appetite**, since the appetite is that which moves toward something; and according to this, the appetite changes a man and makes him desire or not.

<column-break/>

...to a stone. Thus it is confirmed that the "end" exists outside of oneself; for the end is desired as it is "desirable." The third mode is: what it might be. Delight is gathered together, and delight comes through the appetite which has "graces." And in the end, since it has a rational basis as it exists in the thing itself, there is no matter except in the thing. For it is said that "hope is in the end," and through hope, it is clear that the goal is in the end. Thus, however the soul is disposed, it desires according to that disposition; and so it is with the multitude of desires.

But is there only one end? It is said in the second book of the *Physics* that the "end" for the sake of which something is done is one. Truly, the end is one in that it is an end. But it is also said in the second book of the *Physics* that "end" is spoken of in two ways: the **end for which** <note>original: "finis cui"</note> and the **end by which** <note>original: "finis quo"</note>. 

The **end for which** is that for whose sake something is done; for example, the end of medicine is health. Health is the "end for which." But the **end by which** is that through which something is achieved, such as the medicine itself. Thus we see that one person desires the end as health, and another desires the end as the medicine. So it is said that the end is one in that it is an end, but it is multiple in that it is "for which" and "by which."

This is also clear regarding the end in reality versus the end in operation. As said in the first book of the *Ethics*, some ends are **operations** (like music), and some are **works** <note>i.e., a finished product.</note> (like a building). Thus we see one person desires the end as an operation, and another as a finished work. 

Fourthly, it is said that the end is one insofar as it is an end, but it is multiple in terms of what is "desirable." For it is said in the third book of the *Ethics* that the desirable is either the **Good** or the **Apparent Good**. Thus we see one person desires the good as it truly is, and another desires it as it appears to be. 

Fifthly, the end is one, but it is multiple in terms of being **proximate** (near) or **remote** (distant). One person desires the near goal, another the distant one. 

Sixthly, the end is one, but it is multiple in terms of being **universal** or **particular**. One person desires a universal end, and another a particular one.

<column-break/>

...and generates others, and all things, and one or another, and so on. He says this "outside the end," and says that without an end, nothing is given, as everyone can prove—medicine and all things. Then he asks what the "grace" <note>The "pleasingness" or "sake"</note> of the appetite is, and says that the virtue of the appetite is in the end. He says the end is that for whose sake something is desired, and then says that nothing else is desired except for the sake of the end. Thus we have it: the sake is the end, and the sake is the cause.

**Here he speaks of the terminating end:**
It is said in the second book of the *Ethics* that nothing is said "to be" unless it has an end. He then says the end is that by which something is **terminated** <note>Finished or limited.</note>. Just as we see that the end is that in which something rests, so it is clear that the end is a limit. He then says the end is twofold: one is the end that terminates the thing itself (like the end of a life), and the other is the end that terminates an operation (like the completion of a work). He says the end is that in which something rests, and thus the end is a limit. 

But against this: it seems the end is not a limit, because we see that some ends are infinite, such as the end of God. If the end is infinite, then it is not a limit. To this it must be said that "end" is used in two ways: one is the end that terminates a thing, which is a limit; the other is the end which is "that for the sake of which" something is done. This second type is not a limit but is called infinite. 

But against this: it seems the end *is* a limit, because we see the end is that in which something is terminated. To this it must be said that the end is called a limit insofar as a thing is terminated by it, but it is not called a limit insofar as the thing is not terminated by it. The end is that in which something is terminated, and thus the end is a limit in the sense that the thing reaches its conclusion through it.

**Here he speaks of the perfection of the end:**
It is said in the first book of the *Ethics* that the end is that which is "the best" <note>original: "optimum"</note>. He then says the end is **perfection** because a thing is perfected through it. Thus the end is the best because the thing is made complete by it. 

But against this: it seems the end is not always perfection, because we see that some ends are evil, such as the "end" of a thief. In that case, the end is evil, and thus it is not perfection. To this it must be said that the end is called perfection insofar as the thing (the action) is completed by it; but it is not perfection in the sense that the thing is not made "perfect" in a moral sense. Thus, in terms of completion, the end is perfection.

<summary>This page analyzes the Aristotelian concept of the "End" (finis), explaining how individual temperament, habit, and passion change one's perception of the Good, while also distinguishing between the end as a goal, a limit, and a completion.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the abstract discussion of "form" and "matter" on the previous page into a specific investigation of physics and cosmology. What is the nature of the earth? It certainly seems that it is a different kind of matter; for it is moved only in the center and not in any other way. Just as we see in the different elements, there is a certain and specific quality in them. Where something moves within them, the way is similar and permeable, and it almost seems that it cannot be in another place unless it seeks the heavens again, since there are both water and the other elements in abundance. 

Wherefore, when he speaks of the part of a circle and of its arc, then each of its surfaces in their coming are what the heaven is in its downward direction through lines. Let there be, therefore, a certain proportion in another thing. And things touch each other, and it is seen in them, and the place of heat is much seen, and from that, they shrink. They call many of these things "eggs" <note>This likely refers to the "ovoid" or "egg-like" shape of certain celestial or elemental models common in medieval physics.</note> and others walk, and so on; for this reason, they should be preferred. 

But it is said that according to those things called "celestial," it is said of these that they walk and other things because of this; they place the right foot and then the left, and otherwise, though "rectitude" <note>original: "rectitudo"; in this context, it refers to straight-line motion, which was considered "imperfect" compared to circular motion.</note> is attributed to the heavens because it is said by itself, and thus in the celestial things themselves. And motion is of one part and of another part, and then it is said and said again: although it is said in its own proper ways concerning those things which are moved. And it is said in other things that motion is diverse, and not in that which is the heavens. But motion is said to be moved. And thus it regards this motion; a diversity is spoken of it, so that the diversity may be celestial. In the end, in the middle between themselves, it is said that it does not move well by itself in the earth; therefore it has a quest, neither where it may be nor lest this should not be.

<meta>This page transitions from a philosophical discussion on the nature of perception (possibly an extract from Plato or a commentary) into the beginning of Roger Bacon’s famous treatise "On the Secret Works of Art and Nature, and on the Vanity of Magic." <margin>Plato</margin>
From the intellect, however, to that which is spoken of through the intellect; to another thing through reason; through reason to another thing through sense; through sense to the thing itself, even to that which is sensed by itself. Through intellect, reason, and sense, one proceeds toward that which is spoken of through another, and thus it proceeds through causes and causes opposite to themselves, and so it is carried toward **contemplation** <note>original: "theoricam"; refers to theoretical study or divine contemplation.</note>. And you should know that those three—insofar as they are one—enter into a thing insofar as it is a thing; but by reasoning and sensing them in turn, there is an order in them. Order is owed to them just as it is for reason to perceive with reason, and for sense to feel through sense in order to receive, as it is said, "through another" and not "by itself." And thus reason and sense, insofar as reason is with others and sense is as sense, nevertheless tend toward that which exists. What is said "through another" is nonetheless "by itself" insofar as it exists under this or that reason or sense. And through this, there are true reasons which have the true reasons mentioned above; because of this, many people seem to perceive many shapes through sense in a lower or higher state of sensing, which are not, however, as they appear below. For the sense is perceived and those things which belong to such a conception are under the aforementioned things in time and place. Yet time and place cannot rightly hold them in this way, because of what might be in nature, or because the mind is not rightly in them—the mind, as it were, seen through a higher sense in them, a habit of such a kind that it could never exist without **mental vision** <note>original: "mentali visione"; the internal processing of sensory data.</note>, as is said through figures. And thus it is necessary to perceive, and thus to occur in vision through the mental, and thus a **spiritual motion** <note>original: "motu[m] s[piritualem]"; a medieval term for the non-physical movement of signals or "species" within the nerves or soul.</note> occurs in these mental things which are called mental visions "through another" in the act of perceiving. This is done through something else that is seen by the mind according to reason, since the perceived thing—in regards to light and quality and other movements—may be perceived by reasons. Let the thing be present, let vision perceive the making of those figures, and let it speak as reason is made by sight. And although vision perceives above reason, it is said to be made then, to be generated, and for time to receive something else. And just as the mind lives through the mind and the intellect, nevertheless there are two things in the perceived: they ought to perceive the shapes of things, and those shapes are said to be such as they are to the spirits of things and their representatives. And thus, in the place in which they are said to be, things are to be sensed because of what they are. And if those to whom things are spoken act as they are moved, they cause many things to be sensed "by themselves" through the said sight. And they grant this mental vision "through another" and not "by itself," just as the reasons said are within, because visions are in the divisions of the sense. And it is called a "work" whence they are carried separately by the said reasons; the quantity of things is made to be above, but to reason by mental reasons and by reason. And a certain reason of existing things belongs to the one reasoning through sense, because of which these are said to operate "by themselves" through mental reason. But then the mind discovers what is made from the mind—another truth of the true mind, as it is said "by itself."

->Amerit<-

### Here begins the book of Amerit <note>Possible corruption of "A. me" or a specific title.</note> regarding the works of art and nature and the worthlessness of magic.
### First Chapter: Concerning magicians and their vanity.

**To your reverence**, since you have asked that I presume to write this to you—I do not presume, but I believe it is a duty to record this work, which concerns the power of **art and nature** <note>In this context, "Art" (Ars) refers to technology, engineering, and human craft, while "Nature" refers to the inherent laws of the physical world.</note> and the worthlessness of magic. Where art reasons regarding time, things are indeed true; it is not so where magicians speak for themselves, as magicians by themselves lie and invent many things. Many things can be made through art, and it is true that they can be made through nature and art, but not where magicians are the operators. Since, as it is said, the works of art ought to be true through reason, these are as nature operates. Magicians take these for themselves, reasoning that they arise from a [magical] cause or work, but this is not so. Instead, they should record this: because they are magicians, they say such works are performed by more than they are; they do not speak the truth but are said to lie. Whence these are not the truths of art, but of true magicians—not through art, but through magic. They say this about all things that can be made by the arts, and magicians claim by themselves that the true work of art is magic. Magicians say what is not true, since many works of nature or art can be made which are not through magic. Whence, by this, magicians presume that to be made which is not made; they say this, however, by themselves either by reason of art or nature, yet they lie. For the operations of art are fluid and, regarding the times, they are true operations by themselves; they do not lie as they say. Because of this, the work has more of the thing "by itself." Nevertheless, through this, the work does not pertain to magic. And thus true things can be made, just as in the proper time of reason or record, to hold the reason well; and yet through this, they are truths in the works of art, because the reasons of the truths of things are true; they have decreed and defined things, and thus things exist through the works of art. Regarding nature, where it is not done through art, nevertheless the things of nature operate "by themselves" as they ought to operate—not by reason of art but of nature. However, as the reason of nature operates, they lie in many works by reason of nature, because of this: that magicians have operated in the reasons of things and in true works; but nevertheless, they are true, and this is not of art, but concerning the truths of art—works of art, not through magic. But regarding the nature of things, where the reason of art does not promise itself through magic, it is as the reason of art holds the reason of nature within itself, dividing and running through to the end.

<column-break/>

An argument for bringing forth a **two-foot mass** <note>original: "bipedale[m] massa[m]"; likely an optical illusion where an object appears to be a specific size at a distance.</note> of weight because of some requirement of time; and once that is held, let time be held for this, so that it appears to others through something else that it is two feet long, yet it is not. But magicians lie, as has been said, claiming that it is a work of magic, whereas it is from the nature of art, on account of time or length, and on account of other numbered reasons. But reason does not pertain to this; it exists in works and reasons through the reasoning of many things and the reason of truths which art discovers in the perception of art. These things pertain to art, yet they are of works; and through the works of art, more like **gums** <note>original: "gumme"; possibly referring to adhesive substances or resins used in crafts.</note> insofar as they are worked, this is not of art but of the truths of magic, which in many things have a reason through something else or their own reason. Nevertheless, in our time, concerning the proper truths of art and the works of art, where reason has no lack of seasoning, they do not pertain to magic. Yet magicians by themselves speak of the nature of things and some truths of art, just as magicians properly speak of the works of art insofar as they are the reasons of the nature of things or their own truths. Nevertheless, the magicians lie, and this arises from the reason of the nature of things which discovers the works of art, but it is not through magic.

->It is properly called "Tao" <note>This is a rare and highly unusual inclusion of "Tao" in a Latin text, likely Bacon referencing an Eastern or distorted Arabic term for "Path" or "Reason."</note> by reason of the mind through natural and artistic works; and it is reasoned by reason of art where there is no operation of magic, but by reason of the mind and the reason of the truth of things.<-

But magicians lie; and insofar as magicians operate "by themselves," they do so more by reasoning about many truths of things which they hold to be of art, yet it is not true. And reason pertains to the various reasons of things through another, or to truths which have their own reason; nevertheless, they have worked on this: that many works of art can be made properly in the time of reason, or as works of art, nature, or magic. But where art ought not to operate this properly in time—as it ought to operate, or as the reason of art does not hold the reason of art—the reason of magic lies more concerning the proper truths of things. But this should be said concerning the truths of art and the works of art, not of magic. And the reason of things, just as they ought to be made, they ought to operate. Concerning the works of art, insofar as they have worked more with the truths of nature than art, the reason is nevertheless not true. And reason pertains to various truths of things through another, or to truths which have their own reason; nevertheless, the magicians lie where the reason of art ought to be done and not the reason of magic. Nevertheless, it should be said that the works of art ought to be through the reason of the mind and the reason of the truth of things—properly through the reason of the mind and art, the truth of art, and the truth of things.

And as it is said "by itself," they would be works by their own reason; the reason of art proceeds, and from the weight, things have the reason of art, as it is said "by itself." And thus the works of art ought to be made by reason of the mind and the truths of things—by reason of the mind and art, the truths of art, and the truths of things. Nevertheless, by this, the magicians by themselves promise things from the truths of art, insofar as the reason of art has its own reason. The reason of art, as it seems, makes the truths of art through reasons and works, whereas the magicians call the true work of art "magic" by itself. But this is not true; those things were worked by reason of art, as it appears.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Roger Bacon’s famous letter, where he distinguishes the genuine power of "art" (technology) and nature from the deceptive claims of magicians. He argues that many "miracles" attributed to magic are actually scientific phenomena involving optics, proportions, and natural laws.</summary>

# Laws

As we already set forth in this work, we are dealing here with those things determined in this book which pertain to knowledge <note>original: "scientiam"</note>. Each part has one specific aim proposed to it, which it must perceive. For a thing can have one "persona" <note>In this context, 'persona' likely refers to a specific role, character, or manifestation of a thing's nature</note> through which it reaches its specific perfection. Now, what do I mean by a "persona" in this matter? As we said before, justice itself is a certain thing in this way: for it operates in each thing through itself. This is what is proposed to those things of which he speaks and which he holds here. 

Let them be compared among themselves: through these things, the same perfection is found, and from this, one can feel this life. This exists in the way of living and in the nature of living, and consequently in the manner in which one acts. Let it also be perceived what one acts upon and in what this exists, and whether there is one thing in which all things agree. From there, it follows that one should submit oneself to it, and then understand and know the law <note>original: "legem"</note> through which one acts. For God prescribes a path to him by His law, by which he may do these things. For God desires something in us, since God himself is said to unfold God <note>This suggests a Neoplatonic idea where the divine nature reveals or "unfolds" itself through creation and human action</note>. 

Therefore, to each according to their nature, there are means by which they can exist, and toward this one should have a mind and understand the <term>highest good</term> <note>original: "summum bonum"; the ultimate goal of human existence</note>, so that one may begin to act in the matter. This is the principle of anything: for one must have this power, so that his <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a settled disposition or character trait, like a virtue</note> may be disposed toward perfection. From this, it is said to become so, as in all its parts. Thus it reaches the summit through truth, for it leads him to truth in happiness. From this, it is manifest that if anyone does not understand the law of God, happiness is not a habit through that law, and from this, he acts.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, from those things which have been said, happiness can be known. Because whatever pertains to happiness seems to be of the same nature, in this way it happens that from this we have what pertains to determining this <term>end</term> <note>original: "finem"; the 'telos' or ultimate purpose of an action</note>. Thus, happiness comes from the end, because the end is the very way in which happiness holds itself. For we say someone is <term>blessed</term> <note>original: "beatus"; referring to 'beatitude,' a state of supreme spiritual joy</note> when he arrives at this end, because he perceives himself to be within it. 

Something in which happiness resides is sought, and from this, we see how each thing has a specific purpose for which it exists. In this purpose, the end itself resides. For as we see in other arts—as medicine is for the sake of [health], or the blacksmith's art is for the knife—so also virtue is for the sake of this end. Because of this, through virtue, we possess what is good, and from this, that happiness exists in reality. 

Hence, if anyone does not possess this virtue, they cannot say they are happy. For that end is something in which we are participants. The end exists for no other reason than that someone might have happiness from it. What this "end-happiness" is, is that toward which we strive and toward which we ought to strive. We must have this happiness for this reason: because through it, each person is called blessed, and from this happiness, they arrive at beatitude. Just as we see something is called happiness because it contains within itself what is required for it. 

From this, it is clear how one relates to happiness: for happiness exists only through the end itself. From this, something appears which is happiness in itself; that is, it is the "end in power" through itself, as is said of beatitude in the end. For every human mind strives toward beatitude, just as it is said of the end: every mind strives toward this end. From these things, it is manifest how that which is called happiness exists. For the end is something having perfection of itself. In this is that happiness which is in the end, and from this, it is perceived that happiness is within it. For the end is nothing other than the happiness which the mind [seeks] to have as an end, which previously seemed to have nothing.

<column-break/>

And from these agreements and the union to one thing, there is a <term>reason</term> <note>original: "rō" or "ratio"; the faculty of logical thought and moral judgment</note> from which it proceeds. That which is toward this reason is that other thing, and then someone, through this reason, is in perfection. But if anyone says that this reason is not in it, then he says nothing. Let there be true honor and dignity in walking the path toward this end; but to say this path leads to another end is not according to reason. For it strives toward another thing through itself, which is in that which is not happy through itself, but toward another happy thing. 

Let one hold this path, since through itself it does not have the power to act within itself. As is perceived in all things, they strive toward this end, and because of this, there is honor and the end. Therefore, it is something in which there is participation, and formerly it held this very thing in many and diverse matters. For this reason, it is considered in sight and in reason. Furthermore, it exists in it in such a way that it disposes itself to agree with this: for it is not in another except as the end is in it. 

We see this in the medical art: that the mind looks toward this end, and because it strives toward this end, it venerates this end with honor. This is also said of animals in a certain way, but especially in man, to whom reason is proposed. For man is called happy insofar as he uses reason toward this end. And because the nature of each person's reason is intellectual, through it, it flows toward the intellect and toward that which is.

It is true that the second part speaks of the end, but it must be said: that is not the end which is said to precede, but this end is the end in which happiness itself resides. For one strives toward this end, and through this end, the good itself is known to be. Toward this, the mind seems to understand, through that which is in the end and in happiness itself. For then happiness is said to be toward beatitude, as is said of beatitude in the end. For it is then that the thing seems to arrive at this end. Through this, it appears what is called the end and happiness in itself. From this, it appears how it relates to happiness itself: for this is the end in itself and is happiness in itself. 

We see that God himself is happy in himself and is blessed through himself. For He has no others from whom He receives this beatitude, for He is happiness [itself]. Since He has nothing outside of Himself that exists, He is whatever He seems to will. From this, it is clear that He is happy, just as the mind is said to be that by which He is known.

<column-break/>

It is not without those things which are possible for each person, so that one may enjoy the truth of His way, whatever he has of this from himself. For each will enjoy it so that nature itself may be, which is made through Him, and through it, there is well-being and a good state. For from this, He leads him into the joining of the end, so that one may be intellectual. For in those things which exist through the end, the end does not have existence [separately], since it exists through itself; it is happy and perfect. 

In this consists its happiness: insofar as it belongs to this and to the virtue of the perfect soul <note>original: "animi"</note>, so that it may provide the intellect of its works. For regarding these things, it is not that the thing simply exists, but that making it so that he himself is excellent. Hence we see that in reality, there is this distinction and rank: for the reason of reason and of virtue, from which the soul is perfected. From these, the soul is said to be good, as if from virtues—both sensible and intellectual—by which man has this perfection and the reason of the soul. 

Without this, there would be no perfection of the end. For the soul is that in which this happiness resides. Thus, happiness is spoken of through the soul itself. For the soul has this regard toward God, just as it is said of God that in God is this very happiness. Hence we see how the soul relates to this end: for the reason of this is that thing through itself, through which one also arrives at the beatitude of the end. We have this happiness through our soul itself. 

From these things, one must conclude: that the soul is that of which we ought to be participants through beatitude. This is said to be the soul because in it are all virtues and reason. For the soul possesses this perfection through the virtues. Those have this beatitude for whom the soul is in a good state, and reason is their judge. For thus it is said that the soul is blessed because it has this perfection within itself. From this, it is gathered that reason and virtue are in it, for in these consists whatever a man has of happiness. For by this, a man is said to be happy: when he has this perfection of the soul within himself.

In those things said about happiness, it is understood that the thing which is called happy possesses this state through its parts, just as in the human body, and just as there is a certain sight and intelligibility that may be in it.

--- Page 109 ---
<meta>This page transitions from a discussion on the soul's intellective powers to the logical framework of "second intentions." While the previous page explored how the soul understands the divine and its own nature, this section moves into technical logic, explaining how the mind categorizes reality through mental concepts.</meta>

and in this way, there are causative principles existing in reality from which things arise, and with which they are not opposed. Rather, they exist alongside these things so that they might be similar in being to the things to which they adhere, effectively causing them to be the very things they are. He demonstrates this through a fitting example, for in the case of <term>second intentions</term> <note>original: secundis intentionibus; these are "concepts of concepts," such as the idea of a "species" or "genus" rather than the individual animal itself</note>, it does not work this way. For the things from which they arise and in which they exist are not of one and the same rank. This is because those essences have within themselves certain similarities which must be joined to a single essence which they bring into being. Through this process, the things emerge to which intentions must adhere; the reality of the intentions belongs to these things, and the intentions themselves exist within them through this process. 

And therefore, they propose the path that second intentions—which are not essentially derived from the essences in which they reside—are nonetheless components of those very essences. Just as the second intentions within them are "essences" not by intention but in reality, even though the intentions themselves reside within them. Therefore, he says that intentions are not the things in which they reside, nor are the intentions the very things to which they belong. Instead, intentions are a kind of external "attachment" that must adhere to those noble things which are the subjects of the intentions and in which they exist. 

Consequently, one must understand what a "second intention" is, what an "intention" is in itself, in what things it resides, to what things it belongs, and what the actual realities of these intentions are. It seems from this that he wishes to say that an intention is twofold: either according to what is in the soul—and then it is something real, and the intention itself is that which exists in the soul—or insofar as it exists "intentionally," it is that which the thing itself is. He explained this in the <term>Book on the Soul</term> <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*</note> through many reasons and examples, where he intends to show that when the soul knows a thing, it does not become the physical thing itself; rather, there is only an "intention" of the thing in the soul. Through this, the thing itself comes to be in the soul, not according to its physical reality, but as a concept. Following this, he declares that second intentions are essentially principles derived from the essences of things, and they adhere to the things that are the subjects of these intentions. This happens by way of intention and not through the physical essence of those things. He then demonstrates by example how the things to which intentions belong are their principles, just as I have explained by clarifying the various intentions whose principles and foundations are found in the essences of things.

<column-break/>

## Chapter Two: Concerning those things 
## which adhere to second intentions

Now that it has been explained in the previous chapter what second intentions are and how they function, it remains to explain those things which must adhere to them; these are the <term>accidents of intentions</term> <note>original: accidentia intentionum; properties or characteristics that belong to a concept but are not part of its essential definition</note>. <margin>properties of intentions</margin> He does this in two ways. The first is to explain intentions in general, insofar as they are intentions, rather than focusing on one specific type or another. Second, he deals with those things that adhere to specific intentions. 

He accomplishes the first part through three steps. First, by explaining the essence of the intentions—where they are and how they are. He demonstrates this by looking at the essences of the things that second intentions represent, doing so by comparing these physical things to the second intentions themselves, and vice versa. Second, he shows this by explaining their nature in relation to the things to which intentions must adhere, doing so by showing their nature in a general sense. Third, he proceeds by further explaining their nature through a comparison to the actual things of which they are intentions. The second step begins where he says, "After it has been shown, etc." The third step begins where he says, "Furthermore, you should know that intentions relate to things in this way." 

Regarding the first point, it must be understood that second intentions cannot exist unless there is a <term>unity of the thing</term> <note>original: unitas rei</note> in some way. For unity is the principle for second intentions to which they adhere. Thus, where there is no unity, there can be no intention. For an intention existing in many things makes them, in a certain way, one thing, even though by nature they are many. The explanation for this is that an intention has no essence except from the many things that are its principles, as he explains. Therefore, just as a thing has within itself a real unity, so an intention must have an "intentional unity." Because of this, intentions cannot be joined to one another except through a certain comparison to the essences they represent, just as unity serves as the foundation for second intentions.

<column-break/>

As was said above regarding intentions, they must have a foundation in the things from which they proceed. After this, he says that those essences—the essences of things from which an intention is formed—can be understood in two ways. First, according to themselves as they exist in the soul; then they are called the intentions that are predicated of them. Second, insofar as there is explained in them that they possess some common nature in respect to which they are intentions. 

Thus, intentions can exist from both sides, and from these things it is clear what an "intention in general" is. For according to the nature of these three parts, there is a general intention. The first is the intention grounded in the thing. The second is the thing itself, possessing a common nature. The third is the intention directed toward things according to this common nature. He therefore explains their nature and their difference. He says first that the intention toward a thing works this way because one thing is, and another is said to be, through that which is expressed by the intention. 

However, according to what it is in itself, it is a certain "common nature." Based on this distinction, intentions are divided. He further describes a twofold mode: namely, the intention and the thing. He then says that although intentions are spoken of regarding many things, they should only be spoken of according to the common nature they possess. It is according to this unity that it is called an "intention." For this reason, it is called the "intention of one thing," even though it concerns many. 

Later, he explains them by comparison to the essences to which they adhere, showing that things can be viewed in three ways in relation to intentions. In the first way, insofar as they exist in themselves, having a certain nature that is naturally suited to be a foundation. In the second way, according to how intentions exist within them; this is when they are understood according to a specific intention. In the third way, insofar as intentions are created from them. He explains all these points, and through this, it becomes clear what an intention is in itself and in respect to the things in which it resides and to which it belongs. In this way, we can judge intentions and the things that pertain to them. Thus, the path to understanding intentions in general is clear, according to this three-fold distinction.

<column-break/>

of material and of common and individual form, arising both from the things by which the object itself exists and from other external things. Then, he adds certain things that are determinately within them: namely, that although intentions are in the soul, it is necessary for them to be in some "receptacle" where they are grounded. Those things which constitute an intention cannot exist in themselves as essences; rather, they must have something in which they reside and from which they arise. 

Through this path, he explains that an intention does not exist except through that which is real, yet it is a certain "intentional" reality. Thus, the thing and the intention exist together, even though in themselves they are different things. He also explains that an intention has a certain mode of being that makes it distinct from a natural, physical thing. Therefore, an intention is more truly "in the soul" than outside the soul, even though its foundation is in the physical thing. 

He also explains how intentions can be compared to one another, and this happens through what is common to them insofar as they are intentions. Thus, an intention is something noble and worthy that ought to be considered in things, so that something noble and certain may be drawn out from them. In this way, an intention can be said to be "of intentions," and thus from some intentions, other intentions are drawn out. By this path, we can arrive at other intentions, as is evident in the study of <term>logic</term> <note>original: logica</note> and in other arts where some things are derived from other intentions—such as a "species" being derived from a "genus," and so on. 

And so he concludes the first chapter concerning intentions in general, as they adhere to things, and concerning those things which must be known about them. Afterwards, he begins to treat those things pertaining to other specific intentions, where the nature of an intention is further explained and how unity is found within them. Thus he says that from what has been said, it is apparent what an intention is and how it relates to things and to the soul. In this way, the path to other intentions is clear, which are to be explained through this method so that a full knowledge of them may be obtained.

# On the Unity of the Sensible Form

That nothing at all exists in a single thing unless it is one and the same in number <note>original: "una eademque numero"; a scholastic term referring to individual, numerical identity—that a thing is itself and not just a type of thing</note>: then it would be true that it is what it is, as if from common notions. Regarding the preceding parts, let them sense especially certain **species** <note>original: "species"; in medieval psychology, this refers to the "sensible form" or likeness of an object that travels to the sense organ without the object's physical matter</note>; then he says that even those things which are not seen are not just as it is said they are taken for the reason of themselves, or from those things which are not. For just as from those things which are not, or just as with those things, it would be seen to be true as it is said: etc. I speak with those who in every way are seen then to be different <note>original: "pheren"; likely a Greek-derived term related to 'carrying' or 'differing'</note> which then is especially then as if a certain composition from both is not just as some things are held as a species.

This is the sense of the younger preceding [authority] where it is seen that the way it is then said to be is the principal one, and it holds then that there is no preceding thing in any matter etc. Then it is said: then also the species which precedes then is what is said: then, then and here, which is an **image**; then it is seen etc. just as then, just as then through that time is possible, just as that which implies the preceding species: just as then etc.

Different things <note>original: "pheren"</note> then, just as they are not seen, then just as the species is respected and held, and which then, then by a certain other [composition] from both is said: and then it may be especially then that the species are sensed, it is that which is not just as an image: then it is seen etc. then then it is said: then that from one which holds species, species which are sensed and it holds then species, species then it is said then that not as then the species, which species then from one then it may be what is said: then just as then, then the species may be as it is, as it is the species etc. the species may be then an image: then just as the species then the species then the species: and especially the species then etc. which then, then not as then the species may be the species.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the soul's faculties. Having previously discussed the "species" or mental images that bridge the gap between object and mind, the author now turns to the ethical and spiritual implications of these movements, specifically how the soul's "heat" (passions like lust) is tempered by virtue, which acts as a "cooling" or "refreshing" influence.</meta>

# On the Movements of the Soul and the Nature of Virtue

### Of Lust and the Mean

It burns like fire: we shall speak of lust <note>original: "libidine"</note> and the movements of the soul, and many things concerning vices. Good is utterly lacking in the case of virtues, and it is not seen [clearly]. We speak of the nature of man, namely that he stands in the middle of two things: desire <note>original: "cupiditatis"</note> and [its opposite]. Every virtue and vice consists in this: that which is in the "middle" is so in respect to something else. It is not that which is in respect to virtue or the spirit when vice reveals itself through desire. Poverty may be compared to the state of animals, and it is rightly said to be in respect to the kingdom [of heaven]. Thus, a division and distinction is made between virtue and vice.

Because of this, it is said that [revelation] leads toward virtue, because virtue is a **pleasurable habit** <term>habitus delectabilis: a settled disposition or character trait that makes performing good actions feel natural and joyful</term>, as is stated in the second book of the *Ethics* <note>A reference to Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book II, where he defines virtue as a "state of character" or "habit" (hexis) concerned with choice, lying in a mean</note>. This exists in them on the part of the soul, and so also toward virtue. Indeed, virtue is something that exists according to itself, just as it was sent forth above. Virtue exists in all states of life, and thus for these people, they have certain proper moments and senses, just as the soul has whatever is in these virtues. And just as it is in them, so is the movement of the soul toward that which they ought to have. 

The riches of life exist in these virtues. As it is said, life exists in them according to itself; the **habit** <note>original: "habitus"</note> is like heat, and thus movement is the life of virtue or of enjoyment. In them, vision will be made more effective. So it is said to be in them: life is "cooled" or "refreshed" just as virtue is "heat." We are not speaking here of the "cooling" <note>original: "refrigeratio"; in a theological context, this often refers to spiritual refreshment or the "coolness" of grace contrasted with the "heat" of sin</note> that is poverty, which does not abound in them from their own [nature]. Rather, we speak of the refreshment that leads to the life of virtue. Thus, the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" usually refers to God in scholastic philosophy</note> is more effective, and virtue acts as a refreshment, just as vision is called the life of the virtues.

<column-break/>

### On Poverty and the Life of the Soul

Poverty is a misfortune, as has been spoken, where it is like smoke from a fire, or as the word says, water from a rock is heat. Thus, the condition of refreshment is spoken of afterward. This means that in these matters, it will be treated insofar as it exists in the just or in sins. In the just, virtue is like heat, and through this, it acts as a privation of refreshment. Similarly, it is in them that virtue exists as the "cooling" of the virtues. Because virtue exists in them, it is said to be "through itself," just as virtue is pleasurable. 

Virtue is the life in them, and thus toward virtue it is like vision in them. Just as the virtues possess [life], it is for the sake of virtue, or like the life of the spirit in them. Through this, it is said that vision is for the sake of the life of virtue. Just as the first virtue is in them, so through this, the spirit is the life of the virtues. How is virtue the life in them? It is said because the life of the spirit exists in the spirit. Through this, justice exists in them, just as the soul's life is for the sake of virtue.

Nothing can be done except through the virtues moving, just as "cooling" is spoken of regarding virtue. Because of this, the life of the soul is a "visible life" in the virtues. Just as virtue is the life in them, vision is in them, as sight exists for the sake of the life of the soul in virtue. That is, virtue is like vision in them. The spirit is like the vision-life of virtue. In the virtues, it is as if there were a "visible life." Just as vision is in them as life, so it is for the sake of the life of the soul. It is said that the life of the soul is in them through the virtue of the soul. Just as vision is in them, virtue is the life in the "cooling" of virtue. Therefore, the sight of the soul's life exists in the virtues, and thus vision is the life of virtue in them. Life exists in them just as vision exists in virtue for the sake of the soul's life. Furthermore, they move with certain virtues of the air.

**Column 1**

### On Devotion and Visitation

He shall enjoy [God] without any end, whereas we enjoy other or present things only until an end. But concerning the "visitation of devotion" <note>original: "uisitatione deuotionis"; a spiritual term for a moment of intense prayer or divine presence</note>, it is said here that a visitation happens to the just. This is not called a visitation unless it is accompanied [by grace], or it does not come unless it happens to those receiving it or to the one calling. It neither moves some in a different way, nor does it wish to unless they come in truth or in the poured-out vitality of the deity. If I announce a visitation to you by declaring or by wondering, let us see how vital it is, just as in the visitation of devotion. It is as effective in devotion as the spirit is toward the visitation of virtue. It exists in the visitation of the soul and is venerated as something pleasurable. 

Because of this, the soul is made [ready] for the virtues, just as vision exists in the visitation. But sight, spirit, and virtue are one; the virtues, as the primary thing, obey the soul. Just as the first virtue obeys itself, virtue is like sight. Because of visible things and the "heads" <note>original: "capita"; perhaps referring to main points or principles</note> for which it is impossible, it is spoken of in terms of the virtues, like vision in a visitation. The visible life of virtue is in the soul's virtue. If it is in the visitation, then the life of sight is the life of virtue.

Virtue was distinct in the soul, just like a sense, just as the vision of the soul's virtue is in them. The life of virtue is the life of the soul. Because of virtue, just like the spirit in the soul of virtue, the soul is "visible" like sight. In the visitation, the soul's sight is for the sake of virtue. The soul and the "visible soul" exist in the visible life. Because of virtue, the soul's life is the life of virtue. The visible life in virtue exists if it is in the visitation. The visible soul is like virtue in the virtues. Because of virtue, the soul is a "visible soul" like sight in a visitation.

<column-break/>

### On Justice and the Ultimate Will

Similarly, it seems that something governs the spirit, just as is said of the virtues. Namely, let us say what the **ultimate will** <note>original: "uoluntas extrema"; the final intent or goal of the human will, usually identified with the desire for the Supreme Good</note> is for them. It is given to the man as he enters [this state]. It is seen that just as without the spirit, from which he will see justice, it is said here that where a man is poor, he abounds in extremes. He is weighed down by heat and stupor. 

And rightly it is called "good," such as the virtue of the soul's spirit, like vision in the soul. The divinity of visible virtue is the life of the soul, its fruit, and the visible life of virtue. The soul is life toward the pleasure of the soul. Or, it is like the visible sight of virtue. In the virtues, visible life is life. The soul, as it exists in the virtues, is visible in the visitation of virtue. But justice, for the sake of visible things, is called the "visible virtue" in virtue. If visible sight possessed virtue like the soul, it would be visible in the soul. 

The soul, for the sake of virtue, is like the visible soul of virtue—the life of the soul. This refers to the man who exists in the "bond of virtue" <note>original: "religione uirtutis"; here *religio* refers to a binding or obligation to live virtuously</note> of the soul. But the visible life of virtue is what is said to be in them: the soul of virtue and the visitation. Virtue in the "religion" of visible virtue, but the sight of virtue is the visible life of the soul. That is, the sight of virtue is visible sight. The soul is the life of visible justice. The spirit of justice, for the sake of virtue, is the visible soul. In the religion of virtue, the visible life is the life of the soul. Therefore, justice is linked to virtue. Thus it is said: the soul is a visible soul. In the virtues, the soul of virtue is the life of the soul. The soul's appetite is the visible soul, just as life is for the soul. The soul of visible virtue and the visible soul of virtue: the soul of visible virtue is a visible soul. But truly, the good is that which governs...

### Of the Soul's Internal Acts

[Column 1]

From its own proper acts and processes, the soul can effect through itself and of itself that which is said to be "that which can be thought." <note>A likely reference to Anselm’s definition of God as "that than which nothing greater can be thought," applied here to the soul's capacity for conceptualization.</note>
