Then, since essence, like light, produces and communicates whatever is clear in time, you must respond to the reasons that ask and seek; and one responds if it discusses and carries out for others, and it is said to do so in this way. If a thing is said to be "made" <note>original: "factum"</note>, just as it is said, let it be silent and confess that as it is said, it is silent in its own intuition. 

This is just as Blessed Gregory says in his 25th Homily: <note>referring to Gregory the Great's *Homiliae in Ezechielem* or *Homiliae in Evangelia*, commonly cited in medieval texts to discuss the nature of visions</note> that which is "made" will not belong to prophecy unless it is a fantasy, and the mind proceeds beyond itself and becomes "extant" <note>original: "extans"; standing outside itself or ecstatic</note> through itself for an infinite time. Who does not know this? And just as that essence would be most poor if it were so inhabited, is it not thus established? Whence it is not said that it sees, because <unclear>in being</unclear> it is held to perceive a mode which is from time; and so indeed, just as that essence serves in that life, it is a matter of predestination. This same thing is declarable: that which is in time is true in a temporal sense, and it would rule prophetically. Then the state flies through the arts so that it may be seen; or as problems are stated, each would be true then if it knew that it was from a body of time, as is said "in life." And if it is said that the same problem is given, as much as it visits, it is made repugnant in the following words. And although he says it is as it is with bodies, they are always being involved with the vice of the world to which it is undeservedly owed.

First among the questions, it is said that the fateful one is dividing how, since essence is a whole **simultaneously** <term>simul: "at once"; a key concept in medieval metaphysics describing how God or the soul's essence exists outside the linear flow of time</term> in whatever things are there, just as if it were in time—namely, imperfectly, as it is fulfilled. But thus he responds to this division: if he knew the being as a subject, because the subject which is separate is said to be and is contained by him, since he always produces in time. Just as it was made in time, so it is communicating to many; and the same life is either truly being (as it exhibits the present "made" thing) or being as it exists in the divine, which would be involved in the simultaneity of truth. Just as by merit it quickly follows devotions of this kind, it is spoken of by voice, reason, and simultaneity. It is arrived at in this way: that according to the mode of perceiving, things are true in time; for a thing is true in time just as it is.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the human mind receives divine truths. Having previously discussed the mind as "pure water," the text now moves into the formal scholastic mechanics of "illumination" and the necessity of mental images (phantasms) for the soul while it is joined to the physical body.</meta>

...by **illumination**: According to him <note>likely referring to St. Augustine or Thomas Aquinas, the standard authorities on divine illumination</note>, it is from such things which follow that the mind is moved toward certain determined forms. Or rather, these forms are necessary; without them, it is impossible to **contemplate**. This presentation does not merely measure the mind; these are the remnants <note>original: "reliquiae"; refers to the traces or impressions left by an object in the memory</note> of the whole aforementioned concept which are found there. What measures the thing does not only measure the spoken word, but the presentation within the mind. Frequently, these remnants do not constitute anything else; rather, they exist within the mind so that they might not fail to constitute it. They are nothing if not for this. Elsewhere, they are much more: they are the presentation that measures, not merely the thing itself. Here, he will speak of the thing, because such a **revelation** <note>original: "reuelato"</note> is not signified except in those things in which they exist. It is customary to reveal why they are or why they are not. These are not merely for the sake of the mind's presentation, but for the presentation of the thing more presently, and the experience of this fact creates it. It is through the mind that these things possess what has been said, and what the mind does not have, it possesses through the presence of the presentation. In these matters, they say: it is not the remnants of the thing that this mind possesses, but the remnants of what was said in the mind, having the presence of the thing in the mind.

<column-break/>

...of **cognition**. But it is said that for many reasons, the **soul existing in the body** <note>A central tenet of Medieval philosophy: while the soul is embodied, its way of knowing is limited by the physical senses.</note> is nonetheless at the same time unable to understand except through <term>phantasms</term> <note>original: "phantasmata"; mental images derived from sensory experience. Scholasticism held that "the soul understands nothing without a phantasm."</note>. This is clear from its own determinations. It is perfected without the presence of those things which, if they persist as individuals, the phantasm is taken up—and not by the soul—from the phantasm. Inasmuch as in the presence of these things, the mind is moved, and these things are in this way able to move the **reasons** <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the intellectual principles or categories of the mind</note>. In this way, the mind can be moved, and by this reason, it will know them, even if it were to be destitute of them. But because of this, it nonetheless does not lack the means by which the reasons for knowing are established. They would be destitute of the reasons for knowing me in this way; it can happen that it ought to be moved, yet it ought not to produce then a failing **light**, but a flash of the mind. Either it is moved and does not know me, or it shall know. They say this signifies having time in such a way that the reasons are moved; they will know by this reason just as it is possible to be moved in the mind. And by this reason, it is confirmed that these divisions are the reasons of the mind, and by this reason, they are the divisions under which the reasons of the mind are measured. The soul is confirmed by what has been asserted then in respect to **imaginations**, for it appears they are individuals. It would not seek the reason why it is sensible; they do not have their own reasons by which they can be well-powered.

<column-break/>

...to construct, it shall take up. And because of those things which move in cognition, it is the case that they exist from their own senses, which can be fixed to this or that. Then, in this reason, all is certain: this multitude or perfection cannot be seen by **vision** <note>original: "visioni"; refers to intellectual or spiritual sight</note> except for the purpose of perceiving that which is led to be in the mind. And through this, there is this **disposition** <note>original: "dispositio"; the state of readiness or arrangement of the soul to receive grace or knowledge</note> in respect to that disposition, being in this through presentation. And yet, they lead these things—

->But it seems this is not the presence<-

He will understand: from that time, he is moved toward perceiving this within me, and they are in the thing in respect to it. Then, however, there is a way to set the thing aside—with which there is much that is hindering in vision. And it is said in respect to the thing, let it be in the mind by this reason. In respect to it, it is certain that this multitude or perfection cannot be seen by vision, except for the purpose of perceiving that which is led to be in the mind. And through this, there is this disposition in respect to that disposition, being in this through presentation. And yet, they lead these things—

<column-break/>

...to be perceived rather than the act of perceiving, most poorly, just as in this determination, these things are received in the **light**. This is because it has the presence of things; for it possesses these, nor is there **happiness** <note>original: "felicitas"; often used in a scholastic context to mean "beatitude" or the ultimate fulfillment of the intellect in God</note> in the present in respect to what they call their own derivation. And if they receive by looking, and being in such a way toward the one who measures, it is placed through the one who measures toward the influence of this determination. And they are only as much as they are disposed. Then, if this disposition were placed, they are in their own reason, because it is not placed in this division. Because of this, it could not measure, nor does it have it in this—and yet they lead this time as a disposition in respect to the one who measures. They are received by looking, because he possesses this, nor is there happiness in the present in respect to their own derivation, even if they are received.

<meta>This page transitions from a general discussion of "illumination" and mental remnants to the specific Aristotelian framework of knowledge. It marks the beginning of the "Metaphysics," exploring how human understanding ascends from basic sensory perception to the heights of wisdom and the knowledge of causes.</meta>

**[Left Page, Column 1]**

All men by nature desire to know. A sign of this is the delight we take in our **senses**. For even apart from their utility, they are loved for themselves, and most of all the sense which is through the **eyes**. For not only that we may act, but even when we are not intending to do anything, we choose sight, so to speak, above all others. The cause is that this sense, most of all, makes us know and demonstrates many differences.

Animals, therefore, are born possessing sensation. From sensation, in some of them, **prudence** <note>original: "prudentia"; in this context, it refers to a type of practical intelligence or "animal wisdom"</note> is produced in memory; in others, it is not. And because of this, some are prudent, while others are capable of being taught <note>original: "disciplinabilia"</note>—those which are unable to remember, such as **bees**, and any other similar genus of animals. They are prudent, yet they cannot learn unless they have the sense of hearing. Those which possess memory along with this kind of sense [hearing] are able to learn.

Other animals, then, live by **imaginations** and **memories**, and participate only a little in **experience**. But the human genus lives by **art** and **reasoning**. Experience is produced in men from memory; for many memories of the same thing produce the power of a single experience. And experience seems almost similar to **science** <note>original: "scientie"; referring to systematic knowledge or "scientia"</note> and **art**. Through experience, science and art result for men. For as **Polus** <note>A student of the rhetorician Gorgias, mentioned by Plato</note> rightly says, "experience indeed created art, but inexperience created chance."

Art is produced when, from many experimental conceptions, a single universal judgment is formed concerning similar things. For to have the judgment that "this [medicine] was beneficial to this person having this disease," and to this person...

<column-break/>

**[Left Page, Column 2]**

...was beneficial, such as to **Callias** and to **Socrates**, and to many others individually, belongs to **experience**. But when one determines that it benefited all such persons according to one single form—such as the **phlegmatic**, or the **choleric**, or those suffering from burning fevers—this belongs to **art**.

In regard to action, therefore, experience seems to differ not at all from art. Indeed, we see that those who are experienced are more successful than those who have the theory <note>original: "rationem"; meaning the rational account or "reason"</note> without experience. The cause is that experience is the knowledge of **particulars**, while art is the knowledge of **universals**. Now, all actions and all generations are concerned with particulars. For the physician does not heal "Man," except by accident; rather, he heals Callias or Socrates, or someone else called by such a name, to whom it happens to be a "man." If, therefore, someone possesses the theory without experience, and knows the universal but is ignorant of the particular within it, he will frequently fail in his treatment. For it is the particular that is more "healable."

Nevertheless, we judge that "knowing" and "understanding" belong more to art than to experience, and we deem the practitioners of art to be **wiser** than those of mere experience, as if wisdom follows more from "knowing." This is because the former know the **cause**, but the latter do not. For the experienced know the "that" <note>original: "id quod est"; the fact that something is so</note>, but they do not know the "why" <note>original: "propter quid"; the reason or cause</note>. The others, however, know the "why" and the cause.

Wherefore we also deem the **master-builders** <note>original: "architectores"</note> in any craft to be more honorable and to know more, and to be wiser than the manual laborers, because they know the causes of the things being done. The laborers, however, are like certain inanimate things: they act, but they do not act through knowledge—just as fire burns. Inanimate things, therefore, do such things by a certain nature, but manual laborers do them through **habit**. Thus, they are not wiser according to their practical skill, but according to the fact that they possess the theory and know the causes.

In general, the sign of one who knows is the ability to **teach**. And for this reason, we think art is more a science than experience; for the former can teach, but the latter cannot. Furthermore, we do not think any of the senses are "wisdom," although they are the primary knowledges of particulars. But they do not tell the "why" of anything—for example, why fire is hot, but only *that* it is hot.

---

It emphasizes the process of generation, the role of "intellectiones" (mental acts), and the hierarchical mastery of the mind over various genera of concepts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the human mind's nature, shifting from the mechanisms of memory to the "Active Intellect" (intellectus agens). It explores how the soul, while acting as the form of the physical body, maintains an unchanging essence that participates in the divine reason. The text relies heavily on the Aristotelian tradition, likely commenting on his work "On the Soul" (De Anima).</meta>

<margin>
Marginal notes referencing Aristotle’s "On the Soul" <note>original: "De Anima"</note>
</margin>

Secondly, because within the body there is both a single act of striving and a single act of remembering that existed before. Namely, there is a desire <note>The "desire to know," a fundamental concept in Aristotelian thought.</note> which, when it returns, recognizes through an act what it had seen before. It responds and is nourished by goodness. Even a child in its early stages, though the time is uncertain, perceives neither ambiguity nor acts within an act. However, the "continuous" is what is described according to the act of the **active intellect** <note>The "active intellect" (intellectus agens) is the power of the mind that transforms sensory information into abstract concepts.</note>; just as in the act of perceiving, the soul is granted existence by grace. This mode, which belongs to the intellect, is immutable. Even if by the reason of the soul it cannot be prepared for itself, the essence of the intellect is perceived through the "doing" and the "undergoing" of the mind. For just as the intellect possesses that which is mutable and can be troubled, it is also an image of the intellect <note>meaning a reflection of a higher, divine intelligence</note>. And it is said that the **passions of the soul** <note>In this context, "passions" (passiones) refers to anything the soul experiences or undergoes, including emotions and sensations.</note> are true through us, as they are known in themselves. The rational intellect is known to know what is said of the soul through us; it is an essence and is immutable. Whatever the soul must understand through some "home" of the intellect belongs to a superior order. The intellect has the capacity to perceive the form of the soul within itself, just as an intellectual form is understood through the participation of reason. This is the intellect of God through reason, which is the immutability of blessedness. Thus, it desires a similar form, like a figure impressed by light, which in the rational part is said to be the soul’s existence. It is the perpetual form of the **active intellect** in the rational part—or more clearly, the "higher soul" of immaterial contemplation. And so, when a thing is perceived to exist as predicted, it is true of the soul; for just as nature retains something separated, something not separated is also known. This is how the intellect perceives existence through the mediation of the "agent" <note>the active intellect</note>, from which it is called the "active intellect." According to this, all things are unchanged. Just as in every nature there is something that acts as **matter**, to act is to be an **active being** <note>original: "activum"</note> similar to the immutable. Thus, the whole likeness of the immutable arises from the reason of the intellect from without. It must be answered that the intellect in itself, like the soul, is something continuously unchanged; through reason, it understands itself to have its being from the soul. Thus can the intellect perceive what it is, just as superior beings do when they perceive the intellect to exist within a body.

<column-break/>

Moreover, this can be understood regarding the soul in terms of those things which are "ferial" <note>original: "ferialia," likely meaning ordinary, worldly, or non-sacred matters</note> where it perceives **separated substance**. For the intellect in itself, by the grace of God, communicates through itself. Just as it possesses a form through itself—as seen in the generation of things—it first communicates the existence of this form within them. Thus it perceives form as was said before. The reason of the intellect is found within them; the intellect is found in these rational things. Here they say that the "superior" is twofold, just as it is in "act" <note>A technical term meaning "actually occurring" or "fully realized."</note>. Here it is said that when the intellect perceives, it is the rational intellect—the "knowing"—just as reason is in the intellect. Here it is said that the aforementioned does not wish to be through knowing in the way a soul is a "degree." As they are in the intellect, existence is contested; so it is with the intellect of God when it perceives.

[The text continues with repetitive dialectical arguments regarding the intellect and soul]

The soul is understood thus: the intellect is not the form in the way that existence is in the intellect. The **separated active intellect** perceives presence in "act" as was said before; it perceives immutably in that presence. It is said not to be like a perceivable thing, but as it is true according to the "act" which is in the intellect. If anything is perceivable, it is perceived by reason through itself; the intellect perceives it as a degree of existence impressed upon it. Yet there is a degree that corresponds if the essence of the soul is in the intellect. The intellect perceives that the intellect exists according to its own act. Thus, the desire of the soul is the act: to respond that the intellect is itself the desire of the intellect. The rational intellect is within the rational intellect; thus it is said that the intellect is unchanged. It is found in the intellect and perceives its existence as such. It is said that the **immutable form of the intellect** is unchanged...

---

<column-break/>

As long as the soul is through itself the **form of the body**, it exists from the immaterial side. But as long as it is joined to the body, since it is a rational form, it must by nature be "through itself" <note>original: "per se," meaning independent or self-subsisting</note> and immutable. For as it is said, when they are a form, they are not of this [material] kind but must possess the intellect within them. As predicted, the soul must be independent and immutable—that is, the soul's "degree of existence" is desire, perceived as the active intellect in act. The active intellect must not have "communication" <note>In a philosophical sense, this means it does not mix with or get corrupted by the material things it acts upon.</note>. One must respond that the intellect in act is independent and immutable because it exists through reason. The rational intellect is also a **form** that must be immutable; the aforementioned reason is immutable in itself through the intellect. Thus it perceives existence in act; thus desire perceives that it is immutable.

[The manuscript repeats the formula regarding the intellect being "per se and immutable" several times for emphasis or as part of a formal logic exercise.]

...one must respond that the intellect in act is independent and immutable...

<column-break/>

And the **passions of the soul** <note>emotions or experiences</note> are directed toward this; when all things are explained here, they then knew the reason by which they could become perfect. The reason is that they must be "pre-written" <note>original: "prescripte," perhaps meaning innate or ordained</note> as existence is exercised and announced. This is well perceived from the desire for existence; nevertheless, the soul perceives something as if through itself by reason. It perceives it as being "through itself." Another point at present is that the intellect is a form according to "act." The **active intellect** is like a degree of existence; thus they are the form. Also, as it perceives, it is an immutable reason. The immutable reason is within the things of God; thus the degree of existence must have what was predicted. The aforementioned reason perceives according to act, just as it is the nature of reason to perceive what is in the intellect. Thus it is found that the intellect in act is independent and immutable. The rational intellect is also a form that must be immutable... it perceives existence in act; thus desire perceives that it is immutable.

<summary>This page presents a dense scholastic argument defining the soul as the "form of the body" while asserting that the active intellect remains immutable, independent, and participating in divine reason. It emphasizes that the soul's desire for knowledge is a reflection of its immaterial and unchanging essence.</summary>

<keywords>active intellect, soul, rational intellect, form of the body, immutability, scholastic philosophy, Aristotle, passions of the soul, divine reason</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the abstract discussion of the "active intellect" to a specific historical and moral application through the figure of Socrates. It contrasts the natural philosophy (physics) of the pre-Socratics with the ethical turn (morals) introduced by Socrates, ultimately linking human virtue to a divine light.</meta>

# Socrates

Socrates alone is the first of all philosophers to whom, as they say, pertain those things which belong to life and to morals. For before him, others spent more effort in investigating and searching out physical matters <note>original: "physicis rebus"; referring to natural philosophy or the study of the material world</note>. Indeed, Socrates was the first to transfer this entire study toward the cultivation of morals and life. He judged that this philosophy was the most useful for the whole republic. On the other hand, he judged the other kind of study—which was for inquiring into the heavens—to be either of no utility or a vain and destructive knowledge beyond human understanding. 

He was the primary author of this persuasion; and he is said, for that reason, to have taken philosophy down from the heavens and placed it in the city <note>A classic trope found in Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, describing Socrates' shift from cosmology to ethics</note>. And one would have hastened toward this opinion, had Socrates himself, persisting in his view, not refused to follow the ultimate cause of each thing. From this, it seems that the ultimate end and happiness <note>original: "felicitatem"</note> of man is to see the one and the same essence of God and our Lord; and he recognized this God to be the proper and perfect God. 

Whence, with him as the author and teacher, and with that light shining among us, we have cast off the darkness of these mortals. By the vision of the human mind, he knew God as perfect. By the mention of him, he is said to have recognized that the virtues were illuminated—those which we call the four: **Justice**, **Wisdom**, **Fortitude** <note>or Courage</note>, and ignorance <note>The text mentions "ignorantia" here, likely as the vice Socrates sought to cure, following his famous maxim that "virtue is knowledge."</note>.

<column-break/>

Socrates, therefore, as a philosopher in the proper sense, followed divine things in this way through the senses... through which, by the oracle of Apollo, he was held to be the wisest.

And the certainty of what it is through this is to measure nothing but this kind, and through something that is not from elsewhere, which holds the soul toward the cognition of the human mind... just as in the body of this thing... this mode must be perceived... and through this mode the mind does not perceive this perfection just as it has this perfection.

And since that essence must be perceived, our mind has this perfection through something, through the reason of the mind, and thus to have it through some reason, and since it is said to have it through the mention of the mind.

<meta>The previous page concluded a section on Socratic ethics and the "ultimate cause" of things. This page shifts abruptly back to natural philosophy and cosmology, specifically the arrangement of the celestial spheres and the positioning of the Moon relative to the planets and the zodiac.</meta>

#### Column 1 (Folio 136v)

<margin>1</margin>
We see that the **Moon** does not always maintain the same position relative to the **Sun**; rather, it turns itself toward other stars in such a way that it is seen to cover them, positioned beneath it. Indeed, if their appearance is more distant, we see then that the one which cuts off the sight of those same stars is the Moon. And thus, it is eventually revolved back to the sight of those same stars. We can be certain of this matter from those things demonstrated in **astronomy** <note>original: "astronomia"; referring to the mathematical study of the heavens</note>. From these demonstrations, it also appears that these are not "new" moons always being created, as some used to think, but rather the same moons are repeated through their certain movements at fixed times. Therefore, it is not believable that the Moon is revolved back to that same position in which we see the stars themselves unless it is a recurring cycle. Thus, it is clear that the body of the Moon is **below all other bodies**, just as some in the past have suspected. To those who observed these things, we have demonstrated that it is certain because the Moon is sometimes seen to pass under other stars, such as under **Mars** or **Saturn**, or under any other of them. Then, the sight of the Moon is seen to cause an **eclipse** of those stars. In this way, because it is placed as if "above" the other star from our perspective, the body of the Moon is believed to be **below** that star <note>In the medieval geocentric model, "below" means closer to the Earth, while "above" means further away toward the outer heavens</note>. Whenever the Moon is not only between our sight and the Sun, but also between our sight and a star, then that star is believed to be "under" the Moon. Thus, the body of the Moon is seen to be below the body of any star, and the body of the Moon is said to be below the Sun. By every reason, it appears that the body of the Moon is **closer to the Earth** than the body of the other stars; and thus, since the body of the Moon is below all bodies, the Moon is seen to eclipse the other stars.

Indeed, it appears from the movements of the stars that they are farther away from it. For even if we see some stars when the Moon, in its course, is seen to proceed under them—as was observed in ancient times in **Egypt and Syria**—we see it to be true through certain demonstrations and observations in astronomy. Thus, it is clear that the Moon is below all bodies, and so we have <unclear>demonstrated the movement of the moon through astronomy</unclear>.

<column-break/>

#### Column 2 (Folio 136v)

Whence it appears that those stars which have movement of their own relative to other stars are seen such that their movement is compared to another. Just as it appears through this—because the bodies of those stars then cover other stars—it appears that the body of the Moon is below all bodies, and this appears in this manner. And thus, it has been determined elsewhere in astronomy by this method: that the sight of the Moon is seen to sometimes eclipse those same stars. And so, in this manner, we see the Moon cover other stars in its course, and then the body of the Moon is seen "above" the other star <note>meaning it obscures it from view</note>, and thus the body of the Moon is believed to be below the other star. in others, that of nourishment, as in herbs
and grains. But in all there is
matter in which this power exists: just as
we see different plants born from the same earth,
and different fruits from the same seed;
but this is from a certain power
which is in them, which calls them to this
diversity. Just as again in animals
we see different acts and works;
and all these things tend toward one end:
namely, that life in them may be preserved
in its vigor, and again in others be
propagated. And thus let it be said of the generation
of herbs and trees.

### Chapter on the generation of each tree and the manner of each.

The universal power and force 
of grains is in the seed: for
again, as it is in others, so it is in this:
nature indeed is a force in them, and if
it is compared, it will be seen to be in the seed.
For just as concerning earth and water, so it is said
concerning seeds; and the substance
is thus nourished from them; and again they are procreated
from the figure within that, and in this
is something like the power of form. The fruits,
moreover, which are again from them, are nourished
from matter, just as in animals, which are
again nourished from bread and water and other things.
For from those things which plants nourish, and
by which they live, this nature of life appears:
for in them is the power of matter, and if
this were not present, plants would not live. It
is likewise with matter, that power may be in
these things: for also in animals, just as it is nourished
from the same materials, so also in plants: just as
power is in them and in the seeds,
so also in existing plants. For in
them too is a certain power, from which life
flourishes, and this is from the nature of seeds. And
it is also seen in trees: for some
are perpetually green, and this is of their nature;
and again some every year
put forth leaves and lose them again;
but this diversity is from the matter,
just as in animals: some live
a long time, and others die quickly.
And so let it be said of this. And this is of the
nature and power of animals, as if of
this power by which life is preserved in them.
It is also in plants, and their power
consists in nourishment and growth:
and such is the matter of plants.
For the power of the nutritive soul is in them,
and in all things is this power of the soul.
And as we see in animals different
acts and movements, so also in plants.
And again, we must speak of the modes of their
generation. And since life in them
consists of the nutritive and
augmentative power; and again in plants there are diverse
kinds of fruits; and this is of the nature
of the matter in them. And also we must speak
of the fruits, and how life again
arises from them. And then
concerning the seeds of plants, and again
concerning other things which are in them; and this
from diverse modes; and thus let us speak
of the generation of plants, and of their
modes, and how they are diverse among themselves.
For again they are diverse by the multitude and variety
of things; and diversity is seen to be
in those things which are diverse. And so let the
aforementioned description of them be, and let this be the full account of them.

<summary>This page explores the astrological influences of zodiacal signs and stars on material substances, using a highly formulaic and repetitive logical structure. It posits that specific celestial configurations (stars within or outside the zodiac) result in "equal" or "double" effects on different parts of an object's nature.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on celestial influences to a more physical, earthly exploration of plant biology. The text continues the Aristotelian tradition, likely from the work "On Plants" (De Plantis), discussing how the qualities of heat, humidity, and the "temperament" of the soil allow for the generation of different types of vegetation, especially in marine and river environments.</meta>

Something similar also happens in temperate earth: before all else, it is necessary that the earth possesses the humidity from which a thing is created, and likewise a measure of heat that governs that which has been created. In order for a thing to be preserved, it is further necessary that the earth be contained and clean <note>In this context, "clean" refers to soil that is free from extreme qualities or impurities that would disrupt the "temperament" or balance of the plant.</note> from every substance by which a thing might lose its middle temperament <term>temperamentum</term> <note>The "middle temperament" refers to the ideal Aristotelian balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. If this earth is well-warmed and temperate, it soon produces its own seed, and then plants such as grass and the like. This is seen in land that is in the middle of the seas where water is very sparse, and soon in that land which is situated toward temperance, and then land which is contained near the water of the seas. Soon it becomes like the land in certain marine islands, and soon that land gives birth to a plant from the neighboring earth. 

However, the plant which is in the sea is red and is neighbor to that which is born in the sea; this neighborliness exists through all things for those for whom it is proper to be in temperate earth. And just as there are certain ones in marine islands where, as we said, the plants are red and black, they also require fresh water to be contained within them. Just as there are certain plants in rivers, specifically those on the banks, their properties are soon varied in all things; just as those which are on the banks are found on the banks, those which are in the sea also have their own properties. Just as certain marine things and those which are in the seas, the earth indeed which is at the bottom of the waters does not produce anything except plants. This is because the earth at the bottom of the sea does not lack heat and humidity since the earth is near to them, but the water does not permit the wind to reach them. Where, however, the earth is dry and heat is excessive, soon in that land nothing is generated except red or black things, since their heat and humidity and dryness are like the color of the sea and the water in the sea.

<column-break/>

There is a diversion in places where the water is fresh, and there is earth which is not in the water but is born at the summit by the sea in those places where there is little proximity to rivers in the sea. Specifically in those places where there is a mixing of fresh and salt water on the shores of the seas, that water is soon called "sweet" <note>original: "dulcis"</note>. Similarly, there are many species of plants that are born in salt water, and there are some that live in salt water because a little bit of fresh water suffices for them. Some desire fresh water, and soon there is a mixing of those waters; then their variety in salt water is evident. Soon their variety and density, where the heat is advanced, varies through all things: both the location of the places and the waters that are in the sea, and the location of the places and the redness and variety through all things. 

Just as there are herbs in the sea that are red and black, and there are red ones in various red parts of the seas; they are varied in various places by their length. There are certain herbs, but they are not wood, and some which have much of the nature of wood, such as the red coral <term>emtora rubea</term> <note>The term "emtora rubea" likely refers to red coral, which ancient and medieval naturalists often classified as a "stony plant" or a marine growth with the nature of wood.</note>.

And the water in the sea is transformed just as the water in rivers; and their natures are various just as the earth’s. There are certain plants in rivers of many species, some of which are in rivers where the water is above the vicinity of the earth. These are from the land which is in the middle of the seas, as we said, because in the land in the middle of the seas there is little earth but much water in which there is much heat and humidity. Soon there are similarly those which live in salt and bitter water, because there is much salt water in them, and a little fresh water suffices for them—just like the herb that lives in places where there is dryness and variety through all things. And there are some that live in salt water, and there are those born in places where there are "seats" of waters <note>This likely refers to stagnant or settled pools of water.</note>; they are through all things just as we said regarding their own nature, like those that live in salt water. Because a little fresh water suffices for them, like the herb that lives in places where there is dryness and variety through all things, and there are some that live in salt water.

***

In plants, also, the roots of trees are similar to those which are in the earth. Some of them come from earth and water, such as those in the seas; some indeed from clean earth and the humidity of the earth, such as plants born in clean earth where there is heat and humidity. Some indeed are born in red earth because it is dry; some indeed are those born in their own earth, which are green, such as those born in springs and rivers in which the water above the vicinity of their earth has much of the nature of wood, such as red coral <term>emtora rubea</term>. 

As for plants born in the sea, such as heat and cold and dryness and humidity—of which one nature is water—the clean earth, if it has been tempered, and the heat, if it has been tempered, soon plants grow in the water. Just as the water which is in the sea, such as heat and cold and dryness and humidity—of which one nature is water—the clean earth, if it has been tempered, and the heat, if it has been tempered, soon plants grow in the water <note>The text here is highly repetitive, likely a result of the manuscript copying process where various definitions were merged.</note>. And certain species of plants are born in salt water, and there are some that live in salt water, for a little fresh water suffices for them, like the herb that lives in places where there is dryness and variety through all things. Just as there are herbs in the sea, red and black, and there are red ones in various red parts of the seas; they are varied in various places by their length. There are certain herbs, but they are not wood, and some which have much of the nature of wood, such as red coral <term>emtora rubea</term>, just like those born in a place where there is heat and humidity.

<column-break/>

Regarding their natures: many plants grow in waters and seas, and others in streams and rivers, especially in those that flow continuously. Others are "woods" <note>Lignous or woody plants.</note> that are in the waters, such as the willow <term>salix</term>, and those born in rivers and where the water is near to springs. <meta>The previous page discussed theological and philosophical inquiries into the nature of vision, perception, and the will, specifically how humans and angels "see" the truth. This page shifts toward natural philosophy, moving from spiritual perception to the physical composition of the world according to the four elements and the distinction between physics and astronomy. The catchword "secun" at the bottom of column 4 matches the first word of the subsequent section (secundum).</meta>

...through which they receive each other in turn by generation and corruption. For from this mixing of the four simple elements, bodies are formed, in which there is not an equal distribution of elements. Instead, one element predominates over another, and through this kind of joining of elements, they exist from diverse parts. For just as from the mixing of milk and honey nothing follows but a certain third thing <note>This refers to the Aristotelian concept of *mixtio*, where ingredients combine to form a new substance with its own properties.</note>, so it is said that just as there are four elements of the same nature, so there are four mixed bodies. But this is not true, for in these four elements nothing appears except a right angle; and in this way it is said to be a mixture: because just as mixed bodies are made of simple bodies, so elemented bodies are made from the parts of those elements. 

And if it is said that elements can be circular, the response is that a circle is not found except in circular motion; and this is evident in the motion of the heavens. By this reasoning, the four elements cannot exist as a circle, nor can circular motion occur through them, because the motion is circular; and this appears in the motion of the heaven and in the motion of simple bodies, and in elemented bodies, as is clear in the earth, because its motion is circular <note>The author is navigating medieval geocentric physics; while elements usually move in straight lines (up or down), he is debating the complexities of their "natural" movements.</note>. And by this distinction, it is said that mixed bodies exist in elements; and if their motion is circular, the elements should also be found in them, as appears in the motion of the earth, which is a circle. 

And according to this, circular motion is in the motion of the earth, as appears in the motion of the earth surrounding the water; and in this, the circular nature appears in the earth and in the water, as is clear in their motion around the earth. Furthermore, it is asked about circular motion simply in bodies. And if it is asked why circular motion is found in the earth as in the heaven, it is said that just as in the earth existence is circular, so its motion ought to be circular; and according to this, motion is said to be in the earth as in the heaven. And by this, it is clear that the circular motion of the four elements is "per se" <term>per se: intrinsically or by its own nature</term>; and according to this, their motion is circular just like the motion of the heavens. And so it is clear that mixed bodies are made of the four elements. But it is said that this is not a true mixture, because diversity does not yet seem to exist; but according to one mode, all things are one, because according to one mode, all bodies are one. But this does not seem to have a reason, because just as...

<column-break/>

...they would follow diverse essences. And since each thing is one, they also follow a multiplicity of essence, and therefore according to one form or another. And this is what he says: as is clear in animals and plants, because in them there is a diversity of form, in which there are diverse elements. The multitude or diversity of bodies and diversity according to substance is clear in those things made from mixed elements, through whose mixing follows a diversity of forms and their accidents. 

But against this, an objection is raised, namely a question about motion: whether motion is spoken of according to one mode in all things? And according to this, it would follow that there would be no diversity of motions. But this is not true, because we see that every thing is moved by its own proper motion, such as fire upward, water downward, and so on for the others. And by this, it is clear that there is not one motion in all, but there are diverse motions through the diversity of the nature of bodies. 

Furthermore, it is asked about those things found outside; and he says that there are certain bodies that behave according to the same mode in all bodies, as appears in shapes. And it is said that diverse shapes cannot be in the same elements; but just as there are diverse bodies, so there are diverse shapes. And it is said that the shapes of natural bodies are from their nature, as is clear in minerals, animals, and plants. And it is said that the shaping of bodies is from their nature, as appears in the shapes of the bodies of elements: just as fire is of a pyramidal shape <note>Medieval science, following Plato's *Timaeus*, often assigned geometric shapes to elements: fire was pyramidal or tetrahedral because its sharp points "cut" through the air.</note>, air is of a spherical shape, water is said to be of an oval shape, and earth is said to be of a quadrangular shape, and so on for others. And it is said that these shapes are not natural "per se" in the elements, but according to the mode of their motion; because just as motion is natural, so the shape that follows motion is natural. And therefore it is said that there are no diverse essences of shapes in the elements, except according to the diversity of their motions; and thus it is clear that mixed bodies have diverse shapes. 

But it is said that simple bodies do not have diverse shapes "per se," but according to the mode of the place where they are. And it is said that air has no shape except in the place where it is, and so for fire, and water, and earth. And by this, it is clear that elementary bodies have diverse shapes "per se," just as from the multitude of motion and the place where they are found; for according to this diversity, a diversity of essences also follows. And so it is clear that elemented bodies are diverse, according to the diversity of elements from which they are composed, and according to the diversity of motion and the place where they are found. And this is what he intended to conclude: namely, the diversity and composition of elements.

<column-break/>

...something moved is another thing; and more so in animals and plants, for as we see many and diverse shapes of animals and plants. Shapes also exist not only according to themselves, but also according to the diversity of places, and other things of this kind; because as is clear on the earth, certain animals are in water, and certain on land, and certain in the air, and so for the others, which have diverse shapes. It also follows that in water and earth and other elements, there is a certain matter that relates to diverse shapes and diverse motions. And it is said that this matter is not other than the nature of the elements, but it is the elementary nature itself, which receives diverse forms and diverse shapes according to the diversity of the mixing. 

And this is said concerning the mixing of the element: because mixing is nothing but the commingling of elementary forms and qualities according to a certain proportion. And therefore it is said: that the forms of mixtures are diverse according to the diversity of the proportion of elements. And it is also said: that shapes are diverse according to the diversity of the mixtures themselves, as is clear in animals and plants, which have diverse parts and members that do not have uniformity, as is the case in elements. And by this, it is clear: that in mixed bodies there is a composition of dissimilar parts, as in animals and plants, where the parts are diverse according to shape and power <term>virtus: power, capacity, or inherent quality</term>; and this is not in the elements, in which there is uniformity, as appears in water, in which any part is like any other in nature, power, and shape. 

And by this, it is clear: that mixed bodies are composed of diverse parts, and according to this, they are of diverse natures. But against this, an objection is raised concerning minerals, which seem to be uniform, such as gold, silver, and other things of this kind. To this, it is responded: that although in minerals there seems to be a certain uniformity in the parts, nevertheless minerals themselves are from mixed elements through a certain composition and proportion of nature. And it is also said: that although the parts of minerals seem to be similar, yet there is not such uniformity there as in simple elements, because mixing creates diversity; even though the parts are very small—which we do not perceive by the senses—yet also according to reason, there is said to be composition and diversity in them. 

And by this, it is clear: that all bodies that are below the sphere of the moon are composed of elements, such as minerals, animals, and plants; and each of these has its own proper nature and proper power, according to the proportion of elements that are in them, and according to the mode of their mixing. And so it is clear: that all mixed bodies are from the four elements according to diverse proportions; and according to this diversity, diverse forms, diverse shapes, and diverse powers follow, as appears in the diversity of natural bodies which are found in this lower world, which is the place of generation and corruption.

<column-break/>

Wherefore one thing is physical <note>original: "phisicum" — referring to natural philosophy or physics.</note> and another is astronomical. For the astronomer considers bodies according to their motions and according to their positions, such as the distance of the planets from the earth, and according to their motions through the signs <note>the zodiac</note>, and according to those things that follow from this motion, such as the aspects <note>geometrical relationships between planets</note> of the planets through which we see bodies changed in these lower regions. The physicist, however, considers bodies according to their nature and according to their composition from the elements, and according to their qualities; and according to this, there seems to be a difference between them. 

Furthermore, it is said that the physicist ought not to involve himself in those things that are outside his consideration: namely, the motion of the heaven, because this motion is not natural to lower bodies, but is celestial motion which has its own proper nature diverse from the elements. But against this, it is said: that although the motion of the heaven is proper to the heaven itself, yet that motion causes many generations and changes in these lower things, as is clear from the motion of the sun through the signs and through the aspects of the planets; and therefore the physicist ought to consider these causes of generations and corruptions, as Aristotle says in the book *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "in libro de generatione et corruptione."</note>. And so it is clear: that although the astronomer considers these according to one mode, yet the physicist ought to consider them according to another mode—insofar as they are the causes of these lower things. 

And it is also said: that these two do not exclude each other, but one helps the other. Because astronomy teaches us to know the position of the celestial bodies and their motions, and through this, the physicist can know the reason for the diversity of things that are generated in this world. And therefore it is said: that astronomy is necessary to the physicist, so that he can properly consider natural things. But this is not true: that the physicist ought to consider all those things that the astronomer considers, because the measurements of the heavens do not pertain to the physicist, nor the size of the planets, nor their distance from one another—unless insofar as these seem to have some causality in the generation and corruption of these bodies, as is clear concerning the power of the sun, and the moon, and the planets. And therefore it is said: that the physicist considers those things that pertain to natural causes, but not those things that pertain to pure mathematical quantities. 

And so the difference between these two is clear, and how one uses the other for his consideration. And by this, it is clear: that the end of this science is to know the nature of bodies, both simple and mixed, and their generation and corruption, and their properties, according to what we can comprehend by reason. And so ends this first part, in which it was determined concerning bodies in common, and their nature, and their motions, and the diversity of the elements.

The Almond is a tree and is bitter, which is so named in the Greek language <note>The Greek word *amygdalos* was often associated in medieval etymology with the bitterness of the wild variety.</note> because of the bitterness of its fruit. It is found especially in Judea or in similar warm places; then it possesses all its beauty in its flowers, but in its fruits, it produces blossoms before the leaves. Because of the maturity of its fruit, it precedes all other trees. However, the fruit is said to be bitter because of the soil: yet the fruit itself does not receive this in exchange. Instead, it makes the land fertile and enriches the earth where it grows. Moreover, compared to any other trees that bore fruit before, its fruit is more able and powerful to heal. Its bitter fruit, when placed in the earth, makes the tree bitter and oily, yet the fruit becomes sweet; just as with Wormwood,

which is bitter above the ground because of the earth, while that which remains deeper within the earth is mature and perishes as mature: just like this tree, by the liquid it emits. <meta>This page continues the philosophical and alchemical discourse from Folio 151. While the previous page focused on the "material soul" and the revival of the spirit, this page introduces the allegory of the Alchemical Tree and the Holy Mountain, blending botanical imagery with biblical citations to describe the creation of the Elixir.</meta>

<margin>
alkodarye <note>Likely an Arabic-derived term, possibly *al-kudariyya*, referring to a specific alchemical state of "turbidity" or "muddiness" before purification.</note>
</margin>

This tree, which brings forth healthy fruits from within itself, does not accomplish all things solely by its own power; rather, it renders all things <note>original: "rem," referring to the alchemical "Matter" or "Work"</note> in a state where they ought to be judged by their labor and art. There is, moreover, a similarity in the wood of the **elixir** <term>elixir: the sought-after "philosopher's stone" in liquid form, capable of healing or transmutation</term> to that which is taken from the Book of Revelation, chapter 22. There it says that the Tree of Life is that wood whose leaves are opened for the healing of the nations; and you may consider whatever fruit is contained within to be the same.

The tree itself grows on a mountain, of which the Scripture says: *I will ascend the mountain of Lebanon* <note>original: "mōtē libani," a reference to the Song of Solomon 4:8</note>; that is, into a certain high place of **wisdom**, whence it is said: *I will ascend and gather flowers.* Thus the Scripture speaks, and just as in its own time it never ceases to be fruitful, this same tree also possesses a grain. For as it is said: *unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth shall have died* <note>original: "grānū frumenti," referencing John 12:24</note>, and so forth. Thus, it is demonstrated from this one thing, and from there the fruit is gathered and sent back into the earth so that it may be multiplied. This is said to happen at that time. The tree of which we speak is of the nature of the **four elements** in practice, just as it is recognized through the art. For it is said that the aforementioned wood has a root: that is, the **materia** <term>materia: the raw, physical substance used at the start of the alchemical process</term> itself, from which the mountain of the elixir generates fruit from itself. It also has a trunk, which is **justice**, which stands founded upon the foundation—that is, upon the *materia* itself. This justice also makes the thing a true thing. Furthermore, it is said to have four branches, which are the diversities of the four elements produced from a single trunk. Thus says **Wisdom**: they proceed from one root and from one body. Whence it is also said in Scripture that we are all made from one body. And then it is said in Wisdom that this thing is fourfold, through the four branches which are the virtues of the four elements. And so it is situated on the mountain with its high branches reaching toward the heights in accordance with its virtue, etc.

<column-break/>

Know also that it holds the mountain and great places, and no enemy land should be made of the mountain. Whence, in the allegory: *I will ascend the mountain.* And through the mountain, the earth in which there are precious stones is said by comparison to be **minerals**; and all minerals are called stones. Of this, we have the final part of Genesis, where it is said: *and the Lord said to Moses: ascend the mountain of the Lord* <note>original: "ascende i mōtem dōnī," referencing Exodus 24:12</note>; namely, the mountain of the **elixir**. And from there, gather the fruit of life. Of this, Genesis says: *behold, the spouse of this thing of the elixir.* The same thing is then the thing of fruits. This mountain is said to be called the **Gift of God** <note>The scribe uses "dōnū dī," which could be read as "Donum Dei" (Gift of God) or "Dominum Dei" (Lord of God); "Gift of God" is a standard alchemical title for the Great Work.</note>. Since there are four spouses, so it is spoken of in the mountain of the Lord. And so says **Wisdom**: from whatever place you think the mountain grows, from that place you shall gather the fruit of the Matter. It is said to be of the earth, and the earth is the light of the Matter. The mountain is called the *materia*; for it is spoken of regarding the entire mountain, and thus then is the time for gathering the fruit. Know also that there are gifts, the branches of the Matter of the mountain, and certainly those are the fruits. Since no one rules the art and operation of the Matter, one must then know that there are diverse kinds of fruits. For it is said the mountains are stones, and stones are the fruit of the tree. Again, it is said that the countryside is the field; let this art rule. They are the gifts of the mountain just as they are the branches of the tree, and they are the gifts of the mountain: that is, the *materia*. For as it is said: God established this art in nature. For it existed before time, just as it is written. And again: *God created them*, in which he speaks of the *materia*. And certainly, from the end of time, he says again: let it have its operation and let it rule this Matter, as the Scripture says. And so the end is as it is said in the Wisdom of the mountain. This mountain is said to be called the **Gift of God**. The Matter of the mountain, the Matter, the Matter, the Matter, the Matter <note>original: "rēs... rēm rēm rēm rēm," a repetitive emphasis on the physical substance or "the thing" being worked upon</note>. It is said to be the fourfold gift of God; it gives the Matter, the Matter. Thus the Matter is spoken of, the Matter, the Matter, the Matter, the Matter. Whence, in the mountain of the Lord, it is so said: the Matter, the Matter of all things; the Matter, the Matter, the Matter, the Matter; the Matter, the Matter.

and it is evident through putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactionem"; in medieval science, the decay of matter was seen as a necessary stage for the release of its internal "virtue" or life force</note> and from this it is more clearly evident how it is with a herb and with other herbs which are discussed in this matter; it is better seen, and this is through that which is better to feast upon and to be made from it, and to perform many other works.

### First, it should be known according to the nature of the soul

First, it should be known according to the nature of the soul which is the "end" <note>the final purpose or goal</note> of herbs; namely, that the vegetative power <note>original: "vis vegetabilis"; the lowest level of the "soul" in Aristotelian biology, responsible for growth and nutrition</note> which is in them is the sensible end, and this occurs when a thing that is a herb by itself performs its work better because it exists <unclear>by itself</unclear>, as is evident in other things. And this is through what is said in the *Book of Herbs* <note>original: "libro de herbis"; likely referring to a generic herbal or perhaps the work of Dioscorides or Macer Floridus</note>: that herbs ought to be gathered with observance of the time in the proper manner, because their power <note>original: "virtus"</note> is then in its <unclear>vigor</unclear>, while on other days <unclear>which</unclear> then they are in debt <note>meaning they lack their full potency</note>, and then it is said to be gathered; and thus we ought to perceive the <unclear>difference</unclear> between herbs.

Therefore, since we must know about nature and about the herb, <unclear>if</unclear> you wish to know another science, it must be known that just as the herb is small, so too is nature small, which is like a single light, namely <unclear>of the soul itself</unclear>; and that light <unclear>proceeds</unclear> from the root of the soul just as the light of the sun goes to bodies. But because the herb is small and modest, the herb in its small body receives many qualities, specifically the power of the powers of nature, through which the herb is green, flowers, and produces fruit. And because, as it is said, nature does not fail in the <unclear>smallest things</unclear> <note>original: "natura non deficit in minimis"; a common medieval scientific maxim</note>, so it does not fail in a small herb, since it is like a <unclear>great</unclear> thing in its virtue. And this is evident through the fact that in a small herb the whole world <unclear>is seen</unclear>, because matter and form and the power of nature are there, which is the mover and maker for the whole world.

It must therefore be gathered according to what is in the *Book of the Virtues of Herbs*: that if you wish to have the power of the herb itself in full, it ought to be gathered when the herb is in its flowering, and then the herb is in its highest vigor and its virtue is then at its best; and this is evident in a small herb just as in a large one.

Therefore, it should be known that if you wish to know the nature of herbs, you must know the nature of those things which are in the earth, such as minerals, and the celestial bodies, because all these operate in herbs, giving them virtue and vigor. This is evident through what is said in the *Book of Vegetables* <note>original: "libro de vegetalibus"; likely referring to the pseudo-Aristotelian *De Plantis*</note>: that a herb receives power from heaven and from the earth and from the elements, and therefore there is in them a power for healing man or for performing other wonders which are seen in them.

and this is evident in the *Book on the Nature of Things* <note>original: "libro de natura rerum"; possibly the encyclopedia by Thomas of Cantimpré or Bede</note> where it is said that nature is like a certain power implanted in things from which all bodies proceed to their end, and this is most greatly seen in herbs which, as some say, have a hidden <note>original: "occultam"</note> power for working which is not seen except through experience <note>original: "experientiam"; here meaning practical observation or testing</note>.

And this is also evident through what we see in herbs: that certain herbs are hot, and certain cold, and certain dry, and certain moist <note>these are the four primary qualities of the humoral system</note>. And this is according to whether some element dominates in them, or some quality which is in them, as is evident through what is said in the *Book of Herbs*, where the virtues of individual herbs are enumerated, along with those things which are necessary for knowing their nature and their qualities.

Therefore, whoever wishes to know the nature of herbs must be diligent and studious in inspecting their natures and in testing their virtues, just as the wise men did who wrote about herbs, as is evident in their books.

<column-break/>

Which is because whatever has more of the "soul," to that extent it is more perfect and acts better, and this is evident in us. Whence the soul, which is the fountain of life and the end of the herb, is the soul which is in the root; and with its vegetative power, and from that proceeds the vegetative power and flows into the herbs, just as where there is water which proceeds from a fountain and flows through the whole earth and gives vigor and power to things that are in the earth; so also the vegetative soul which is in the root of the herb flows through the whole herb and gives it vigor and power for growing, flowering, and for producing fruit.

Therefore, when we wish to have the power of the herb, we ought to gather it in its vigor, and then the herb is at its best and its power is then at its greatest, as is evident in herbs that are gathered in summer, because then their vigor is at its peak and their power is then stronger for working.

According to this, we also see in other things that are in the earth, such as animals and other bodies which receive vigor and power from nature, as is evident in the *Book of Animals* <note>original: "libro de animalibus"; Aristotle's major work on zoology</note> where it is said that animals have their vigor according to how they receive power from nature and from the elements; and thus we see in all things that live and grow on the earth.

# The Recognition of Species

## Characteristics and Medical Uses

<page-num>178v</page-num>

The well-known species is quite long, and it is customary for it to be recognized and known in many ways, wherever it may come from. It is used in medicines and has properties from the heavens <note>likely referring to "facultatibus que sursum sunt," implying celestial or astrological influence on the plant's potency</note>; its appearance is as follows. It grows here and there in damp and wooded places, especially in areas that have been cleared, because it puts forth long red flowers and small roses. It ripens red-colored ruptures <note>original: "rupturas rubei colore"; likely referring to its use in healing sores or inflammatory breaks in the skin</note>. One species is red; its water is effective for constrictions and mouth-sores <note>original: "rincturas," a variant of ricturas, referring to fissures or openings in the skin or mouth</note>. Those signs are seen in what is called field lavender <note>original: "aspicus arvensis"</note>: and it is spat out by cattle. It dries the gut, but its whole root is for the fingernails; for one should seek this herb in whatever places it grows before it flowers, so that its best benefits may remain. It is a dry herb which the ancients loved and which those who are most cautious used, because it is harsh and rough as it spreads upon itself. In Rome, it is found both in gardens and in the woods. It has properties for weak teeth and heals differences in breathing <note>original: "adspitationis," likely a corruption of "aspirationis"</note> in the gums. If there should be any pustules in the belly, the water of this herb is effective. Also, its juice can cause paleness in that part [of the body] according to many readings. For this reason, the nature of the herb itself is for burning-heat and is used in a multitude of works. All its material is of a golden color, used for internal bedding and dried. In a wound, this herb is very soothing; its thinness is most effective for wounds when the herb is in water. This herb with vinegar restrains blood from the belly if any should flow from it; without which, one of these things will be profitable, such as the juice of the one who has ground it, and this will be a single powder.

<margin>Horse-hoof <note>original: "Ungula Caball."; common name for Tussilago farfara or Coltsfoot</note></margin>
Let it be without a mother <note>likely "sine matre," an idiomatic or technical term for a self-seeding or wild plant</note> for those who have the plant which is also called <term>nightshade</term> <note>original: "trychnos"</note> and it is able to dry. For mouth-sores in [various] parts: there are also those for hills and fertility and <term>homeopathy</term> <note>original: "alleopatia," though used here in a pre-modern sense of "like curing like" or "opposing cures"</note>. And when this has been given on an island, it loves what is soaked in water and honey; its juice is boiled again and made from a storehouse <note>original: "apothesu"</note> and for the tooth for that person, even without any other [remedy].
[Symbol] A "hot" herb is the herb which poisons every herb of the hare, and the hare's path is—as it is said of two of these in an herb, and it is called the hare's [herb] too much, and it is bitter. It can be tempered in moisture. And it is called a "fish in the herb," this herb of the hare, just as this and that is called; and it is also the acid herb of the hare <note>likely Wood Sorrel</note>.

---

Hare’s Herb is <term>Coltsfoot</term> <note>original: "Tussilago"; literally "cough-chaser"</note>: because the hare eats it willingly. Another is "Hare’s Face," a small "Hare’s Foot" commonly called *cacioloporo* from its leaves shaped like a hare's foot: or because it is made by those of the hare, as some wish. Another is the true <term>Hare’s Foot</term> <note>original: "Lagopus"</note>, with leaves very similar to a hare’s foot: it is often called <term>Wood Avens</term> <note>original: "gariophillata"</note>. The whole of its root smells like cloves.

<column-break/>

[Known] by the name Wood Avens. It is found in valleys and in places where it mostly grows over oaks. It is hot and dry, and its utility is proven with honeyed herbs.
Furthermore, there is a small herb of the sun growing in high places, called by two figures, and it is both hot and one is called the aquatic herb. It puts forth long red flowers and roses: its shape is hot. Some seek this so they may be cured in water, and from its juice this herb is effective for <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagram"</note> without any doubt.
Likewise, there is an herb as they read and seek; they are harsh and long, and in the part where there are fissures, the leaves are small like a bed, and its flower is red and it puts forth its rustic flower. It is red, however, and similarly produces fruit in those places. While the previous page debated whether plants possess a soul or sensation, this page shifts toward the physical composition of plants—specifically the role of the "pith," the "clothing" (bark), and the nature of seeds and fruit.</meta>

### Folio 202r

**Column 1**

It follows, moreover, concerning all kinds of trees: something indeed about the **composition** of the tree. But this is to be done where it will be seen, just as it is said regarding this matter. For when it is both mixed and spoken of, the vital part will be resumed; and since plants have less "flesh" <note>In medieval botanical analogies, "flesh" refers to the soft pulp of a plant, contrasted with the "bone" of the wood.</note>, there are thus kinds—both [animals that] bray and all the kinds of which were spoken in the preceding remarks. 

But here truly, let [life] be and live in every part of plants. However, he wishes to speak of another thing, namely this: although truly both the **pith** <term>pith</term> <note>original: "medulla"; the central, spongy tissue in a stem or branch, often compared to animal bone marrow.</note> and all the sides are essentially necessary to plants especially—even if it is so in truth for other plants as well—which we wish to call trees. In the treatise concerning these, he says that life is in some way "clothed" <note>The author uses "uestiri" (to be clothed) to describe how the vital essence is covered by the bark and wood.</note>. 

There is a property of the pith belonging to the tree and a property belonging to another plant. And then, and in another way, it is used properly. And in those things which are said in this place, we wish it to all turn so much toward that. And in a certain way, it is said of these things regarding plants which are named from their **matter**. And thus, as if distinguishing the matter, he mentions the **sap** <note>original: "sapia"; the vital fluid of the plant.</note>. 

And some things seem to pertain to those whose nature is of the root and the shoot. But it is another thing that the roots of plants have. And we wish to see where it truly has [its place]; that is, in place of the pith, the wood is said to be "clothed." Another thing is said of the "clothing" in the tree. But although it is as in plants which are above—that is, what is between the "clothing" and what is called the "vital part"—namely this: all things are made from the **four elements** <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>. 

As is written above, whoever speaks of those things which breathe, it is said truly to be from water and earth, and indeed from the ancients just as above. It is to be said that in these things—the elements in these are called "innocuous" <note>likely meaning "passive" or "non-sentient" in this context.</note> more than in plants. It is clear that just as they wish to be generated, so it happens. And he wished this just as plants do. But it happens near the nature of other plants which, when he wished, are of themselves. 

Thus it is said, from which they truly flee from becoming. And he wished life to be present at whatever time. But this, just as in the ancients, is life—the thing which he says clearly signifies this. Unless it was then... trees by their inclination, and it is said that either **leaves** or **roots** are spoken of in these plants, and the **fruit**. Although more from where it is made—the "power of the fruit" is spoken of concerning these. Some are from the fruits of the four kinds. When he says "more from where," just as plants generate by the likeness of the... it is what he says: just as the plant brought forth according to its **species**, and it attained the generation of plants, and similar things were generated.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

In some plants, however, fruit is not found, but the plant has these properties in itself. And of these it is soon spoken; and these are the things said in this place concerning fruits and foliage. Yet other things are said in other places, just as here it is spoken of in the foliage, and as in others in which they are not spoken of, but it can happen. As in another place, in its own time, it does not perish. 

In those where this fruit is not found, it nevertheless has what is said in some to be these properties. But in others, truly, in the **seed** (which is the fruit), it has its own fruits. And yet, in the seed of others which nature did not have, something is found—as in **pine trees**. And there is found a specific pith which is hidden away, just as in nuts. 

And in others, just as in the seed, as in nuts, it is not called "pith" (medulla) although it effectively *is* pith; rather, it is called "seed" because it is closer to **perfection** <note>original: "perfectioni"; in the Aristotelian sense, the final, fully-realized purpose or "end" of the plant's growth.</note>. And truly, it does not take the place of the pith although it is in the seed. And they are properly called "fruit" in truth, just as it can happen in time. And truly soon, just as in the seed, something is found which is called pith. 

Truly, it is near to being a property; it is not more properly called so in truth, although it is near to perfection. And they are found as pines, and just as it can happen in nuts. And yet they have something in truth which is called pith in the interior part. Yet another thing is said, as it has a property in truth, and because something of the property is found which is called "smoothness" in other parts. And it has the property of pith, which is closer to perfection. 

And truly, just as something is found which is called pith in the interior parts, they are properly called so. And truly in these things which are spoken of, it takes the place of pith, although strictly speaking it does not have the property of pith. And these are the things said in this place about fruits and leaves. In some, however, pith is soon found; in others, it is found in the seed. 

And yet they do not truly have this property. For just as pith in a part does not have this property as it does in the seed, some of the pith is as a **perfect fruit** in truth, which does not have this property called "pith" in the seed—as in pines and others. And they are properly called "perfect fruit" in truth, but in others it is not found, as it is said in some parts that it takes the place of pith in the perfect seed. And in others truly this pith of the fruit is not found, which can happen in truth.

Namely, that others have life, which are forms of **perfection**; they have life as can happen in truth. It seems that it has in itself infinite things; it has life, and truly the property belongs to some part, which are found in themselves, just as they have **vital parts** in themselves.

The author uses Aristotelian logic to categorize different reproductive structures, such as those in pine trees and nuts, based on their level of biological "perfection."</summary>

There are some fruits that consist of flesh, or have only a certain likeness to flesh, such as in the small flowers of the legumes which they call <term>beans</term> <note>original: "fauas"</note>.
