Some have flesh, such as <term>peaches</term> <note>original: "mala persica"</note>, <term>pears</term> <note>original: "pira"</note>, <term>apples</term> <note>original: "mala"</note>, and <term>citrons</term> <note>original: "citria"</note>, and others which are like pears or apples. Some have "bones" <note>In this context, "bones" refers to the hard pits or stones inside fruit.</note> such as the <term>olive</term> <note>original: "oliva"</note> and <term>dates</term> <note>original: "dactili"</note>, and others which are like <term>nuts</term> <note>original: "nuces"</note>, <term>chestnuts</term> <note>original: "castaneæ"</note>, and <term>almonds</term> <note>original: "amygdala"</note>. There are some whose shell is on the outside and the hard part is inside, such as nuts and almonds; and there are some whose fruit is entirely made of flesh. There remain those things which were said from the aforementioned, namely, in the bodies and vital powers <note>original: "virtutibus"</note> of plants according to those causes by which one recognizes the diversities of trees and their generation from seeds; and this in the distinction of herbs and fruits from those things which Aristotle narrated in his books on nature and *On the Generation of Animals* <note>Aristotle’s "De Generatione Animalium"</note>. And in this, we have determined what ought to be determined from the ancient writings, and in many things more than these, since they explained them better so that we might have a declaration of these matters and what their causes were: for the ancients narrated little concerning them and not fully, as it seems; and for this reason, we have written this book so that the reasons might be given concerning those things which were not fully said, as will be clear in the following; and we wish that it may come by favor and let there be lacking that which favors coming; and concerning those things which are through the windows and are retained; and concerning those things which are at a distant voice; and concerning those things which are substance and concerning the power of some form; and power and power and what their things may be, and what may be from them in every generation and in certain of their generations, from which things they come and how things are born from which they are made and found, which are in others; and concerning the locations in which plants are produced with their names; and concerning the generations of a thing known with certainty in locations, and where certain fruits are held; and from those which are grainy; and concerning the resolutions of woods; and also concerning these fruits and concerning the diversity of all fruits which happen naturally, whether they might lead or lead little; and they are deservedly required according to the diversity of the location and diversity; and since things arrive from which plants and branches and fruit and leaves are made; and all things which are born upon the earth which are certain things from which both branches and fruit and branches are made.

The fourth book on plants ends <note>original: "Explicit quartus liber de plantis"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the botanical and philosophical inquiry into the nature of plants, moving from the practicalities of planting discussed on the previous page to a theoretical analysis of plant "perfection" and the "vegetative soul" as described by classical authorities.</meta>

For just as nature generates things in a certain proportion according to their use, even though among them some plants may appear superfluous—as if they lacked perfection <note>original: "pfectio"; in this context, it refers to a thing reaching its full natural development or purpose</note> or were not intended for the purpose for which they came to be—it is still said they are produced by nature. This is evident in things that are rare and not common, which are said to be full of "exhalation." Thus, within these same plants, there is a perfection according to their specific nature. To increase their perfection, however, seems to be a part of their overall development, since they are rooted in the earth and from them comes the food by which things are made fit. The grain is that which proceeds and produces others of its kind through generation; and this is perfectly described in the books *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "de cęlo et mūdo"; a reference to Aristotle's cosmological treatise</note>.

Another point concerns the variety seen in plants due to a certain diverse nature that arises in some of them, which distinguishes and nourishes their kind. Because of this, there is something of the power <term>power|virtute; the inherent biological or "soulish" capacity of a living thing</term> found in rare plants, as is said of gum and the "parts of the earth" that come from the very matter of those plants. From these, something equal emerges. There are also certain plants that come from the same parts when the parts of the earth are poorly formed; in these, the vegetative power <term>vegetative power|virtus vegetativa; the lowest level of the soul in Aristotelian philosophy, responsible for growth and nutrition</term> is divided, although it strives for the perfection of living within itself. This produces a plant from the nutrient. In the chapter concerning perfection and generation, it is discussed how plants are generated, as **Plato** says in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the universe and the nature of physical bodies</note>. He says that this plant has within itself a certain rational principle <note>original: "rātionē rōnalē"</note>, claiming this arises from the distinction within this rational power.

Just as in them there is a power found in other perfected things, regarding this genus of things, they speak of the "perfect man." It is said of them that, due to their magnitude and growth, some call them "melancholic." Some say that the rational part, while it possesses a "feminine" quality, is nourished by such a reason through motion, so that a sensitive power <term>sensitive power|the capacity for sensation and movement, which distinguishes animals from plants</term> cannot be generated from them. This is called by them the "sensitive part," which plants lack. Hence, **Aristotle** says that plants are like animals in that they do not have what is said of plants in that same function—namely, that they lack perfection and movement, except for the movement of generation. For plants to be perfectly generated with sensitivity and other traits that come through the sensitive power is a different matter. But since generation then appears to be rational, and life is as life is, it appears that those of good generation possess a perfect reason.

<column-break/>

To this end, however, so that it may reach its goal, the plant extracts substance <term>substance|substantia; the underlying material or essence of the plant</term> from things. Plants are by no means nourished nor increased if their substance is too small and is resolved, or if the rooting is external. Regarding this volume, it is said that from these things mentioned, there is finally a "nod" of reason from plant to plant. They are received like food, and therefore the reason for them is to be perceived; for in them, there is no reason regarding generation, but rather regarding power. In these things, it is said that there is a perfection of the power of reason and production.

In these, there is no account of generation regarding perfection such that there is movement (as is said of rational perfection). However, it is also said that another kind of nature returns to this reason. He says that, from this perspective, things like gum and the "milk" <note>original: "lac"; likely referring to sap, latex, or resin</note> seen in plants belong here. When this "milk" is distinguished within the plant, such a generation nourishes it. This nature of reason and perfection comes from the earth. By nature, things have what they do not have by perfect reason; thus, they are of the plant itself. On one hand, there is no perfection of the thing as a plant unless it is generated from the nutritive and productive power. Thus, kinds of plants are by reason, as is said of the generation of this according to perfect reason.

Furthermore, they have this reason within themselves—namely, the power of generating—so that it belongs to the nature of natural perfection. In this way, they are "rational" in their own way. In them, there is no perfection through themselves as plants; it was a great matter that a tree should exist by the reason of its consumption in the generation of plants. From this, it follows that they have a power of generation from which generation is perfected. They possess a certain perfected state, which they do not have through this [external] view. They see the perfection which belongs to reason. They have this reason beyond both generation and growth. Then, in plants, it is seen through this that they are not [merely] "true," but it is seen that this belongs to the nutritive, generative, and productive power. For those which are in truth are seen to possess this nutritive and productive power by reason. They are seen at the end of generation to be within the nature of things. And the generation that is seen exists by reason of those things which are generated, as is said by <unclear>the author</unclear>.

It explores how plants achieve a form of "perfection" through growth, generation, and the production of substances like sap and resin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the underlying "spirit" of natural things. While the previous page focused on the vegetative spirit in plants and its circulation, this section shifts to a philosophical defense of teleology—the idea that nature acts with a specific purpose (an "end"). It uses Aristotelian concepts to explain why elements move as they do and why biological structures, like teeth and roots, take their specific forms.</meta>

<column-break/>

...otherwise the process would go on to infinity. It is established, therefore, that the end of that which must be made of itself is its general form. For this reason, the earth seeks the lowest places, because such a form underlies it, by which it reaches those places; just as gravity is called the "form" that carries it there. This is that "natural appetite" <note>This refers to the inherent tendency of an object to move toward its natural place, a core concept in Aristotelian physics.</note> of which the <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: physici</note> speak with great focus in the first book. So also the elements in turn give way to those proportionate compounds, according to the matter within them, so that through them the "end" may be achieved. To become more substantial, they reach toward those differences belonging to things whose nature is finite—such as certain actions. Among these, there is something that serves as a spirit, and because of this, it is asked whether that which is the "end" is the same as that which is the "spirit," since it is certain that things are made for this definite purpose.

In this same way, rare and dense things, and other physical phenomena, are made for a purpose—just as hands [serve] for fish <note>likely referring to fins as the aquatic equivalent of hands</note> to propel them, and teeth [are for chewing]. Again, the ear has this purpose: for capturing sounds and the like. Again, the tongue is an instrument for food and for speaking, and likewise for any other parts. But one must not merely think they happen by chance; they must be seen as being made for an end. Although rare and dense qualities exist in growth and generation, they do not arise in that part of the plant by accident; for instance, a root is in the earth because such is the nature of a radical consistency intended for nourishment. It does not exist for any other reason once these things are revealed. Thus they have said that nature is the way these things happen—that plants are generated this way—and one must suspect that they are made for an end. Because of a certain stability, that which is produced for a reason finds its "end" in the very nature that is carried toward that purpose.

<column-break/>

In the front part of the head, however, which is called the forehead, there is that which is not far off, and a <unclear>greave</unclear> <note>original: ocrea. This may refer to a protective structure or a specific anatomical feature likened to a piece of armor.</note>.

<margin>accidents</margin>
Here, however, someone might wonder whether it was necessary for every finished thing to be made from its own <term>matter</term> <note>materia: the physical substance from which something is composed.</note> or not. For matter is rather the thing for whose sake the rest have to be made, as Aristotle says, just as we see in the construction of buildings. Let us say, therefore, regarding those things made by the craftsmanship of nature: whatever the mode of that thing appears to be, if that thing is to be produced, then its "whatness" <note>quidditas: the essence or "what-it-is" of a thing.</note> will be of such a kind. And in the process of becoming, those things which intervene are necessary. For the things from which it is made are necessary; if the thing is to exist, it is necessary that something be within it, and the remaining essence is for the sake of completion. Whether it be a seat or whatever the soul desires, it is thus multiplied in the matter, just as must happen in the appetite—

<margin>Matter of the end</margin>
—for if a thing ought to be made for a purpose, it is necessary that such and such matter exists. Just as a <term>saw</term> <note>original: serra</note> of its kind must be made, it cannot be made if the matter is not present. To remain a saw and to be made as a saw, it does not appear as such unless it is made from iron (or something else within the iron), or from the refined matter of the saw. The "end" is the saw itself, which must be made because, as he [Aristotle] says, things are made by nature.

<margin>The soul is the [form]</margin>
Because things are as they are, matter is necessary—not only for the end but for what they are. Unless the thing were of such a kind, it would not be made, because it possesses nothing in itself except that nature. For plants would not become earthy unless they were made of such matter. But again,

<margin>Nature generates plants toward an end, namely for nourishment: roots: teeth: etc. <unclear>to be made for a task</unclear></margin>
for a thing to exist is not only to be made of such matter, but insofar as it ought to be made for a specific end. Thus, in the case of saws, as was said: if it is to be a saw, it is necessary for iron to be that from which it is made. But it is not a saw simply because it is iron; rather, because it is a saw, it must be made of such things so that it may be of that kind. And so it is in other things, just as in nature: in the parts of an animal, if it is to be such an animal, it is necessary to have such parts, like teeth; and so in all other things. But whether nature is the "end" or the "matter" is clear from what was said above: it is the "end." For that for the sake of which a thing must be made is called the "final cause." Just as if someone builds a house, he is said to build it for the sake of a dwelling, not for the sake of the stones. Thus nature makes something not for the sake of the matter, but for the sake of the end, which is the "form"—and this is the cause. For it is the "end" that is desired, not the matter.

<summary>This page discusses the Aristotelian concept of teleology, arguing that nature acts with purpose ("the end") rather than by random chance. It explains that while matter (like iron for a saw or stones for a house) is necessary, the true cause of a thing is its intended function and form.</summary>
<keywords>teleology, Aristotle, matter and form, final cause, natural appetite, anatomy, vegetative nature, physics</keywords>

The **Cypress** and many shrubs and jointed plants <note>original: *geniculæ* — referring to plants with "knees" or nodes like grasses or reeds</note> do not have this [pith] at all. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the elemental composition of plants, specifically how the balance of fire, water, air, and earth determines a plant's physical substance, taste, and medicinal "virtue." It follows the previous page's discussion on the role of pith and roots in plant development.</meta>

From this, it is clearly seen that some expectation arises from a certain **form**, yet it is no less mixed in its substance—unless it were taken as a whole. Then again, from this proximity, there remained... unless it passes away in a warm heat, and from that which remains, something is found. In this, it seems that there are **four [elements]** in one: fire, and this also has water and moist air, in which it is seen to be strong. And it shall be and is turned in some manner... out of plants, after the middle part is dried out, more remains from the water, and some from earth; and earth and air are present. However, that which has more from **fire** is corrupted by its own abundance <note>original: *felicitate* — literally "happiness" or "fruitfulness," but in this context referring to an over-abundance or over-ripeness that leads to decay</note>. 

Furthermore, from that part of the restoration which occurs in the plant’s **savor** <note>original: *sapientem* — can mean "wisdom" or "savor/taste"; in medieval botany, the taste of a plant indicated its internal elemental logic</note>, if it were to happen: it will be as it can be; that is, in many words <note>original: *sexcentis uerbis* — a Latin idiom meaning "infinitely many" or "countless words"</note>. And if it shall be, it is turned just as the nature of time was, so also are those things which are accustomed to happen either from the day, unless it should wish to be beneath a single affinity. From the forms, it appears moist when it is near water; therefore, every part of the plant, if it be as it is said of that part, and if it willed to be generated or near to that which is called "to become." And when it is doubled, it appears if it is said to be from one thing: from the winds, or another is brought forth... and it is seen... this ought to partake of the **nature of fire**. 

It is said, if the generation of the plant occurs in cold water, these things are agreeable, and to this, all things may taste of the moisture, by which the plant itself is "wise" <gloss>savorous</gloss>. Because the plant cannot naturally nourish or have heat for the same cause, just as it prevents the fruit of such plants from being formed from water—those which are of this nature. As it is said, where the **natural heat** does not endure until desiccation, and that water is swallowed up by the flowing matter, it is seen to live. They stand in the way of the power of heat; and there are sweet powers, but the power is not of the mind's water <note>The text here becomes highly abstract, likely discussing the "anima vegetabilis" or vegetable soul</note>. If afterward the plant is seen and remains, the parts are held back in turn (in the Greek manner), it was in the water, yet it is seen to be of the plant in both parts. Fire, indeed, for that time, speaks within the boundaries; but to be made indeed seems the boundary...

<column-break/>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of plants, moving from their elemental composition to their growth patterns and the internal "soul" or vital force that governs them. It compares plant anatomy—such as bark, pith, and veins—to the limbs and organs of animals.</meta>

Sometimes these are in the fruit, as in **citrons**, **chestnuts**, **mistletoe**, **figs**, and similar plants. Usually, the fruit appears after the leaves, as nature intends; however, sometimes it appears even before the leaves, as in the **almond tree**, certain types of **laurel**, and in **apple trees**. In these, the "hairs" <note>original: *pulli cappillarum* — likely referring to fine buds or the filamentous parts of blossoms</note> are seen before the leaves, and the leaves follow afterward. 

In stalks and those things born from seeds, the leaves precede the sprout. In woody plants, there are seen in them shoots <note>original: *blasti* — a Greek-derived term for new growth or buds</note>, branches, twigs, leaves, flowers, fruit, and those parts that emerge such as bark and pith <note>original: *medullae* — literally "marrow," referring to the soft central tissue of a stem</note>. All such things are seen; the plant also seems to have a "heart," and the fruit is like a heart. For there is a **power** <note>original: *uis*</note> in plants which belongs to nature and which acts: there are natural things, and a **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note>, and **virtues**, just as in animals. 

Therefore, the plant appears as a living being <note>original: *animal* — here meaning any "animated" or living entity</note> with the power to live. The fruit and the things born from them—such as stalks, twigs, or branches—burst forth from a single nature. Just as one thing has leaves, so too another has branches. Branches grow above the earth, along with twigs, shoots, and boughs, but the **root** is below, descending into the ground. 

Thus, we say there is a similarity between this nature and that of an animal. Among the members of an animal are those belonging to nature and lying within, such as **veins**, the **physical constitution** <note>original: *phisnomia* — a corruption of "physiognomy," referring to the bodily structure</note>, and **arteries**, which are very similar to each other. In other things, there appear to be, in like manner, wood, bark, twining parts, and leaves or branches. Just as in animals, these parts in plants are like spheres and are universal. 

But the branches and shoots, including those from the roots, are not called "parts" in relation to the body, but in relation to the **species**. Four properties appear in them, like four limbs: wood, branches, twigs, and leaves, along with their sprout. Branches are in the wood, so all these are within them, as are the small twigs found in shrubs and the small branches, as is seen, in their tree. The leaves are also branches and are born from them. These four parts are nearly universal in every tree. Branches are in the wood and act as the material from which the fruit and seeds of the plants are born. For those...

<column-break/>

...vitality is seen in them just as in animals: there is **virtue** and a **soul**, which is called the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*</note> formed within the plant. Indeed, there is a virtue like that in a seed, and a **moisture** <note>original: *humor*</note> like that in the loins, which acts and creates. Thus, its nature appears to be just as the nature of humans is, and it seems to itself to be worthy and close to it. 

These parts are enfolded, and within them is the spirit, a specific part present in all members. Therefore, it seems the "sense" is warm, like a power flowing through them. So it is in all plants and herbs: moisture and power exist, and the soul is in them, but it is the same thing enfolded within. That which is in them comes from the spirit and from many things enfolded. 

There is a power that removes what is pure and retains what is purified within them. There is also spirit in them, and virtue, and a warm fire and virtue, which is in them just like a soul. The spirit is in them like a power. But this is perfected in them: the soul that is in them, the heat that is in them, the soul that is in them, and the power that is in them—which is called **force** <note>original: *uis*</note>. 

It is said that there is no power there, according to those wise men who speak of the "way of plants" and the virtues within them—such as those in wood—and they ask if it is present. They say it cannot be, and that no "virtue" exists in them. Yet, it is called virtue, and nature, and it is called a "plant"—that is, something that cannot live without **heat** (being warm) nor without **moisture** (being humid). 

Thus, some say that because a soul and power are within them, and virtue, they absolutely cannot live without these things. But they do not have another "intention" <note>original: *intentio* — meaning conscious will or mental focus</note>. Though some say they have souls and the virtue of a human, nothing is in them except spirit, and not intention. 

However, some say that certain parts in them seem to want to come forth and act like animals. But the truth is, there is virtue, yet there is no spirit in them that follows the "way of animals." Because the soul that is in them is not a "power" in that animal sense, yet it is in them. There are souls in them—or perhaps there are no spirits and souls and natures and spirits and souls. For it is said that in them...

<meta>This page continues the botanical and medical exploration of plant life, shifting from the elemental and "demonic" influences discussed previously to a more taxonomic and dietetic analysis of fruits. It draws heavily on the authorities of Aristotle, Hermes Trismegistus, and Galen to classify fruits by their physical structure and their humoral effects on the human body.</meta>

<margin>something concerning fruits etc.</margin>

And he speaks generally of every fruit that does not have a pithy heart, such as medlars <note>original: *sedamina*; likely referring to the medlar or a similar stony fruit</note> and dates, which are called in Arabic *al-thimar* <note>original: *allethemar*; from the Arabic "al-thimar," meaning "the fruits"</note> etc., where **Aristotle** says:

> The fruits of trees are either pithy and without a limit <note>original: *sine fine*; perhaps referring to fruits without a hard stone or boundary</note> like dates and medlars—where the part outside the tree is sweet and nourishing—and those like nuts and acorns which are red [internally], and then according to their fruit, then according to their flavor, and so on.

And the aforementioned dates and fruits are found in islands—that is, dates that have a nut <note>original: *nucem*; referring to the stone or pit</note> in their heart, and dates that are without it, and dates that are in the middle, etc. And fruits are found in regions and provinces where there is great heat and humidity, etc., and these fruits do not provide nourishment except for a short time, such as the dates found in the seas of the Arabs. Furthermore, he says natural trees in islands where the air is hot are sweet and have large and good fruits, etc., as in certain islands where there are trees like vines, and their leaves are as large as a king’s dish <note>original: *scutella regum*; likely describing the massive leaves of tropical plants like the banana or lotus</note>, and they are called figs, and their fruit is in the likeness of a melon and the flavor is sweet like honey, etc. And some of these bring forth other fruits from the root, like the fig, and others from the top, etc.; others are those that bring forth their fruits from the bark, etc. And there are others in a certain island in valleys called the Gallic ones, and others which have fruits in the likeness of purgatives, etc.; others that are like peppercorns; and there are others that are only harvested at a certain time and then stored for eating and preserved for a long time; and here he says something about fruits and the fruit of the tree, etc. He says, therefore, that certain trees produce other plants like vines which have a widespread heat and dryness, and are like the chaste tree <note>original: *vitices*</note>, dates, figs, and so on. Likewise, he says that fruits [can be] hot and moist, such as citrons <note>original: *citrea*</note> and so on. Likewise, he says fruits [can be] hot and dry, such as the fruit of the balsam, etc. Likewise, he says fruits [can be] cold and moist, such as plums, peaches, and gourds; and fruits [can be] cold and dry, such as galls <note>original: *gallae*; oak apples used in medicine and ink</note>, pears, pomegranates, and so on. And he says, therefore, that hot and moist fruits spoil quickly, etc. And he speaks of fruits that do not have rinds, such as the fruit of figs and peaches, etc. And he says that there are some that cannot last long enough to be eaten [later], such as the fig.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, he says that trees in hot places bear fruit frequently because the heat provides them with much nourishment for the fruits, etc. And as in hotter places like Egypt and Ethiopia, etc., and elsewhere, etc., he says that in Egypt there are certain trees in which fruits are produced that have within them something in the likeness of honey, such as dates and figs and so on. He says, therefore, that dates and figs are "living," hot, moist, and nourishing; and as it is said, when dates are green, they are like fruits that have a [harsh] flavor, and then they are not eaten, and if they are eaten, they bring about harm, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that are not well-ripened are bad because they are not well-digested, and therefore they ought to be cooked so that they may be better digested, etc. Likewise, he says certain trees do not bear fruit except rarely because of the coldness of the air, etc., as in cold provinces where there are trees that do not bring forth their fruit except every other year, and in the other year they do not fruit, etc. And he says certain trees in their parts bring forth two fruits in a year, like the fig in Egypt and the fig in other places such as Sicily, etc. And he says certain trees bring forth their fruit more rarely over many years, such as the terebinth <note>original: *terebinthus*; the turpentine tree</note>, and trees that in other places do not bring forth fruit except once in a hundred years, etc. Likewise, he says that there are fruits that have a marrow <note>meaning a meat or kernel</note> within them, like walnuts, hazelnuts, and chestnuts; and he says that these fruits nourish well and are of a strong substance, etc. He says, therefore, that sweet fruits like dates and figs are very nourishing and produce good blood, etc. And he says that bitter fruits are bad and are not nourishing, such as galls and the wild pear, etc. And he says that sour fruits are cold and dry, such as citrons and sour apples, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits ought to be eaten when they are ripe, etc.

<column-break/>

<margin>Hermes the Egyptian</margin>

And he mentions **Hermes the Egyptian** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with alchemy and ancient wisdom</note> concerning the date tree which is in Egypt and Arabia, etc. He says that there are dates there that have [a substance] like honey in them and are red; and he says that dates are of many and diverse kinds, such as dates that have a nut <note>pit</note> in the heart and dates that are without it, etc. He says, therefore, that dates nourish much and produce good blood, etc. He says, therefore, that there are certain dates that have a laxative virtue in them, such as the dates that have a nut in the heart, etc. He says, therefore, that dates that are green are bad and harm the stomach, etc. He says, therefore, that ripe dates are good and nourish the body, etc. And he says there are certain trees that have large and broad leaves, such as the trees in the islands of India, etc.; and he says that their leaves are like dishes; and he says that their fruits are like melons and are sweet like honey, etc. He says, therefore, that trees in hot and moist places bring forth their fruits quickly and frequently, etc. He says, therefore, that trees in cold and dry places bring forth their fruits slowly and more rarely, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that have much humidity spoil quickly and cannot be kept for a long time, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that have little humidity can be kept for a long time, such as walnuts and hazelnuts and so on. He says, therefore, that fruits that have a sweet flavor in them are hot and moist and nourishing, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that have a bitter flavor in them are cold and dry and are not nourishing, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that have a sour flavor in them are cold and dry and are not nourishing, etc.

And **Galen** says in his book *On the Capacities of Simple Medicines* that:

> Fruit that has a bitter flavor in it, such as the rind of the pomegranate, galls, and the wild pear, etc., are cold and dry and have an astringent virtue, etc.

He says, therefore, that fruits that have a sweet flavor in them, such as dates, figs, and sweet grapes, etc., are hot and moist and nourishing and have a laxative virtue, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that have a sour flavor in them, such as citrons and sour apples, etc., are cold and dry, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that are ripe are better and more nourishing than those that are not ripe, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits should be eaten after food and not before food, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits that have much humidity ought to be eaten before food, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits ought to be well chewed and well digested, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits ought to be clean and cleansed from all filth, etc. He says, therefore, that fruits ought to be from good trees and from good places, etc.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on plant physiology and moisture to a psychological and philosophical examination of "appetite"—the internal drive or desire within living beings. It draws heavily on Aristotelian and Thomistic concepts of the soul, distinguishing between sensory desires and the rational will.</meta>

...should agree: since one and the same appetite, in relation to the same end <term>end|Latin: *finis*; the goal or purpose toward which an action is directed</term> from which it derives its unity, does not have different objects except by accident. This is clear in other powers of the soul, such as sight; for something is seen because of something else, just as a thing is visible in itself when seen in the light—though in an unordered way, as one who sees color in the light. Although it is one thing in itself and another thing because of something else, sight is not said to behold two objects, but one. And so it is in this proposal: because he who loves something for the sake of another, that which is loved is only one thing; and there is one love in both, though in one way for one, and in another way for the other, since it is for one in itself and for the other through something else. Hence it follows that according to this way of speaking, our appetite is not distracted toward different objects, but is proportionally directed toward one, which is the end. Because in matters of desire, the end is in a certain way "formal" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "formal" aspect gives a thing its specific identity or "species."</note> and gives the act its species; and since the end is unique in itself, hence it is that our appetite is also one. Regarding what is said about friends—that they "will the same and do not will the same"—this must be understood as concerning the same end. In this way, we are said to be "one spirit with God," insofar as our willing and not-willing is conformed to the divine will. Regarding what is said about contrary vices, it is clear that the end of willing is different, or at least is diversified by the goal. This appears in the liberal man, the prodigal, and the miser: for the liberal man desires to give for the sake of decorum and honesty, and to retain so that he does not lack elsewhere; the prodigal gives for empty, common glory; and the miser retains beyond what is honest. Hence it is clear that the will cannot be the same in diverse and opposite things, for then contrary forms would be given in the same subject, which is impossible. This can be seen in other things, such as in sight, which is the same and uniform in all; and yet in different things it sees different things in themselves, because each thing is seen in itself under its own species. So it is in this proposal: for the same will may be loving in one instance and hating in another, just as in the same person it may love the way of God and hate the way of iniquity. For the reason for loving good and hating evil is the same,
<margin>Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book 3</margin>
as is clear in the third book of *On the Soul*. Because he who wills one of two contraries, by that same act rejects the other; and hence it is said that hatred is "willing evil to someone" and love is "willing good." Therefore the appetite, which is "willing," is seen to be given to the soul so that it may be its index and the rule of its own perfection. For just as sight was given to the body to discern those things that are helpful or not, so too appetite was given to the soul to attain those things that are harmonious with it and to flee those that are contrary, as is clear from Aristotle and others. It seems that friendship is nothing other than a certain unity of souls; because from the fact that someone loves himself, he wills all good things for himself, and from this follows a perfect unity, as will be shown below. Since, therefore, the soul is simple <note>"Simple" here means not made of parts, a standard philosophical view of the soul's nature.</note> and appetite is something simple belonging to the soul, it seems that in itself it regards only one object, and others by accident. This is as in other things, like sight, which in itself sees color, and accidentally sees other things, such as magnitude and the rest. Consequently, we must speak secondly of appetite in itself, as it is divided into the sensory and the intellective. For although both have the nature of appetite, yet in themselves they are diverse and differ from one another, as will be shown. Therefore, beginning from the sensible and then proceeding to the intellect, we must first look at the sensory appetite in itself, and afterward at the intellective appetite, as will be said in the course of the discussion. This appetite they call "desire" and "concupiscence."

<column-break/>

They call [this]: first, we must speak of the nature of desire. Wherefore it should be known that "appetite" in a general sense is used for any appetite whatever, so that it is the "genus" <term>genus|The broad category that includes several specific types or "species."</term> for everything that is desired. And thus Aristotle accepts it in the second book of *On the Soul*, saying: "Appetite is desire, anger, and will." Here he says that appetite is the genus, of which the aforementioned are the species. And it should be known that appetite is a certain "passion" <note>In medieval philosophy, a "passion" (*passio*) is not just an emotion, but any state where a subject is acted upon or "suffers" an influence from an external object.</note> insofar as it is taken from the desirable thing; for the desirable thing moves it like an agent, while the appetite is moved like a patient. Hence it is clear that appetite is a passive power; and for that reason, it is called by Aristotle a "moved mover." For if it were only a mover, it would not be a "moved mover," but would be a mover of the moving only, as the "end" is. But appetite is a mover insofar as it moves toward a place, toward a certain desirable form; and it is moved by the desirable thing, whose form <note>original: *speciem*</note> it receives, just as the sense receives the form of the sensible. Thus, just as the sense in act is the sensible itself, so also the appetite in act is the desirable itself. This appetite, which is "desire" and "concupiscence," the Greeks call *epithymia* <note>original: *epithymian* (Greek: ἐπιθυμία), referring to the sensory desire for pleasure.</note>; and we call it concupiscence or desire. For it is called desire (*desiderium*) from the absence of a thing, so that it is an appetite for an absent thing, as Augustine says
<margin>Augustine, *On the Trinity*</margin>
in his book *On the Trinity*: that the appetite for a present thing is love, but for an absent thing it is desire. Hence it is that appetite in general is divided in this way: for it is either toward a present thing and is called love, or it is toward an absent thing and is called desire. But the "desirable" is spoken of in two ways: in one way, that which is according to the truth of the thing, and thus it is called "good"; in another way, according to appearance, and thus it is called that which "seems good." For example, what is evil but seems good; and this appears in drunkards and in other vicious people, to whom that seems good which in truth is evil. From this it appears that the object of appetite is the good in itself, or in appearance, as Aristotle maintains in the third book of *On the Soul*, saying the end of appetite is the "good or the apparent good." And this is what Aristotle says at the beginning of the *Ethics*: it is called "good" because the good is what all things desire. This appetite, so understood, Aristotle says is "desire," because the end to which it is directed is to attain a perfection which it does not have. For appetite is only spoken of regarding a thing that is not possessed; because what is possessed is not desired, except as to its conservation. For then the thing is not desired, but rather the conservation of the thing. Hence appetite in itself is for a thing not held; wherefore Aristotle says that appetite is for a "good not held." And that it is a "passion" is manifest from this: because the appetite is said to "suffer" from the desirable thing, since from the fact that it is seen as good, it moves the appetite to its pursuit. Hence it is clear that appetite is a passive power in that it receives the "species" <note>original: *speciem*; the mental image or form of the object.</note> of the desirable thing, just as sight receives the species of color, and as the intellect receives the species of the intelligible; so too the appetite receives the species of the desirable good. For that which is good would not move the appetite except through its species which it creates in the appetite. Hence it is clear that appetite is said to be nothing other than a certain inclination toward some thing, according to which some speak; and it is said that appetite is the inclination of any thing toward its own proper end. And thus it is in all things, because all things have a certain inclination toward their own perfection, as appears in heavy things, which desire to seek the center, and in light things, which desire the heights. Hence it is said that appetite is twofold: one is "natural," which is in all things; and thus the theologians also speak, as Thomas [Aquinas] says in the *Prima Secundae*, in the question on appetite. There he says that appetite is the inclination of a thing toward the good; and this he consequently divides: one is natural, as in inanimate things; another is sensual, as in animals; another is intellectual, as in men. Of this appetite, therefore, we must treat in this place: that which is sensual, and according to Aristotle is called *epithymia*, and is called concupiscence or desire.

---

Hence it should be known that not only does the soul have this appetite, just as it has sight and other powers; but it is also said of the appetite that it is an "active power." For after it has the species of the desirable thing, it moves itself toward the pursuit of that thing, so that the desirer and the desired become one. But in this way, there appears to be a diversity; because the appetite is called "mover" and "being moved," just as the intellect wills, and as Aristotle teaches. Hence some say that appetite is a certain active power; others say it is passive only. To this I say: that appetite according to its essence is a passive power, just as the sensitive power is; for it receives the species of the desirable, just as the sense receives the species of the sensible. Wherefore Aristotle says that the appetite receives the species of the desirable as the sense receives the sensible. But that it is a "mover," it has this through the species; because the species of the desirable existing in the appetite is the principle of moving toward attaining that thing, just as heat in fire is the principle of heating. So the appetite, having in itself the species of the desirable, moves the desirer toward that which is desirable. Hence it is said that the appetite is "moved" like a patient and "moves" like an agent. But it is moved by the desirable thing, and it moves the whole soul and body to the pursuit of the desirable thing. This appetite, then, which Aristotle calls *epithymia*, we call concupiscence or desire. It is also said that this appetite is called "desire" and "concupiscence" by others; for this appetite is said to be for an absent thing, because the thing which one desires is absent; hence it is called "desire." But "concupiscence" is said to be for a present thing, insofar as one enjoys the desirable thing. So also some say that the appetite is called "desire" insofar as it concerns the "end," but "concupiscence" insofar as it concerns those things which lead to the end. But Aristotle does not make this distinction; rather, he maintains that concupiscence is the same as desire, and is the appetite for a sensible good, as appears in the third book of *On the Soul*. Wherefore he says that concupiscence is the "appetite for the delightful." This appetite, therefore, as it is divided in this way, must be examined. And first, it must be said that concupiscence is said to be twofold: for one is called "natural" and the other "non-natural." And this Aristotle maintains in the third book of the *Ethics*, where he says that some concupiscences are common and natural, and others are proper and acquired. Natural concupiscences are such as the desire for food and drink, and such things as are for the conservation of nature; these are called common because they are in all animals. But the others are non-natural, such as the desire for money, honors, and such things, which are not necessary for the conservation of nature. From this it appears that the sensory appetite, as Aristotle maintains, is twofold: one which is natural, like the appetite for food and such; the other which is non-natural, but is called the appetite for a thing according to what is in the imagination, such as the appetite for honors. Wherefore Aristotle says in the same place that appetite is twofold: one which is "without reason," such as the natural appetite; another which is "with reason," such as the appetite in itself which one has for a thing according to which it is judged to be good by reason. But then the appetite is called "will," as will be shown. This appetite, then, which Aristotle calls

<column-break/>

*epithymia*, and is called concupiscence or desire: it is clear from what has been said that it regards the delightful object, such as is a sensible good. But it should be known that "appetite" is taken here in two ways: in one way for the act of desiring itself; in another way for the appetitive power itself, just as it is said of sight that there is "the sight" (the power) and "vision" (the act). Concupiscence, therefore, insofar as it is an act, is a certain movement of the appetite toward a delightful thing; but insofar as it is a power, it is the sensory power itself through which the animal is carried toward a delightful thing. Now, how this appetite is distinct from reason, and how it is called a "part of the soul," is clear from those things said above: because appetite is said to be a power of the soul through which the animal is moved toward a thing. And since the "desirable" is twofold—namely, the sensible good and the intelligible good—it follows that the appetite is also twofold: one, namely, the sensory, which regards the sensible good; the other the intellective, which regards the intelligible good, and is called the "will." And since in man there are both appetites, it is clear that in man there are two "movers"; for the animal is moved both by the sensory appetite and by the intellect, as Aristotle says in the third book of *On the Soul*. Now we must see how this sensory appetite, which is "concupiscence," is distinct from the "irascible" appetite, as Aristotle also wishes to distinguish. For Aristotle says in the third book of *On the Soul* that appetite is divided into concupiscence and anger. This irascible appetite, which the Greeks call *thymon* <note>Greek: θυμός (*thymos*), referring to the spirited part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and the "arduous good."</note>, we call "anger"; and it differs from concupiscence, because concupiscence is the appetite for the delightful good, while anger is the appetite for vengeance, as will be shown below. But since both are concerning the good—because vengeance also has the character of a good—hence it is that "appetite" is said to be the genus for both of these. And so Aristotle says in the second book of *On the Soul* that "appetite is desire, anger, and will." Here it is clear that appetite is the genus, of which the aforementioned are the species. But that concupiscence and anger are two distinct powers is clear from this: that they have different objects. Because the object of concupiscence is the delightful good; whereas the object of anger is the "arduous good" <note>The "arduous good" (*bonum arduum*) is a classical concept referring to a good that is difficult to attain or requires overcoming obstacles.</note>; and in this way
<margin>Thomas [Aquinas], *Prima Secundae*, Question 23</margin>
the Doctors commonly speak, as Thomas says in the *Prima Secundae*, question 23, on the passion of anger. But Aristotle seems to maintain that anger and concupiscence are differences <note>In logic, a "difference" is a characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus.</note> of the appetite rather than distinct powers, as can be seen in the third book of *On the Soul*. But then the sensory appetite is called one power which has two operations, which are called "to desire" and "to be angry." But then concupiscence and anger are not properly called "powers of the soul," but rather operations, as will be shown below. Of this irascible appetite, which the Greeks call *thymon* and we call anger, we shall not treat here; because he [the author or Aristotle] only wishes to treat of concupiscence and the delightful appetite. This appetite, then, which the Greeks call *epithymia* and we call concupiscence, Aristotle seems to accept here insofar as it pertains to the conservation of nature, such as food, drink, and such. Wherefore he wishes to show from this that concupiscence is nothing other than the appetite for a delightful thing.

<note>This entire page contains a massive amount of repetitive shorthand. In medieval scholastic writing, students or scribes often used these repetitive formulas to represent complex logical relationships between "Matter" (*Materia*), "Form" (*Forma*), and "Reason/Definition" (*Ratio*). The sequence suggests a dialectical exercise where every possible combination of these terms is tested to define the "finite" nature of a "thing" (*res*). The text effectively argues that a thing's identity comes from its form, while its potentiality comes from its matter.</note>

<summary>This page presents a dense scholastic logical derivation concerning the metaphysical relationship between essence, matter, and form. It argues that while matter itself is infinite or indefinite, it becomes "finite" and defined as a specific "thing" only when joined with "form" and a "principal nature."</summary>

--- Page 243 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the abstract metaphysical definitions of "essence" and "matter" found on the previous page into a discussion on the theology of grace and the human soul. The author shifts from logical categories to the internal workings of the human spirit, specifically how original sin damaged human nature and how divine grace is necessary for restoration.</meta>

Because, therefore, through the first sin <note>original: *peccatum primum*; referring to the "Original Sin" of Adam and Eve in Christian theology</note> the natural powers—namely, the very faculties of the soul—happened to be weakened, man cannot reach those things which pertain to the attainment of **beatitude** <term>Beatitude (beatitudo)</term> <note>The state of supreme happiness or blessedness, specifically the ultimate goal of human life in union with God.</note> by his own strength, unless he is aided by divine grace. Furthermore, the virtue of faith is required not only for the knowledge of truth but also for the performance of good works. For "without faith it is impossible to please God," as the Apostle says <note>original: *ut ait apostolus*; a reference to the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews 11:6</note>. From this, it is clear that through sin, man suffered corruption not only in his intellect but also in his affections. Therefore, he stands in need of restoration through the medicines of grace, which are dispensed in the sacraments.

<column-break/>

<margin>
<unclear>Note that grace is a state (habitus)</unclear>
</margin>
But since man, according to his nature, is composed of soul and body, it is necessary that both be healed. For grace is a certain **habit** <term>Habit (habitus)</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, a 'habit' is not a repetitive action, but a stable, internal quality or disposition that perfects a person's nature.</note> received into the soul, through which man is made a "partaker of the divine nature." From this, it follows that the acts of man proceeding from faith and charity are meritorious of eternal life. For it is not enough merely to know what must be done, but the will must also be upright so that it may be inclined toward the proper end. To achieve this, however, the help of the Holy Spirit is required, who is the love and the "gift of the Most High."

---

### Page 243 ###

It seems rather that grace is not only in the soul, but there is also some disposition in the body for the reception of grace. For just as in natural things a "disposition of form" precedes the form itself, so in man a certain preparation is required so that the light of grace may be infused. This, however, happens not by one’s own power, but by divine motion. Therefore, it is said in the Psalm: *They have prepared my soul* <note>original: *Praeparaverunt animam meam*; likely citing Psalm 57:6</note>. From this, it is clear that grace is the beginning and the end of our entire salvation, without which we can do nothing that looks toward salvation.

<column-break/>

<margin>
<unclear>Concerning the power of the soul</unclear>
</margin>
The soul, therefore, has its own powers through which it operates, but grace perfects them and elevates them to something that exceeds nature. Just as the eye sees color through the light of the sun, so the intellect sees divine things through the light of grace. And just as the sensitive appetite is moved toward what is naturally delightful, so the will is moved toward spiritual good according to grace. Through this, indeed, man is conformed to God, so that he may be a child of adoption and an heir to the celestial kingdom.

The author uses an analogy comparing the light of grace to sunlight, which allows the "eye" of the intellect to see beyond its natural limits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the nature of the soul (anima) and light (lux). Having established the basics of matter and form on the previous page, the author now uses the physics of light—specifically optics and geometry—to explain how the rational soul perceives itself and interacts with time and movement. The text relies heavily on the concept of the "point" (punctus) as a symbol for the soul's unity.</meta>

from itself to itself—and they proceed and are generated here and there through the **division of light** into spirit and flow; but also again from here, conversely, they descend perpendicularly from the light in a straight line, so that they collect themselves again in themselves. And through this movement, they are gathered into themselves again as far as the center, to the point—that is, the **unity** where they consist—and there nothing else seems to be but the center of the point, where they remain as if in the center point and no further. Nor do they move themselves except from the center where light <note>original: "lux"</note> is generated through itself, and not outside itself; and they are only in the one light of the radiating center. And this is the same light, both *intensive* and *extensive*, and there is no other light outside the center except from the center, and it is propagated from the center.

Then light emits itself outside the center in a straight line: and while it is emitted from it, then it becomes **illumination** <note>original: "lumen". In medieval philosophy, "lux" is the essential source of light, while "lumen" is the light as it travels through a medium or fills a space.</note> in the *intelligible spirit*. This illumination in the intelligible spirit is that which extends itself, and where it ends is a point. While that which proceeds from the point then moves through **time**; however, as long as it is in the point and does not move, it is in the point, and what is in the point has no time. 

But time exists at the point where movement begins along a straight line; and what moves thus along a straight line is in time. Because all time proceeds from time, so that time is not *in* the point, but it originates from the point. Movement proceeds from the point along a line, and movement along a line is in time; and thus all time belongs to that which proceeds from a point. Then time is the **measure of movement**, and then time is measured by that movement; then since the point is the measure of time, time measures the light flowing in time along a line. Therefore, then, in the point is the "light of the point" which is flowing in time, and so forth—that is, that time measures movement and the "time of time" is the measure of time. That is, the measure of time in time where the **rational soul**, like light pointed in itself, is a point. It measures itself—that is, it measures itself through time and movement, just as light in time is movement through movement. That is, illumination <note>original: "lumen"</note>, just as it flows in movement through time, so the rational soul, thus measuring itself through time and movement, is thus light flowing in time toward a line. And that which is flowing in time toward a line has light flowing in movement: and that movement is measured by time, just as the soul is in time.

<column-break/>

There is an opposite rudimentary aspect which brings sense to the eyes from where it originates, and to itself only that which approaches the sense. Nothing less can happen here in this which is the soul—that is, from itself and moving itself—and from itself it nevertheless exists; that is, it moves through a **circuit** <note>The "circuit" refers to a circular motion, often used to describe the soul's return to itself in self-reflection.</note> around itself. And here, just as from straight lines moved to points, so again from a point it is **reflected** to the light, as we see in mirrors. 

Therefore, the soul becomes like a reflection of light; it foresees itself and sees itself in itself, just as in a point a point is regarded. That is, as from the unity of a point, it reflects from itself back to itself like a ray of light in itself. This is the **reflection** by which the soul knows itself, and it knows itself as it is light—both the measure and the measured. And it knows itself as it is—that is, as the soul is the soul, as the soul is the **form** in which each thing is contained. As the soul, which is illumination and light, sees and intuits itself through itself, just as light is seen in itself, and just as a point is seen in a point, so the soul sees itself; it sees in its own point its own point.

Just as it is [impossible] for this soul not to be measured except by time, which is extensive—that is, the measure of time toward something, the measure of time toward something measured, which is measured by time, which is measured by light in movement. Therefore, the soul is a measure because the soul is **light in movement**, just as light is light flowing in time along a line. And the soul is measured by the movement of time, just as the movement of time flows toward movement, just as movement in movement, just as light in movement in time. Therefore, the soul flowing toward a line in movement is the measure of time, just as the soul in time flows like light flowing in movement. And that which is in time flowing in movement flows through measure. 

Therefore, the soul in time is the measure of time, just as the soul in movement, just as light is in movement, measures time. Just as time is in time, it measures time; and then time is the measure of time through time. Just as light measures time, just as the soul in time is light flowing in movement, it measures time. Therefore, the soul is light in movement as the soul measures movement; it measures just as light flowing in movement measures time, just as time measures light in time through movement. And then the soul is light in movement as it measures, just as light in time flows, just as the movement of the soul in movement measures time. That which is in time measures time through time, just as the soul in time is light in movement and measures time.

---

And again, he [the Creator or Philosopher] made them so that there are diverse **reason** and **reasoning** <note>original: "ratio et ratiocinatio". In scholasticism, 'ratio' is the faculty of reason, while 'ratiocinatio' is the active process of logical deduction.</note>. And here let it walk from where it might go out to that same illumination <note>original: "lumen"</note>, just as the point went out through this straight line to the center point. Again, let it reflect the light to the point from which it went out through this line, again as from a straight line to the point—that is, from the center to the circle—and again it returns to the center, that is, into itself. So let the soul be in itself, so that from that light itself there is nothing but illumination in itself, just as a point is in itself. And let it be that as illumination is in itself, where there is nothing but light through itself. 

And then light in itself is light that does not proceed from time, unlike the light that is in time flowing along a line. Therefore, as light is light in itself where there is no time—that is, in the point where there is no time—and that which is not in time is light through itself. And then light which is light through itself is light which is not in time—that is, light in itself as light through itself. Thus, light through itself is light in itself, and that which is light in itself is light through itself. And then light in itself is light which is not in time. Therefore, light which is in time is not light through itself, but light through movement flowing along a line, just as the soul in movement flows through movement, just as light in time flows, just as the soul in movement measures time. Just as the soul in time is light flowing in movement, it measures time. Therefore, the soul in time measures time through time—that is, it measures time through time, just as the soul in time is light flowing in movement and measures time.

<column-break/>

[This is] the remaining part, as far as a thing exists in itself; and as it is in itself, as it is nowhere else. And then it is light in itself—that is, light in itself as a point is in itself, and as the soul is in itself, just as light is in itself, and as illumination <note>original: "lumen"</note> is in itself. And then the soul in itself is nothing but illumination, as illumination is in itself, as a point is in itself. And then the soul in itself is that which is not measured by time, because the soul in itself is not in time. As the soul in itself is not in movement, therefore the soul in itself is like light in itself where there is no movement. Therefore, the soul in itself, like light in itself, has no movement; then the **brightness** <note>original: "clarificatum"</note> of the soul is light through itself, as illumination is in itself. And then the soul in itself is light through itself where the soul in itself is like light in itself where there is no movement of the soul. 

Therefore, the soul in itself is what the soul is in itself, like light in itself where time is not the measure of souls. Just as the soul in itself is not measured in time, as the soul in itself has no movement, so the soul in itself is not measured by time. Just as light in itself has no movement, so the soul in itself has no movement; and then the soul in itself has no time, just as light in itself has no time. As the soul in itself is nothing but illumination in itself, so the soul in itself has no movement. Therefore, the soul in itself has no time; therefore, the soul in itself has no time; therefore, the soul in itself is nothing but illumination, like illumination in itself, like a point in itself. 

And then the soul in itself, which has no time as the measure of souls; and then the soul in itself has no measure of time, just as the soul in itself is light in itself and has no measure of time through movement. And then the soul in itself has no movement, just as the soul in itself has no time, as the soul in itself is nothing but illumination. Just as the soul in itself has no movement, just as light in itself has no movement, therefore the soul in itself has no time. Therefore, the soul in itself is nothing but illumination, as the soul in itself has no movement, and then the soul in itself is not measured by time. Just as the soul in itself is light in itself and has no measure of time, as the soul in itself is nothing but illumination in itself, like a point in itself. And then the soul in itself has no measure of time; therefore, the soul in itself has no movement, just as light in itself has no movement. Therefore, the soul in itself is nothing but illumination, like illumination in itself, like a point in itself, and then the soul in itself is nothing but illumination.

# On the Word and the Divine Will

To speak universally of these words: since Christ could not have suffered except through the **will**, just as it appears through the Son of God. This is what is called the "Word of God’s Grace," because in this, the Word of God willed to be the "Word of Christ." Of these things which I spoke of above, the sum is the **truth** and **piety** of Christ. For they <unclear>propose</unclear> Christ as Father just as He is Son, and this is why He is called the "Word of Christ." This Word is of the **flesh**, and into this Word the **soul** comes, just as Christ came. Thus the soul comes to God through this spirit, and in this, Christ is the **will** of the soul, just as Christ is the **will of the Father**. So the soul ought to be the **will of Christ**. And in this, the will of Christ comes into the soul, so that it may be in her just as it is in the Father. And just as Christ is called the "Word of God," so the soul is called the "Word of Christ." In this Word of Christ, Christ comes into the soul just as the Word of God came into Christ. And as Christ said: <note>original: "qui uenerit ad me..."</note> "Whoever comes to me, let the Word be made in me, just as I am in the Word of the Father." So let the soul be in the Word of Christ, and thus it shall come to the Father just as Christ came to the Father—and Christ came to God. This is the **Word of Truth** and the **Piety of Christ**, for the Word is **spirit and life**. Thus the soul has life through Christ just as Christ has life through the Father. As it is written: <note>referencing John 6:57</note> "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me, he also shall live because of me." This is the **Word of Life** and the **grace** <unclear>given</unclear> by Christ.

<column-break/>

And since it is said here—as it appears—that Christ the Son of God is said to be the **Word** and the **Will of God**; as it appears through the Son, this is the Word of God, and in this the Son of God was **made man**. As it appears through the Word, that Word is of the **flesh**, and in this Word our Christ was made man, as is evident in the Gospel. In this Word, Christ is our **life**, as is clear through the Word—which is the Word of flesh. In this Word, our Christ comes to us, just as the Word of God comes to the Father. And as Christ said: "As the Father has life in Himself, so He has given to the Son to have life in Himself." <note>referencing John 5:26</note> In this Word of Christ is the **life of souls**, just as in the Word of the Father is the life of Christ. And just as Christ is called the Word of God, so the **will of the soul** is called the Word of Christ, as appears through the Word of Truth, which is the Word of flesh. In this Word, the will of the soul is made the Word of Christ, and Christ comes into the soul just as the Word of God comes into Christ. As it is said in the Gospel: Christ came into the world and came unto His own. Just as Christ is called the Word of God, so the will of the soul is called the Word of Christ, as appears through the Word of Truth, which is the Word of flesh. Thus the Word of Christ's Truth is the life of souls, just as the Word of the Father is the life of Christ. And as Christ comes to the Father, and Christ comes to God, <unclear>so</unclear> the soul...

***

# On Spiritual Union and the Deified Soul

I say, clearly, to all these **spiritual** ones: let there be nothing in them except their own procreation—that is, **charity** <note>original: "caritas", meaning divine or selfless love</note> and **piety** in all truth. This is the **grace of Christ**, whom they have said to be both Father and Son, to be the divine essence and God. This Son, and with Him the **sacred water** of His eternal words; for it is nothing but the action which the **will** signifies, and as it wills, those things are brought to pass. Let the will grow cold and let it lust in the living person, from whom the will has long ceased; and then, that which is not the will is nothing. If the Word is made, then the Word is of the **flesh**, which was then made so that it might **deify souls**. <note>The concept of "deificet animas" refers to theosis or divinization, a mystical process where the soul is transformed by grace into a god-like state.</note> This happens through that place where a person is called a "sinner" to be seen as sinning—not of the flesh, but of the **spirit**—so that the will may be made in this spirit for the sins in which souls are entangled. And the Word, which is said to be the **truth**, is the Word of Christ’s mind and will in this world and in the future. Christ comes into God so that the will may be Christ, and He Himself may be in it just as Christ is in the Father. This Word is the **truth**, and "the truth shall set you free." <note>John 8:32</note> I say this concerning the **flesh of Christ**, because this Word is truth; and just as Christ is truth, so the will of Christ is truth in this world and the future. Because the Word of Christ’s flesh was made the Word of God for the sins of the world, this God who thus visited us—the Son of Man—came to the sinner, as is clear in the Gospel. And it is said: just as the Father made the world and all things in it, so the **will of man** makes a world for itself and for other sins. Let us see, therefore, if the will of Christ is in us, as is clear through the **Spirit of Christ**, who is the Word of God through whom all things were made. Thus the Spirit, who is the Word of God and Truth—for the sake of these spirits Christ comes into souls to rule them, just as the Word of God rules the world. For the **Kingdom of God** is not in talk, but in the **power** <note>original: "uirtute", implying strength or miraculous power</note> of Christ, where Christ is King, and the **will of God** is justice and judgment in their midst, just as Christ is in the Father.

<column-break/>

I say that this way is the **way of the will**. He who sins through the will is of the flesh; as it is said to the Corinthians near the end: "Sinners shall not inhabit the Kingdom of God." And as the Apostle says: this is the Son of Man. The souls whom Christ loves, for those He came into the world. And as Christ is, so is the will in Him; as in God, so in this Christ who wills Himself to be the Son of God. Then the **grace of Christ** comes to him, by which, just as the Spirit made this man into God for Himself, so Christ made this soul into God for Himself. This is what my Lord said: "Why have you forsaken me?" <note>Matthew 27:46</note> Because then the **deified soul** <note>original: "anima deifica"</note> shall remain solitary in itself, just as Christ is. And just as the Son was alone, as is clear by that which the Father says: "As I am in the Father, so you are in me." This is the **Word of Truth and Life**, since the soul then shall be like Christ, and its will like the will of Christ, and the truth of Christ like the truth of Christ. Wherefore it is said of Christ: "As He is, so shall we be." As He is in this world, I say that the **will of Christ is truth**, and the grace of Christ is the truth of Christ. And as He is, so the will of the soul is truth, because the grace of Christ made this will, and the will of Christ rules this will, so that the will of Christ and the will of the soul may be **one will** and **one truth** and **one God** in all things. And as Christ said He was the **vine** and we the **branches**, so the will of Christ is life, and the will of the soul is that of the branches. He who does not remain in me, his will shall not be of Christ, nor of the soul of Christ. As He Himself said: "Where I am, there you shall be." For then the soul shall be like Christ, and Christ like the soul, and thus there shall be **one God** and **one Christ** in all things and through all things. Then the will of Christ shall be the will of the soul, and the truth of Christ shall be the truth of the soul. And as Christ is God, so the soul shall be like Christ in God, and God in the soul. Thus there shall be one God in all, just as Christ is one in the Father and the Father in Him. Thus Christ and the soul shall be **one Christ**, and one will, and one truth. And just as Christ is called Truth, so the will of the soul's truth is Christ.

<summary>These pages outline a mystical theology of "The Will," arguing that the human soul achieves union with God by aligning its will perfectly with Christ's. Drawing heavily on the Gospel of John, the author describes a process of deification where the soul and Christ become "one" in truth and purpose.</summary>

This transition from theology to "natural philosophy" was common in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, where the study of light was often seen as a bridge between the physical and the divine.</meta>

<meta>The previous page discussed the nature of light and the heavens. This page shifts toward a more abstract metaphysical investigation of the Aristotelian principles of "Matter" and "Form," and how things transition from a state of possibility (potency) to a state of reality (act).</meta>

<margin>Second</margin> Secondly, it follows from both of these that it is called such at a certain time; just as one does not depend more on the property of one than the other. Matter cannot properly be called "potency" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, 'potency' (potentia) is the capacity to become something, while 'act' (actu) is the reality of being it.</note> in its own right, but it is said to "become." To restrict something from itself is not properly to be limited, and thus matter is said to exist through itself. More properly, however, it is said to be made of two elements; and so there is a reason in this: that matter and form exist through themselves, just as does a generation of such a kind. The main point is that what he says is the subject by which the form of generation is produced, for it is in the middle of them. Therefore, another nature is said to be in generation and change; but through themselves they are not said to be "in act" <note>original: "actu" — meaning in a state of completed reality</note>, about which modes it is rarer to acquire a divine opinion, except that it is certainly said to be implanted, not that it is said of the form. It is said differently that the perfect is not said of the same thing through itself, just as from water comes a horse; here, briefly, it follows that the common thing generated is the form which is in this, just as it is in act. Therefore, it is nature: and matter exists through itself because it can become actual. However, by these notes, nature is nature through its vicinity which it possesses; but to seek its property is something that is in it, or to understand that it is not this, for it is not known. And nature is named as "becoming," and here it is said that nature is perpetuated.
