<meta>This page transitions from the abstract discussion of matter and form to a specific physical application: the spherical nature of the elements, particularly water and earth. It uses Aristotelian physics to explain why the oceans and even small drops of water take a round shape, continuing the exploration of how "form" manifests in the natural world.</meta>

There are, however, various opinions, the first of which is from Aristotle in the 4th book of *On the Heavens* <note>original: "De Coelo"</note>, where he seems to maintain that water is part of a circle in the middle of which is the earth. Because water is part of a sphere for which the earth is the center, it thus encloses the earth with water. For he says that water has a spherical form everywhere around the earth; hence, if one part of the water is higher than another, it immediately flows toward the other until both places belong to a single sphericity and circle. It is equidistant <note>meaning all points on the surface are an equal distance from the center</note> according to what Aristotle says: that water has a spherical form so that the center of the earth is everywhere its center. His reason is what Aristotle <unclear>posits</unclear> in the 4th book of *On the Heavens*, where he seems to say that water has a nature such that it everywhere flows to a deeper place, and thus it <unclear>achieves</unclear> a single spherical form everywhere. Therefore, if one part is higher, the water immediately flows toward the other until each place is of one sphericity, just as "moist things" <note>the "moist" or "fluid" was considered one of the primary qualities of the elements</note> possess by their very nature. 

To this, we then see the reason by which some wish to say that water is spherical and round everywhere; for if one part is higher, the water then flows to the other until both places are of one sphericity, as is the case in water by the nature of the moist. But then this reason is spoken of in terms of the "end" <note>the "final cause" or purpose</note> toward which it tends by the power of nature, just as Aristotle says at the end of the 2nd book of *On the Heavens*. He gives the reason that water has a nature by which it everywhere wants to run to a deeper place, toward the earth, toward the place that is the center. Thus, it has a nature everywhere such that one part is joined to another, and so it achieves a single sphericity. This is the logic of the reason why it everywhere possesses a moist nature; in its totality, it has a nature everywhere such that one part is joined to another, as is said of the nature of the moist.

<column-break/>

And the only thing being questioned is whether the whole aggregate <note>the combined mass of earth and water</note> is spherical everywhere on its surface. The reason for this is what Aristotle touches upon in the 4th book: water everywhere flows to a deeper place, which is the reason for its finish. However small a spherical surface may be, it must be round; and it immediately flows into a deeper place. When it is said that water has a spherical form, it is not to be understood that it is perfectly spherical everywhere and must be round in every single part, but it is said to have a spherical form by reason of the "end" toward which it tends—that is, toward the deeper place—namely, through a straight path by which it tends toward the spherical center. This is so that it may then appear to have a spherical figure on its surface toward the outermost sphere. 

Regarding this, Aristotle speaks at the end of the 2nd book of *On the Heavens*, providing the reason by which he proves the earth is round. And as water here has a moist nature, the reason is that one part has an "appetite" <note>a natural inclination or tendency</note> for another, and thus they achieve a single spherical form. We see this in a small quantity of water, which then takes a round form, as is evident in moist drops. Thus, it is seen that water has a spherical form by reason of its moisture, and so one part "desires" a single sphericity with the other. From this, it follows that the earth and water everywhere create one body by reason of the moist, and thus both places share one sphericity, as is seen by the nature of the moist, since water everywhere seeks the deeper place. And if water has an appetite for another part, one part for another, then we see that it has an appetite for a single sphericity everywhere all around the earth. Thus, by reason of the moist, it has this nature everywhere: that one part seeks the deeper place for another by the logic of the moist. Thus, through this, Aristotle says in the *Book on Animals* that water everywhere has a moist form by reason of sphericity, as it is said of water that one part seeks the deeper place, and thus both places share one sphericity everywhere around the earth.

<column-break/>

Do we not see that even a small amount of water everywhere has the same figure? The logic for this is found in the "end" or purpose: for if water did not everywhere have to flow down to a place, it would have to flow by some appetite driven by an outside agent. But we see this instead: that in water there is a logic of flow in whatever parts it has. For if one part of the water is high and another is low, that which is high immediately flows to the low, and thus both places achieve one sphericity. From this, Aristotle says in the 2nd book of *On the Heavens* that water has a spherical form by reason of the moist; water ought to be round, and the reason for this is that it everywhere possesses a moist form. 

As we also see in drops that are taken from water: if one is placed on a spot of a surface where it has its nature by logic, it then takes a spherical figure. By reason of the "end" toward which it tends, it has an appetite for the center, as if by a straight path. And then, according to the "end" toward which it tends, it is said to have a spherical form because one part has a relationship to another so that both locations share one sphericity. As is said regarding an elementary body, water has this nature everywhere by reason of the moist. Indeed, insofar as the moist has an appetite for another part, it then seems to run everywhere toward the center so that it may satisfy its appetite to have one sphericity. By reason of the moist, it is said through this that water is a moist aggregate everywhere, so that one part has an appetite for another. From this, therefore, we see that water has an appetite by nature for another part, through which there is one spherical form. Insofar as it is moist, it has this nature everywhere: that one part seeks the deeper place for another. By this logic, water flows to the place for which it has an appetite, so that it may thus achieve one sphericity everywhere around the earth, according to what is said of the moist. It possesses the logic of the moist so that it has this nature everywhere. Thus, it seems that water everywhere has an appetite for another part, one part for another, so that both locations are of one sphericity everywhere around the earth by reason of the moist, just as is said of drops of water having this spherical figure.

<column-break/>

Aristotle says, regarding the same moist part of water, in the book *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "De generatione et corruptione"</note>, that the "moist" is that which is filled and bounded by other limits. Therefore, by reason of the moist, water is of such a sort that wherever it is placed, it fills the place, just as Aristotle says of the moist in water. For water does not have its own proper figure, but of itself is such that it flows everywhere unless it is contained by something external. Just as in a vessel, water takes the figure of the vessel, from which it is seen that water has a moist form. Thus, water of itself does not have a figure but takes the figure of other things. So it is said that water of itself does not have a spherical figure by reason of the moist, as Aristotle says <margin>Of a bitter spring</margin> in the 2nd book of *On the Heavens*, but by reason of the "end" toward which it tends, as it seeks the center as if by a straight path. 

And so water has a nature such that it possesses the logic of the moist by reason of sphericity, so that one part has an appetite for another, so that both locations are of one sphericity, having an appetite for the other by reason of the "end" toward which it tends. And thus water has a nature everywhere so that one part seeks the deeper place for another by the logic of the moist, as is said of the elements. Water is by reason of the moist, insofar as its logic is that one part has an appetite for another so that both locations are of one sphericity. As is said of other elements, by reason of the moist, it has an appetite so that one part seeks the deeper place for another. As it is said of water, it has a nature everywhere such that one part seeks the deeper place for another so that both locations share one sphericity, as Aristotle says in the 2nd book of *On the Heavens* concerning water having a moist form. Thus, then, water has a nature such that one part has an appetite for another so that they thus achieve one sphericity everywhere around the earth. As is said of other elements, by reason of the moist, water everywhere has this nature: that one part seeks the deeper place for another by reason of the moist and by reason of sphericity.

While the previous page focused on the elements and sensory signs of knowledge, this page shifts into the mathematical foundations of natural philosophy—geometry and the definitions of quantity—drawing heavily on Aristotle’s Physics and Categories, as well as Euclid’s Elements, to explain how physical bodies are structured.</meta>

I say in a second way: that the point from which a part begins is not the part itself, because a part possesses quantity; but the principle of a part is indivisible in itself, as is stated in the 6th book of the <term>Physics</term> <note>Aristotle's *Physica*, a foundational text on the study of nature and change</note>. This is similarly said of the point in respect to the line, the line in respect to the surface, and the surface in respect to the body. It is said that the principle is not part of the essence of that for which it is a principle; just as a point is not a line, a line is not a surface, and a surface is not a body. Therefore, a point is the principle of a line, but it is neither a line nor a part of a line. And so they say that the point, the line, the surface, and the body are not in the same genus of <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: "quidditatis"; the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</note>, even though they are in the same genus of quantity. This is what <term>Aristotle</term> means in the <term>Categories</term> <note>original: "praedicamentis"</note> when he says that the point, line, surface, and body all belong to the genus of quantity.

<margin>Wisdom 11 <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "But thou hast arranged all things by measure and number and weight."</note></margin>
Secondly, I say that the essence of a part in relation to the whole is twofold: in one way, formally, and thus the part is of the essence of the whole; in another way, according to its essential being, and thus the whole is of the essence of the part. This is what the <term>Commentator</term> <note>referring to Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard in medieval universities</note> intends in the 7th book of the <term>Metaphysics</term>, saying that if the part is of the essence of the whole, then the part is prior to the whole, just as a circle is prior to its portions; however, if the whole is of the essence of the part, then the whole is prior to its parts, just as a human being is prior to his parts; for a single part of a human is not a "human" except when compared to the whole. And it is further said that a "part" is sometimes taken for a surface, sometimes for a line, and sometimes for a point, insofar as any of these is called a part of a body. It is said that a part, insofar as it is a surface, possesses division in two dimensions; a part, insofar as it is a line, has division in one dimension; but a part, insofar as it is a point, is indivisible.

<column-break/>

If, however, it is asked whether a point is finite, or if the end of a line is a point, it must be said: no, because a point is not the end but the principle of a line; and the end of a line is indivisible just like the principle. Thus, a point is the finite limit <note>original: "terminus"</note> of a line; and just as the end of a line is not the line itself, so a point is not a line. And if it is asked "What is a point?", it is said to be the principle of a line, not a part; and the same applies to the line in respect to the surface. It is further said that a point is not "in a place" <note>original: "in loco"</note>, but is in a magnitude which is in a place; hence surfaces, lines, and points are said to be in a place only <term>by accident</term> <note>original: "per accidens"; meaning they don't have a place of their own, but exist within things that do</note>.

<margin>Wisdom 11</margin>
After this, we must consider lines and surfaces. Here it is said that a line is length without width, the extremities of which are two points. A surface is that which has length and width only, the extremities of which are lines. A body, truly, is that which has length, width, and depth, and whose extremities are surfaces. Secondly, it should be known that every line is either straight or curved. A straight line is that which lies equally between its points. A curved line is that which does not lie equally between its points. And a surface is either plane or curved. A plane surface is that which lies equally between its lines. A curved surface is that which does not lie equally between its lines. And a body is either plane or curved. A plane body is one that has plane surfaces. A curved body is one that has curved surfaces. Afterwards, we must consider the angle: where it is said that an angle is the meeting of two lines at one point.

---

First, it must be known what is meant by that which is called a "finite sensible part," of which it is said that the concept exists in the order of things. It is said that a finite part is that which can be perceived by the senses, as in a stone or a piece of wood; and such a part is properly called "finite" because it has a beginning and an end. It is said that a part is a part of the total quantity, not a part of the essence. And it should be known that quantity is divided into <term>continuous</term> and <term>discrete</term>. Continuous quantity is that whose parts are joined at a single common limit, as is evident in a line, whose parts are joined at a single point; or a surface, whose parts are joined at a single line; or a body, whose parts are joined at a single surface. Discrete quantity, however, is that whose parts are not joined at a single common limit, as is evident in numbers.

It is further said regarding figure: where it is stated that a figure is that which is contained under one or more limits; and this is clear from the definition of a figure in the 1st book of <term>Euclid</term> <note>referring to Euclid’s *Elements*</note>. And it is said that a figure is either plane or solid. A plane figure is one contained under one or more lines. A solid figure is one contained under one or more surfaces. It is further said that figures are either rectilinear or curvilinear. Rectilinear figures are those contained by straight lines. Curvilinear figures are those contained by curved lines. And it is said that rectilinear figures are trilateral, quadrilateral, or multilateral. Trilateral figures are those contained by three lines. Quadrilateral figures are those contained by four lines. Multilateral figures are those contained by more than four lines.

<column-break/>

...I would give form to according to only one part of its magnitude, which is in the surface. And it is said that every plane figure is finite, because it is enclosed within its limits. And it is further said that a point is that which has no part. A line is length without width. A surface is that which has length and width only. And all these things are evident in the principles of <term>Euclid</term>. And it is said that every quantity is finite in itself, although it can be called "infinite" in a certain respect; just as a line is called "infinite" in terms of its length.

And it is said that every figure has its own properties; just as a circle has its center, and a triangle has its three angles. And it is said that a triangle is a figure contained by three straight lines, and it has three angles. And it is said that a quadrangle is a figure contained by four straight lines, and it has four angles. And it is said that a circle is a plane figure contained by a single line, which is called the circumference; in the middle of which is a point, from which all lines drawn to the circumference are equal. And it is said that a sphere is a solid figure contained by a single surface; in the middle of which is a point, from which all lines drawn to the surface are equal.

Afterwards, we must consider motion: where it is said that motion is the act of a being in <term>potency</term> insofar as it is in potency <note>original: "motus est actus entis in potentia prout est in potentia"; the classic Aristotelian definition of change or movement</note>. And it is said that motion is twofold: one natural and the other violent. Natural motion is that which arises from an intrinsic principle. Violent motion is that which arises from an extrinsic principle <note>Natural motion is like a rock falling (its nature), while violent motion is like a rock being thrown (an outside force)</note>.

<summary>This page defines the geometric foundations of physical reality, detailing the relationships between points, lines, surfaces, and bodies according to Aristotelian and Euclidean principles. It also distinguishes between continuous and discrete quantity and concludes with the standard scholastic definitions of motion.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on classification, this page moves into a deep metaphysical analysis of definitions. It explains how a general category (genus) and a specific trait (difference) combine to form a single, unified concept (species), using Aristotle's theories of matter and form as a model.</meta>

<page-num>128v</page-num>

<margin>
<unclear>difference</unclear>
<unclear>of genus</unclear>
<unclear>of species</unclear>
</margin>

Here, however, from some single species, they cannot be mutually **per se** <note>original: "per se"; meaning essentially or by its very nature</note> from others, as if there were some species which is **per se** one, just like the forms that are parts of some whole and constitute that whole **per se**. Nevertheless, those species that constitute that specific species are one **per se**. Similarly, that which is one **per se** is composed of things where one is potentiality <term>potentia</term> <note>the capacity to become something</note> and the other is act <term>actus</term> <note>the actual realization or "form" of that thing</note>, just like form and matter. 

In the same way, in these differences, one relates to the other as potentiality to act; for the genus relates to the difference as matter to form, and thus from them, a unity **per se** is made. Hence, a species is said to be one **per se**; but this is not the case for differences if they are taken as many species, because then they would be many, and not a single species. 

So it is clear from what has been said how the species is one and how the differences are one within it. I say then to the first argument: when it is said that differences are distinct among themselves, I say this is true insofar as they are in the genus, but not insofar as they are in the species. For in the species they are united, as was said above; and although they differ from each other, yet in the species they are made into one single thing. 

To the second [argument]: when it is said that differences are diverse things and thus do not make one, I say this is true if they were diverse things existing outside the mind <note>original: "extra intellectum"; referring to physical objects rather than mental concepts</note>, but it is not so in the species. Because the species, although it is one thing in the mind, nevertheless includes many differences which are parts of itself. 

To the third: when it is said that differences are beings in act, I say that differences are beings in potentiality with respect to the species; because the species is a being in act, and the differences are parts of it. Thus it is clear that differences are one in the species, and not outside the species.

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the unity of genus and species, this page transitions into a detailed examination of the relationship between matter (potentiality) and form (actuality). It explores how matter serves as the underlying subject of change while form provides the definition, purpose, and perfection of a being, drawing heavily on Aristotle’s Physics and Metaphysics.</meta>

<margin>matter</margin>
...toward decay: if it should cease to have some specific form, it is not for that reason "loseable" <note>original: "amissibile"</note> simply as this or that specific thing. Rather, because it exists in itself as a potentiality <term>potentia</term> <note>the capacity to become something else</note> to be this or that, it is thus a cause and a principle of being. We do not call that from which a thing is made a "loss," but rather we define the thing according to what it currently is. For matter relates to being just as it relates to the process of becoming. Just as nothing is said to become out of nothing—but rather matter is that out of which it becomes—so too a thing is said to be something else through the matter from which it consists. But before our transformation <note>original: "metathesim"; likely referring to the change of state or substantial change</note>, it is said to "become" or "decay" from that matter; and this is because matter is that *from which* and *in which* form exists.
<margin>form</margin>
Form, however, is that *through which* a thing exists. Therefore, form is directed toward this: it is both the end <term>finis</term> <note>the goal or final cause</note> and the limit itself. For form is the very "being" <note>original: "esse"</note> of a thing. Since form is the perfection of all things, that which is limited is said to have this "end" because it possesses being. Therefore, the end itself is called the form of the thing. Because all motion and every action tends toward form—since a thing desires its own being and whatever it is—form is called both the "end" and "the good." For the "end" is that for the sake of which a thing exists, and for this reason it is also "good," because it is desirable. Since all things desire their own being and perfection, all things desire form. For any thing, insofar as it exists in act <term>in actu</term> <note>actually realized rather than just potential</note>, is thus good and more perfect. Therefore, we have not said in vain that form is divine and optimal. But this form must also be traced back to its origin; and thus we conclude regarding it: for this is the cause and the principle of being, and ultimately, it is what is being sought in the present inquiry.

<column-break/>

...its own and proper being, which is why it does not have this "end" from itself, but rather through the rational principle <term>ratio</term> that is within it. Because of this, nothing should be taken from a substance by way of a universal form, but rather as something that possesses the "what-ness" <term>quidditas</term> <note>the essence or "what it is" of a thing</note> of the substance in itself. As Aristotle says: just as something known can be understood through its magnitude, so he says this part of a thing is different from the thing itself—not indeed in essence, but because both are what that thing is, and nevertheless they possess this character of substance. Therefore, it is necessary for this to be "matter in itself" within the thing, because it exists of itself. Nothing can act upon itself from itself; rather, it is like that in which something can act for its own sake. Therefore, it has this action within itself but not *from* itself. And for this reason Aristotle says: 
It is clearly manifest that from love, those [beings] rejoice in the intellect, and this is being itself and its perfection. It is like that from which something must become, and it is the subject of the action. This is the "that from which," but this other is a "this-something" <note>original: "hoc aliquid"; Aristotle's term for a specific, individual substance</note>. Because of this, Aristotle says: If it is here, it is matter. But it must be both that and the rational principle which, insofar as it exists, belongs to something—not just existing in that way, but so that it refers to something else. 
Thus, matter is a part of some whole, which is called the "genus" of matter. For example, a body, or a straight line, or a figure. And therefore, if something exists in relation to something else—as this is to that—Aristotle says matter exists through its quiddity. It is such that it is a part of a whole; but that is the thing which is not yet in act, but is matter. Just as lines are parts fitting themselves together equally; and Aristotle says this in connection to this principle where he discusses form, at the end of the book titled *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*</note>, Book Three. And since the forms of bodies are said to "vanish" <note>original: "evanescere"</note> when they undergo separation, it seems we must conclude regarding matter that it is nothing other than "sensible matter," which in itself does not possess the rational principle that is understood. For if it is considered as it is in itself, it is entirely formless, and it only falls under a secondary or accidental principle so that it may be understood as the "subject" <term>subiectum</term> <note>the underlying 'stuff' that receives qualities</note>. Therefore, Aristotle says that what he calls "being" is not "being in act" insofar as it is intelligible and has its own proper action, but rather as "potentially intelligible." Therefore, it is an imperfect being. For this reason, the ancients called this "primary matter" <term>materia prima</term>, which is neither in act nor properly called form; but rather, it is related to form as it appears to be something. And since that thing which is the cause in things, having the power of generation in itself, is nothing but that in which the generation is said to occur—because that is the matter of the thing in which it is said to become or to be corrupted... <meta>catchword: nor does it seem</meta>

---

...nor does the opinion of those ancients seem right who prevail, nor those who denied matter, claiming it is nothing but a part of the substance which exists in power and in the element. However, there is another root of generation, because besides the matter which is similar to the rational principle in which the thing exists, the thing itself declares this to be present in generable things. For if it were only in the element, then it would no longer be the thing which is said to be in the element, but rather something else by which it would be constituted. Therefore, this is said to belong to the soul <note>original: "animi"</note>. And because it is in sensible things, it is that thing by which it is named, which is matter. For it is called "matter" in that which is in itself, which is said to be a "part of the thing." And it is said that this [subject] possesses a part of the thing; for thus it is said: matter is necessary. And in all finite things, it does not appear again from matter, but as if from something in itself; it is said to be something other than the thing itself, being only the "matter in which" it exists. Thus, that is called the thing from which the thing is said to be. 
And for this reason, one must place this "end" in things. Therefore, things that come to be do so not entirely from their own part, but from the part of the thing insofar as they possess this part of the rational principle which motion has made known. A thing exists in a thing only insofar as there is matter in it for the sake of which the thing itself is made. If, therefore, this matter is different from the "becoming" of things, then one must ask with fear: how must something be made from matter? And if it is so, it can only be directed toward this very thing: so that we may say this rational principle of generation occurs because the thing itself has being in matter. Whence it passes itself along to this, only so that it may become an "end," so that it begins to be something. Aristotle discusses this matter in his book of *Metaphysics*. 
But that is something else, and this is not the end of the thing, nor does it come again from the substance. Rather, it is because of the part by which the thing is "carried" from this state to its being, just as the element and the quiddity of the thing are. From this, it is clear that this "end" is the cause and the being. And since we cannot [fully] be this end, it is necessary to proceed into the "denials" <note>original: "negu", likely abbreviation for negationibus</note> and it would be called such; and thus of itself, it is "generable" and is properly so-called. But what it might be in things—and concerning this matter in which the thing exists and through which and in which the thing itself is—the thing is different from the matter which is "being." Therefore, it is spoken of as "repairable" <note>original: "reparabilis"</note> and of eternity, where it is discussed: that which is said to be a thing "in potentiality." For as he says, they were indeed forms which are now in the proximities of generation—even in the forms of Lions <note>original: "Leonibus"; possibly a specific biological example used in the source text</note>—where it says things are said neither to become nor to perish by themselves. And thus proper knowledge is had: for in the thing, and in that which is called a "part," the thing is understood neither properly by itself, but as having its own rational principle, just as it appears from itself. Thus, a thing is spoken of in things insofar as it is that very thing; wherefore one must know what is in it and what the property of its genus may be.

<column-break/>

...it cannot be said to come from something, nor to exist by itself in things. Even in the very process which is properly called "generation," it is not said to "be" [in a finished sense], but it is that which is something within it. But that which is in the thing, since it is called a certain "being" <term>ens</term>, and from this the thing itself exists, is part of generation insofar as it is "something." 
Then one must see regarding the thing if it has its own rational principle as it is in itself. If, therefore, something were acted upon in the thing, the thing is not outside of substance, and therefore it is always "being" insofar as it is moved into something—specifically in things, from which it will also become what is said to be "in motion." And just as it is said to come from anything, so too it comes from itself; and this happens frequently in things insofar as it is said to be "that which is," because it is said to be "from matter." 
But if it is "form," from which "being" takes its divided part, then it is "being in itself" <term>ens per se</term> and "being in act" <term>ens in actu</term>, insofar as it is that thing. This is in common, according to which it is not "this" by itself as it is spoken of universally, nor as it is spoken of in substance, but as it is spoken of "in itself" according to this part. Therefore, a thing is not named from its own form [alone], but according to that which it possesses primarily; and thus it is said to be "from form." And properly, at this point, where it is limited in generable things in which it is received, this is said to be "its being through itself" <note>original: "esse sui per se"</note>. Hence a certain part belongs to the thing itself, concerning mutable things and concerning those forms of the elements themselves, so much so that in those things which are made, and again from the elements, and from the thing which is in this, it is proper. 
And since the thing itself makes that which is called "this" and "that," but insofar as it is called the thing itself in which they are made, it makes other things. Therefore, it is spoken of regarding these, and from these it is seen in bodies, so that in its own thing according to itself, form appears to "become" in it, just as Aristotle says. And it is said in the thing: if the thing is defined according to what it does, the thing is said to be "from its own form" as it is. 
And it is necessary to know this "end" in which the thing exists, because the thing itself, insofar as it is in itself—specifically in the thing and in the matter itself where form is—this form seems properly "intelligible" <term>intelligibilis</term> <note>capable of being understood by the mind, rather than just sensed by the eyes</note> insofar as matter is in it. And according to what is said to have this "end," just as it is acted upon in things and in those things which are becoming, so the thing appears where there is being. And how the thing itself relates to this matter and to its own nature—which does not "become" in the thing insofar as it is already the thing—and this is in things. For it is said in this way: that this form might be properly the "end" of the thing. For the thing itself, insofar as it is spoken of in this way, and insofar as the thing is spoken of in it, has this "end" of the thing, as it is taken in the thing and is thus in it.

<summary>This page explores the Aristotelian metaphysical relationship between matter and form, defining matter as the potentiality from which things become and form as the actuality, goal, and "perfection" of a being. It references Aristotle's *On the Soul* and *Metaphysics* to explain how form acts as the final cause or "end" that gives a substance its specific identity.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on matter and form as the fundamental principles of being, this page shifts focus toward the "spirit" (spiritus) and "natural heat" as the mediators between the soul and the physical body. It draws on Galen's medical-philosophical framework to explain how the soul's vegetative power—responsible for growth and nutrition—operates through the physical elements.</meta>

...if they are not withdrawn, they infer from this as it seems: Galen, in his sixth book *On the Spirit* <note>original: "Galenus 6 spiritu dicit"</note>, says that the natural power of heat does not cause inflation; and through the guide and union in one union, it seems its parts—whether of heat or moisture—are seen to be obscured, just as it relates to the form, which is like the form to the moisture of fire. Clearly, just as some power might happen to exist as the fire of the principle for what is external, it is the nature of the part as an element through power. Or, the vegetative power <term>virtus vegetabilis</term> <note>the aspect of the soul responsible for basic biological functions like growth and nutrition</note> itself is naturally pious; thus the power of fire consists in the support of the spirit. For nothing is said to be a body through itself... nor was it perpetual through itself. Or, there is an abundance against fate, a coupling which has been of the moist spirit, while the soul precedes nature. The form is either from the abundance against [fate], or the nature of the "fater" <note>original: "fatoris"; likely referring to a governing or 'fating' principle</note> has been in the form, and thus it holds the power of heat from the nourishment against it. If fire is that which is fate, the soul is the soul and the form which is in itself of the power of fates; through itself, it will be the fates themselves and its parts are the distinct parts of the "fater." If the soul has been, it is the soul of a different "fater"; it is the powers of nature, and the soul is the soul so that it runs into the form of matter. Or, the vegetative parts of nature were another fate, just like the soul which will be; however, that fate is the form of the soul itself, namely fate with the body, or the nature of fates, provided however it is fate.

<column-break/>

...indeed, whoever they may be, <unclear>his</unclear> <unclear>orders</unclear> which are thus through themselves would not <unclear>lead</unclear> the soul toward the form of power. For the soul is the prior form <term>forma prior</term> <note>the organizing principle that exists logically before the physical body it animates</note> which exists through the essence of the plant as power. For matter is the prior form which is the fate of the plant regarding some common matter in the "ray" <note>original: "radio"</note> which is the plant. Thus, nature is the prior form which is in the fate of the bodies of nature, from which the spirit shall be. They are joined by the support of the spirit, so that nature exists, and that which will be is outside the body for the spirit. Thus, the spirit is the soul which, through the power that will be in the common powers of fate, consists in support of the form. The nature of the spirit is the soul of fire, and the nature of fate [exists] through the form of the soul in fate, just as the form which is in the fate of the soul of fire. The nature of the soul is prior to the bodies of nature—it is the power, as said above—just as the form which is in fate is fate; according to fate, the powers of fate, which can [be] the form of fire, is the soul. And of the fire of the form of fates, the nature of the part which is the soul in fate... fate is the nature of the "fater," it is the form itself. And fate is the vegetative power in fate; the soul of the spirit is fate according to that which will be and the powers. However, let that fate become the power of the soul itself in fate; the soul of the spirit is fate, that very fate; the fate of the spirit through that very thing.

<column-break/>

...the operation in the region of the heavens <note>original: "regione celi"</note> should not be according to the powers... it is possible, namely, in the proportion of the higher fates. The form of fire is simple, standing through itself, which [is] before some matter. If indeed there is an abundance of those things which are from the outside, it is not impassive as they regard themselves; for the spirit which will be, they contain and conquer within. They are of the vegetative [powers], or they are toward the form; or the soul is matter, or the soul is not in that spirit for the sake of nourishing it. The power of moist heat flows down into those elements of its own nature; and spirit is joined to spirit through fate. The way of vegetation <term>via vegetationis</term> <note>the biological process of growth and development</note> is itself a perpetual fate; it defines it namely according to that which is in the spirit. The nature of the "fater" is the form itself, and fate is the vegetative power in fate. In the fate of the spirit, the soul is according to that fate which will be, and the powers. However, let that fate become the power of the soul itself in fate; the soul of the spirit is fate, that very fate; the fate of the spirit through that very thing. Let the soul be and the fate which is the form of fire in fate; the soul of fire is the form itself. Let fate be through itself, fate can [be] the soul—namely the soul which is outside. Nature is the powers of the spirit, that very nature; that which is fate through the soul. Let the spirit be for fate; thus nature is fate; let the spirit be the form for fate.

<column-break/>

...of human nature and its [parts], and if it is to have a body, looking toward the body and the homeland, the soul of fire in order. If the soul has been restored, the form yielded, having converged there; may the condition of the same form be better. They are of nature, or that which is more perfect, those parts which proceed from themselves. Nature is such that it exists in another; nor is it such that it is from the nature which exists, but consequently that which is given to each through the paths of the soul which is in the powers of the soul, just as it is of the soul in it. Let the spirit be the soul which is of the form of fire; nature is the fire in the soul through the power which will be in the common powers. And the powers which will be; however, let that fate become the power of the soul itself in fate. The soul of the spirit is fate, that very fate; the fate of the spirit through that very thing. Let nature be, and that which will be is outside the body for the spirit. Thus the spirit is the soul which is the nature of fates... the soul and it seems the form itself. Fate, it seems, is nature; it seems to be the soul of fate. Thus, let the soul be, and that fate for fates according to that which is the powers of fire. That which will be outside is the prior form; the nature of fates is the nature of fates, the soul itself. And it seems the form itself; fate, it seems, is nature; it seems to be the soul of fate. Thus, let the soul be, and that fate for fates according to that which is the powers of fire.

<meta>The previous page discussed the relationship between faith and works. <summary>This page analyzes the duality of the human intellect, distinguishing between its "active" role (which processes information) and its "possible" or "passive" role (which receives and stores knowledge). It frames these functions within the broader Aristotelian concepts of "act" and "potency" as they relate to the essence of the rational soul.</summary>
<keywords>active intellect, possible intellect, potency, matter, form, act, rational soul, essence, prime matter, Aristotelian psychology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of the mind and the soul. While the previous page established the soul as form and potentiality using Aristotelian categories, this section shifts to the methodology of knowledge (scientia). It explores how different disciplines—geometry, astronomy, and psychology—use "reason" and "rational modes" to reach certain truth.</meta>

For those, there is certainly contemplation not only of the sun but also of the true magnitudes and of very many uses. If study and industry are applied to these, the result is certainly not to be regretted; for in this way, there is both a certain path to discovery, a path that is both attainable and concise. This appears first in those matters of the unrefined <note>original: "rudiū," likely referring to basic or foundational principles</note> where there is a certain line on the earth which is said to be equidistant to the heavens, such as on the horizon; from this, that power is evident. Then, in those things which are highest, here is the way of finding: when it is found through something of this sort of foundational principle, or marked on the earth, then it is called the path of assumption <note>original: "via sūptiuæ," referring to knowledge based on premises or accepted starting points</note>, and a certain path; then it is called the rational path, as appears in the work of geometers. Theirs is a certain, rational, and assumptive path, as is said in the *Physics* <note>original: "pīo," an abbreviation for Aristotle's *Physica*</note>, where it says that the geometer tells us this line is such and such, and does not care whether it is so in reality, provided he has the foundation of the mind, where he evidently finds the foundation and truth. For when such a reason is proposed, since it then reasoned—because it is true in the mind—then his reason tells him that it is true in reality; and thus reason is a rational reason and a certain path. 

This also appears in the work of astrologers where they seek [knowledge]. For instance, they give certain things as the logic of astronomy, and they wish to describe these lines and these reasons. Because the path is assumptive and rational, they wish to be certified through reason that those things which are in the heavens are true. But a rational assumptive path is not truly "rational" <note>in the highest sense</note> because it is not the ultimate reason. Where he says "and thus it is rational," reason is that which expresses the underlying cause, as appears in the science of the spirit and the soul <note>original: "scia de spū & aia," referring to the medieval psychological treatise *De spiritu et anima*</note>. There we say that where the reason is, it is rational because the rational assumptive path does not state the underlying cause, but only states a rational mode. Hence he says that power is rational, that is, a rational mode. Thus true science is that which speaks of the underlying cause, as Aristotle says in the first book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de aia"</note>. He says that where there is true science, there the account is called reason, and then it is said to be rational. This is because the rational path is within reason, or because reason is in the power of the mind, or because reason is within reason itself, since it is the science of reason. Aristotle says this in the second book of *On the Soul*; for he says that a rational mode is a rational mode because it expresses the reason. But the rational mode of a science does not [always] express the reason, but merely states a rational method, and therefore it is called a rational mode. Thus, the science which expresses the reason, which is called rational, is that which expresses the reason for the question. Hence this kind of science is called rational, as Aristotle says in the second book of *On the Soul*: place a certain reason of the mind—

<summary>This manuscript page explores the definition of "rational" as it applies to different sciences like geometry and astronomy, contrasting "assumptive" reasoning with the certain "rational path" of the mind. It heavily references Aristotle's Physics and Metaphysics to establish that true science must express the underlying reason of its subject rather than just following a rational mode.</summary>

<summary>This page explores the scholastic definitions of will, desire, and grace, arguing that for an act to be truly meritorious, it must be directed toward an "end" (the ultimate good) through the influence of grace. It distinguishes between natural desire and the specific disposition or "habit" of the soul that allows it to act in accordance with divine purpose.</summary>
<keywords>will, grace, final cause, merit, appetite, habit, scholasticism, intention, moral act</keywords>

<summary>This page explores the ontological nature of the soul, defining it through its relationship to life, essence, and truth, while distinguishing between its existence "through itself" and its existence "in time." The text uses a repetitive, meditative structure to assert the identity of these concepts within the divine and human order.</summary>

--- Page 271 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholastic discussion of the soul’s faculties. While the previous page focused on the intellectual light and the return of the soul to its divine source, the author now transitions into "appetite"—the faculty of desire and striving—explaining how various forms of life are drawn toward what they perceive as good.</meta>

Now there were three principles by which <term>appetite</term> <note>original: "appetitus," referring to a natural striving or desire toward a goal</note> is governed: the first is knowledge, the second is appetite itself, and the third is motion. However, appetite can be understood in two ways: in one way as the power of appetite itself, and in another way as the very act of desiring. Yet the power of appetite does not move anything except through the mediation of the act of desiring. Furthermore, the act of desiring follows knowledge; therefore, if there is no knowledge, there is no appetite. But knowledge can be of two kinds: that which is <term>through itself</term> <note>original: "per se," meaning essential or intrinsic</note>, and that which is <term>accidental</term> <note>original: "per accidens," meaning incidental or through external means</note>. Knowledge "through itself" is that which proceeds from the principles of knowing, such as the knowledge of first principles and logical conclusions. Accidental knowledge, however, is that which proceeds from other things, such as when we know something through the senses.

Therefore, the appetite that follows knowledge "through itself" is called the **rational appetite** or the **will**. The appetite that follows accidental knowledge is called the **sensitive appetite**. From this, it is clear that the will exists only in those beings possessing reason; however, the sensitive appetite is found in all animals. Moreover, just as knowledge is of two kinds, so too appetite is of two kinds: for there is a certain **natural appetite**, and a certain **animal appetite**.

<column-break/>

**Natural appetite** is nothing other than a certain inclination of a thing toward its own end, which does not follow the knowledge of the one desiring, but rather follows the knowledge of the one who established nature. For just as an arrow is moved toward a target by the archer, so natural things are moved toward their ends by Him who established nature. Hence, natural appetite is nothing else than a certain disposition of a thing toward that which is suitable for it according to its own nature. In **animal appetite**, however, knowledge is required, because an animal is not moved toward anything unless it is perceived through knowledge.

Therefore, animal appetite is of two kinds: one which follows the perception of the senses, and this is called the **sensitive appetite**; and another which follows the perception of the intellect, and this is called the **will**. Now, the sensitive appetite differs from natural appetite in this: that natural appetite is determined toward a single thing, just as fire is determined to move upward; but the sensitive appetite is not determined toward one thing, but relates to many things according to the diversity of what is perceived.

<meta>catchword: natural</meta>

<page-num>265</page-num>

It is natural, however, for appetite to follow knowledge, because appetite is directed toward a "perceived good." For in those things that exist "through themselves," appetite follows the **form**; <note>original: "forma," the defining essence or blueprint of a thing that gives it its nature</note> hence, just as a thing has its being through its form, so it has an inclination toward the good through its form. In natural things, the form is the principle of being and the principle of acting; therefore, the inclination that follows a natural form is called natural appetite. In animals, however, the form is twofold: one which is the principle of being, and this is the **soul**; the other which is the principle of knowing, such as a <term>sensible or intelligible species</term>. <note>original: "species," here meaning the mental image or concept by which we recognize an object</note>

Therefore, the appetite that follows a "known form" is called an animal or intellectual appetite. And just as natural forms are determined, so also are natural appetites determined. However, the forms perceived through the senses or the intellect are many and diverse; hence, the appetites following them are directed toward many and diverse things. This is why animals are not moved toward only one thing, but toward many, according to what appears to them as good or suitable.

<column-break/>

There were some to whom it seemed that the will and appetite do not differ except as a genus and a species, such that the will would be a certain species of appetite. For they say that appetite is common to both the natural and the animal, while the will is the "rational animal appetite." But this does not seem to be true according to the opinion of <term>The Philosopher</term> <note>A standard scholastic reference to Aristotle</note> in the book *On the Soul*, where he says that the **will** is in the reason, but the **sensitive appetite** is in the irrational part of the soul.

Hence, the will and the sensitive appetite are distinguished according to the distinction of the powers of perception, namely, the intellect and the senses. For just as the intellect and the senses are different powers, so the will and the sensitive appetite are different appetitive powers. Indeed, natural appetite is not some power added onto the essence of a thing, but is the very inclination of the essence toward its end. The will and the sensitive appetite, however, are powers that operate through knowledge, and therefore they differ from one another according to the diversity of the knowledge they follow.

<summary>This page defines the different types of "appetite" (striving) in scholastic philosophy, distinguishing between natural inclination (like gravity), animal desire (based on senses), and the rational will (based on the intellect).</summary>
<keywords>appetite, will, natural appetite, sensitive appetite, reason, intellect, soul, form, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 272 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous discussion on the soul's appetite and knowledge toward the external influences on the world. The author shifts from the internal "light" of the intellect to a physical and metaphysical analysis of light (lux and lumen) and how celestial bodies act as instruments of divine governance over the Earth.</meta>

Here we also deal with the difference that exists between **source-light** and **radiated-light** <note>original: "lux" and "lumen." Medieval thinkers distinguished between the essence of light in a source and the light that travels through space.</note>. For **source-light** is said to be in a shining body as if in a "subject" <note>the substance or thing in which a quality exists</note>: hence it is called an active and fundamental quality. However, **radiated-light** is said to be the "species" <note>an image or likeness</note> of light which is spread through a medium, and it is a passive and intentional quality. This seems to be the opinion of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of *On the Soul*. In a second way, it is understood as that brightness which is in a luminous body, not as it exists in a subject, but as it is in the process of becoming; in this way, radiated-light is the "flow" of source-light. In a third way, light is used to refer to the ray itself, which is direct radiated-light.

There is indeed a certain celestial influence, which <term>astrologers</term> <note>original: "astrologi"; in the medieval period, this term covered both what we now call astronomy and the study of celestial influences</note> call a certain divine, physical, and natural power, through which the celestial bodies act upon these lower things. This power exists in the celestial bodies as if in a subject, and is spread through the medium as if through an instrument.

<column-break/>

...not only according to my own resolution, but also according to others. **Source-light** exists in the celestial bodies as if in a subject. Astrologers also say that the celestial bodies have an influence on these lower things through light and heat. For there is a certain divine and celestial power which is derived from the sun and stars to these <term>sublunary</term> <note>original: "sublunaria," meaning everything below the sphere of the Moon, i.e., the Earthly realm</note> bodies. 

And although light is in all stars, it is not there equally; for every star has its own proper light, distinct from another. For just as one star differs from another in magnitude, so it also differs in brightness and power. As for the fact that the stars seem to shine less than the sun, this is not from a lack of light in them, but from their distance from us. Therefore, all the learned doctors agree on this: that the celestial bodies are luminous by nature, and that their light is the cause of many effects in these lower regions.

<column-break/>

Just as source-light is in them as if in fountains, so also radiated-light proceeds from them to illuminate this sublunary world. And it is said to be in the sun and stars not only as in a subject, but as in an "effective and preservative principle" <note>the active cause that creates and maintains something</note>. For although the matter of the heavens is one in essence, it is not one in its readiness for light. For one part of the same matter can be more disposed to receiving the form of light than another. 

Hence, in the heavens, there is not the same density or rarity everywhere. For the stars are the denser parts of their celestial sphere, and therefore they shine more and spread light. However, the part of the sphere which is not a star is more rare and transparent, and therefore it does not shine in that way. <unclear>Hence</unclear> it appears that the diversity of light in the heavens does not arise from a diversity of matter, but from the different disposition of the same matter according to "more and less."

<column-break/>

...one part of the same matter <unclear>can be</unclear> disposed to receiving the form of light, as is clear in the fixed stars, which according to <unclear>astronomers</unclear> have different powers and operations. And although the heaven is a simple body, it does not lack "organs" to carry out different operations, just as we see in other bodies. 

Therefore, just as in the human body there are different senses for different operations, so in the heavens there are stars which are like the "senses" and "organs" of the world itself. Through these organs, the heaven <unclear>flows into</unclear> these lower things and governs them according to divine disposition. <unclear>From</unclear> which it is clear that, just as the soul rules the body through the organs of the senses, so God rules the world through the celestial bodies. In this, however, there is no "necessity of fate" <note>the author is careful to avoid suggesting that the stars force human actions, preserving free will</note>, but only a certain natural order established by God for the preservation of the universe.

<summary>This page explains the medieval distinction between the essence of light (lux) and its radiation (lumen), using this framework to describe how stars act as 'organs' through which God governs the physical world. It emphasizes that celestial influence is a natural order of the universe rather than a fatalistic or magical necessity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of knowledge and light. While the previous page addressed the physical and metaphysical properties of light (source-light and radiated-light) and celestial influences, this page applies those concepts to the human intellect. It explores how the soul, as the lowest of intellectual beings, requires both the senses and a "superior light" to attain knowledge.</meta>

<margin>3. On the Soul</margin>
Since the human soul is the lowest in the grade of intellectual beings, it has nevertheless from its own nature the quality of being unifiable to a body, and through this, it is ordered toward receiving the knowledge of things through the senses: and therefore it is said in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s treatise on psychology and the mind</note> that the soul is like a **blank slate** <note>original: "tabula rasa"</note> upon which nothing has been written.
But against this reasoning, there seems to be what
<margin>Book of Causes</margin>
is said in the *Book of Causes* <note>An anonymous work based on Proclus, often attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages, which explores the hierarchy of being</note>, that every intellect is full of forms: but this is understood according to the relationship it has to the **First Principle** <note>God, the source of all being</note>, from whom it receives all its perfection. But that knowledge is not innate to it, but is infused into it by the First Principle according to its own capacity. However, the human soul is not made in this way, but is made to be unifiable to a body: and therefore it is necessary that it receives the knowledge of things through the body and through the senses: and this is what is said in the third book of *On the Soul*, that the **possible intellect** <note>the capacity of the mind to receive or be shaped by new information</note> is nothing of the things that exist before it understands.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Opinion of Alexander and Avicenna</margin>
In this order, we see that what is higher always has power and influence over what is lower: and therefore a superior intelligence has power over the human soul. And thus the human soul, in order to understand, needs a certain influence from superior substances: and this appears most clearly in those matters pertaining to faith and to prophecy. Hence it is said that prophecy comes from divine influence through the mediation of angels. But regarding this, there is a double opinion. For some say that the human soul does not understand except through the influence of the **agent intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentiae agentis"; a separate, external mind that illuminates human thought, a concept favored by some Arabic philosophers</note>: and this was the position of **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a Greek commentator on Aristotle</note> and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath</note>. But against this is what the **Philosopher** <note>The standard medieval title for Aristotle</note> says in the third book of *On the Soul*, that it is necessary for there to be something in the soul by which it "becomes all things," and something by which it "makes all things": and that by which it makes all things he calls the **agent intellect** <note>original: "intellectum agentem"; the active power of the human mind to process sensory data into abstract concepts</note>. Hence, the agent intellect is something belonging to the soul, and not a separate substance.

<column-break/>

<margin>On the agent and possible intellect</margin>
The agent intellect is nothing other than a certain power of the soul, through which the soul makes "intelligible things" actual: for just as light makes colors actual which were only potential <note>colors exist in the dark but cannot be seen until light hits them</note>, so the agent intellect makes things "intelligible" in reality which were only potential in the **mental images** <note>original: "phantasmatibus"; the sensory images stored in the memory/imagination</note>. And therefore it is necessary that in the human soul there is something that is in potentiality to all things that can be understood, which is called the **possible intellect**; and something that makes all intelligible things actual, which is called the **agent intellect**. And this is what the Philosopher intends to say. Hence it is clear that the agent and possible intellect are parts of our soul. But because our soul is the lowest in the order of intellectual beings, it cannot by itself enter into the act of understanding unless aided by a superior light. Hence, just as sight needs external light to see, so our intellect needs a superior light to understand: and this light is the **divine light**. Thus it is said in the <term>Psalm</term> <note>the Book of Psalms in the Bible</note>:
<margin>Psalm 4</margin>
> The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us. <note>Psalm 4:6</note>

<column-break/>

And this is the reason why the soul needs the body and the senses: because it does not have the knowledge of things innate to itself, but must receive it from the senses. Thus it is clear that the human soul is the lowest in the order of intellectual beings. But because it is intellectual, it has some participation in the divine light. And through this light, the human soul judges the truth of things. But this light in the human soul is like a weak light, and therefore it needs help from a superior light in order to understand perfectly. Hence we see that in those things which are above reason, such as the matters of faith, the soul cannot know them except through the **light of grace**, which is a certain supernatural light. And therefore it is said that faith is a gift of God. And this also appears in the prophets, who know things that are future or hidden through the **prophetic light**. Thus it is clear that the human soul needs divine help in all things, as it is said in the *Book of Causes*, that intelligence is above the soul and rules it. And this is what the **Commentator** <note>The standard medieval title for Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the Andalusian philosopher</note> says in the third book of *On the Soul*, that our intellect, in the face of those things which are most manifest, behaves like the **eye of an owl** toward the light of the sun <note>meaning that the most obvious divine truths are too bright/overwhelming for our limited human minds to see clearly without help</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the human soul as the lowest rank of intellectual beings, explaining that it is a "blank slate" requiring the body and senses to gain knowledge. It distinguishes between the "possible intellect" and the "agent intellect," concluding that the human mind requires the aid of divine light and grace to understand higher truths.</summary>

When the **form** <note>In scholastic philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is—for example, the "soul" is the form of a human body.</note> of a thing is considered, it is that from which it possesses its **essence** <note>original: "essentia"; the core identity of a thing.</note>. It is called essence according to the way it gives being to that of which it is the form. It is also called essence according to its status as a form considered in itself, with respect to the being it possesses in itself and the nature it holds among things. 

When considered in this way, it is called the **quiddity** <note>original: "quidditas"; literally the "what-ness" of a thing, or the definition that answers the question "What is it?"</note> of a thing, according to what is stated through a definition. Through this quiddity, the thing exists within a **species** <note>A category of being, like "human" or "horse."</note>. 

Insofar as it is considered in itself, possessing this nature among things, it is called form. And because it has this nature, it is called the quiddity of the thing according to what is stated in the species. Yet, it is not called form in itself in this sense, but rather according to its definition, by which the thing is said to possess this quiddity. It is through this quiddity that it exists in the species.

As if it did not have a superior over itself; but it is possible that the superior of the mind is that which is called **Mind** <note>Capitalized here to refer to the Divine Intellect or God.</note>, and it is through this that one reaches toward God, which is one's own **happiness** <note>original: "felicitas"; in this context, the ultimate fulfillment or "beatitude" of a rational being.</note>. 

The mind is so named because it "measures" <note>A medieval etymological link: "mens" (mind) was often derived from "metior" (to measure).</note>; it measures that which is not above itself, and it measures directly that which it reaches. Nor is the mind directed by passion, but is figuratively the human light.

While the mind is in the Supreme, through the mind, the truth of the mind is the dignity of humanity. The truth of the mind is the good of humanity, which the mind reaches through the guide of the Supreme Human. Above all, through the Supreme, the mind is directed. Figuratively, the mind is the dignity of humanity; the truth of the mind is the truth of the Supreme. The mind, through the mind, reaches toward God and the truth of the mind.

<meta>This page continues the technical psychological analysis of the soul and the intellect, moving from the definition of essence to the mechanisms of perception and understanding. It draws heavily on Aristotle’s *De Anima* (On the Soul) and *Metaphysics* to explain how the human mind transitions from potentiality to actuality.</meta>

# [Left Page]

For they perceive by themselves those things whose difficulty concerns us. Nor are they fit to perceive the reason, or where that reason is, concerning the difficulty of which it is said to be necessary. And there is no **species** <note>In this context, a "species" is not a biological category but a "mental likeness" or "form" that represents an object in the mind.</note> that is made except according to the perfection of the one who established it. Thus, our intellect does not receive its species from **potency** <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to become something else, as opposed to being it already.</note>, nor from some external matter, but rather from another source, as was in some way proven by **Aristotle** in the 4th book of his *Metaphysics*. For he says thus in the beginning: just as our intellect is said to be in potency, so it is essential and operative; so that it receives power just as that which is called a species, which is called **essence**. That species is also called the receiver of power, and it is said to be a species; and that which in some proper way is a species is like the **soul**. And it is called both soul and species, as is any other body in which a species is perceived. Also called species is the intellect that communicates and is handed down; although the intellect is separate, and in this way it is of itself, as the Philosopher <note>Scholastic writers almost always refer to Aristotle simply as "the Philosopher."</note> says: just as the intellect is said to be in potency, so also it is operative. I say, however, that just as "species" is spoken of in many ways, so is there a power whose frequent multiplication is not a proper definition, as he says. And for this reason, there seems to be a definition of this, although some intellect is said to be in potency; just as the intellect which is said to be the intellect **per se** <note>original: "per se"; by itself or essentially.</note>, and the species is the receiver of power, just as our intellect, when it perceives some thing, is said to be **in act** <note>original: "in actu"; currently functioning or fully realized.</note> by perceiving it. This is called "intellect" from one side and "species" from the other; for it is the soul itself perceiving, so that the soul receives and communicates the same essence to the body, as well as the will and the life of the body—that is, this is necessary for its being, and insofar as it is like the soul of a person, he understood the substance of the soul.

<column-break/>

The breaking <note>likely referring to the division of concepts or physical quantities</note> is through the parts from which it is constituted, because through the multiplication of quantity—which is properly called "toward what"—it is only for the wise man, because he sees that what is in something, he wishes to be received into that which is in the soul. And so, by understanding, the thing is **in act** just like the intellect which is called "separate." Our intellect, however, in order to understand, must apply itself to the **operated intellect** <note>original: "intellectui operato"; the mind once it has been informed by knowledge.</note>, and in such a way it is like a species to be perceived, which appears from this: because it perceives, it is called a species in potency and is called "in act." Nothing, however, is corrupted by this twofold understanding of things, just as the soul is said to be "clear" through the fact that it perceives things in species. And these species which are in the soul are said to be in the intellect, but this is only in potency unless it comes from being understood by the intellect itself. It is called "potency"; toward the intellect, it is thus the intellect; in another way, it is the intellect just as the species which are in it are said to be in the intellect. This is clear through another sign: for from the fact that it understands something, it is "in act" within it according to nothingness, because the thing which is called **intelligible** is called "intellect in time," just as there is the intellect *per se*, or the intellect by which something is perceived in the soul and in the intellect toward that which is in the intellect *per se* and that which is in the intellect. And note that because it is a receiver of power—that is, the definition of this is a "species"—and the thing which is in the soul, this is also the species which is in the intellect as it is perceived by it. Thus this species reveals, in a certain way, the potency and that which the soul saw through potency toward the intellect by perceiving the real. This is clear because it is not in it like something received in the soul, but by itself the intellect and the soul are like parts of one whole, as is said of others: namely, that there is a form which is a species, and the soul is in it, and through it something is perceived in the soul through that which is said to be in the intellect, as is clear from what has been said. Because the soul is said to be that which is in act; however, for this to be clear, the soul is in one way a thing in act and in another way not. And so the species which is in the soul is said to be in the intellect *per se*; but by **accident** <note>original: "per accidens"; a non-essential property or circumstance.</note> it is a species to that which is in the soul, and so it is said to be a species in the intellect. It is also clear because, just as the soul, by understanding things in the intellect, receives them into itself in a certain way, so that it is called soul and intellect: which species indeed is called a thing "in potency," just as the intellect is in potency, and thus it perceives the things of which it is said to belong.
