# [Right Page]

<page-num>273</page-num>

For just as it is under the **account of man** <note>original: "sub ratione hominis"; the essential definition or concept of a human being.</note>, and thus has its own essence and being, this principle is said to be that which understands **in habit** <note>original: "in habitu"; possessing knowledge as a lasting disposition, like a person who knows how to read even when they are sleeping.</note> or as intelligible things are in potency; and according to this, there is in the soul some intellect which is in potency. And when the intellect is said to be "in habit," it is as when it understands things, and this is the intellect *per se*. And just as we say that it is the intellect *per se*, it is also said to be that which is "in habit," like a thing which is "in act." Since our intellect is in act, it is called the intellect *per se*. And so the Philosopher says in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*: that there is an intellect which is in potency and an intellect which is in act. And it is spoken of as a thing which is in habit, like a **wise man**; who, at the time when he is said to be "in act," is not spoken of in the same way as one who is called an "intellect in habit." Thus, he is then said to "know" and is said to be "in act," just like that which is said to be wise and to contemplate by its own power. Finally, I say that in this way the soul understands the intelligible thing; its operations are manifold, as the Philosopher says. For some are understood by way of **composition and division** <note>A logical term: "composition" is joining concepts (e.g., "The sky is blue"), and "division" is separating them ("The sky is not green").</note>, such as those things which are true and false, and those things which are **simple** <note>Indivisible concepts, like "man" or "white," before they are put into a sentence.</note>, which it understands by themselves, as is said in the 3rd book of the *Metaphysics*. And it is said that the intellect of "simples" is not false, as is said in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*, where it is said that the intellect of simples is like one "seeing." And this intellect of simples he calls the "intellect in act." He also says there that the intellect is said to be that which belongs to simples, and it is not composite nor false, just as "being" is spoken of in many ways, or as the intellect of simples is said not to be true or false in the same way as other things. In this intellection, there is said to be an intellect which is in potency, like our intellect which understands composite things. As the Philosopher says in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*, there is in our intellect something which is like that which is in material things, or like that which is in matter, and that which is like that which is called the **agent** <note>original: "agens"; the active principle.</note>. This **agent intellect** <note>The "intellectus agens" is the part of the mind that acts like a light, taking raw sensory data and making it understandable to the mind.</note> is thus called *per se* in itself, as is said in the *Book on the Intellect and the Intelligible*: where it is said that there is an intellect *per se* which is in act, which is called "agent," because it is the one that makes intelligible things, which are in potency, to be in act. It appears, therefore, from what has been said, that the intellect in potency is our intellect when it is in a certain abstraction—and it is not abstracted from matter, but is said to be like that which is in matter; and this is what is called "our intellect." But the agent intellect itself is like that which exists *per se*, and it is said to be "in act"; and thus it is said that it is **separate and immortal**.

<column-break/>

Truly, it is perceived through itself, just as the soul, by understanding things that are in the soul concerning "man" and "essence." And according to this, as things are in the soul, so it is said that the soul understands by itself through that intellection, and they are as if in the intellect *per se*; and as things are understood, they are said to be in the intellect. So it is noted, as is said by Aristotle in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*, that there is a certain intellect which is *per se*, which is said to be "in potency," just as it is in matter; and there is another intellect which is called "agent," which is like **art to matter** <note>The way a sculptor's skill (art) acts upon the stone (matter).</note>, or like **light to color**. In this way, the agent intellect is to the potential intellect, and Aristotle proves this in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*. For it is said that the soul is, in a certain way, **all things**. Because it is the species of things—just as the hand is the "organ of organs," so the intellect is the "species of species." And the soul is the **place of species** <note>original: "locus specierum"; a famous Aristotelian definition: the mind doesn't contain the physical things, but the mental forms (species) of them.</note>, but not the whole soul, only the intellect; nor are the species in it "in act," but "in potency." And so it is clear that the soul, according to its intellect, is said to be the place of species, according to the fact that the species are in it. And the species is that which is called "our intellect"; and the species is that which is perceived; and the species is that which is perceived in the soul, as is said in the *Book on the Soul*, where it is said that the species which are in the soul are like the "operated intellect" and that which is said to be in the intellect *per se*. And the species is that which is understood, and this is said to be the intellect which is "in act"—that is, the agent intellect—and this is like that which is in the soul. For just as that which is in the soul is like things that are in matter, as the Philosopher says, so also the species which is in the soul is said to be the agent intellect, as is said in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*, where it is said that the intellect is like that which is "acting." This is clear because it is the one that makes intelligible things, which are in potency, to be in act. But in our soul, the species are in potency; and when they are in the agent intellect, they are in act. Just as **light makes color**, which is in potency, to be "in act" through the light, so also the agent intellect makes the species be in act. This is clear from what has been said: because the soul, according to itself, is said to be in a certain way "all things" insofar as the species are in it. As it is said in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*, where it is stated that the soul is in a certain way all things, and so it is said that the soul is the place of species according to the intellect.

<summary>This page explores the Aristotelian concept of the intellect, specifically the distinction between the potential intellect (the mind's capacity to learn) and the agent intellect (the active power that makes knowledge possible). It concludes that the soul is the 'place of species' and that the agent intellect functions like light, making potential thoughts actual and visible to the mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the intellect, shifting from Aristotelian definitions of "species" and "potency" to a Neoplatonic and mystical exploration of how the human mind perceives God. The author relies heavily on the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite to explain the "Divine Darkness."</meta>

Just as it is in the case of illumination—if light appears as darkness, it is not so that things might seek the darkness, but rather that they might flee from it; so I say in this proposition that light extends itself through privation and removal, but also through excess and eminence, and in this way, it illuminates the darkness. Just as the eye does not properly see darkness, but rather the sun, it cannot see darkness except for the sake of seeing something else, and not for its own sake. Therefore, such things are not the objects of the will. Regarding what is said concerning the **Divine darkness** <term>Divine darkness: or *caligo divina*, a concept from mystical theology where God is described as "dark" not because of a lack of light, but because His light is so intense it blinds the human intellect.</term>; it must be said that just as darkness appears from a multitude of light, so it is here. For although light in itself is supremely knowable, it is not so to our intellects while they are in bodies; hence, to an eye present in the sun, darkness appears. So in this proposition, our intellect, seeing God, sees darkness—not because He Himself is darkness, but because from the excess of light, He appears as darkness to it. As **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian philosopher whose works on "Mystical Theology" were central to medieval thought.</note> says in the *Mystical Theology*, chapter 1: in this, it appears clearly that our intellect is not carried into God according to what He is in Himself, but according to what is in His presence; namely, through excess. Hence it is clear that from the Divine darkness, nothing can be concluded against the previous premises.

And it is clear then, by this mode, what that object is. For it is seen from the foregoing that it is nothing other than the Supreme Truth itself. And so we see that our intellect, since it is a certain mode of being of the soul itself, is called "intellect" insofar as it tends toward that which is its light and subject; but from the fact that it tends toward that which is above itself, it is called **Mind** <term>Mind: original *mens*. In Scholastic thought, "mind" often refers to the higher part of the soul that deals specifically with divine things, while "intellect" handles general understanding.</term>. And then the intellect is said to "be seen." Hence it is clear that "mind" is spoken of in respect to God, and "intellect" in respect to the creature. And then the mind is in the powers of the soul just as the essence is in the soul. Now, "mind" is so called as if "measuring" <note>original: "metiens"; the author is using a common medieval etymological link between *mens* (mind) and *mensis* or *metiri* (to measure).</note> and providing a measure. Hence it is clear that our intellect is called "mind" insofar as it sees itself, and through itself sees all things and rules itself; but it is called "intellect" insofar as it is carried toward external things; and it is called "reason" insofar as it discourses.

<column-break/>

Something can be considered in such a way before our intellect has anything to perceive of itself, and this is insofar as it perceives a certain mode of being which is perfect within itself; as for example it is called "mind" and possesses in itself the fullness of creatures. And from this, the intellect begins to be within itself; and the intellect is that which it sees, just as the essence is the soul. In this way, the intellect is both the subject and that which is seen. Then it has the fullness of a certain light, and that is said to be what is spoken of concerning the Divine darkness. Wherefore Dionysius says: "The Divine darkness is inaccessible light dwelling [within], which no one approaches." And then it is said that the intellect possesses that light for the purpose of seeing all things. This appears clearly from the words of Dionysius in *Mystical Theology*, chapter 1, where he intends this to be the end of our intellect: namely, that it may know God Himself. And then he says that this mode of knowing is above the intellect itself, just as God is above it.

Hence it is clear that the object of our intellect is light itself; and from this light, it sees all other things. Dionysius calls this mode the "unknown deity"; namely, insofar as we see God not according to Himself, but insofar as He is the object. And then the intellect conducts itself like the eye toward the sun. But there is a difference: because the light of the sun is not that which the eye sees [directly], but is that by which it sees. In this matter, however, it is different, because the Divine light is that which it sees; and this is clear because God is light. And then Dionysius says in *Mystical Theology*, chapter 2, that we do not see God like a thing which is below us is seen—such as a stone or a piece of wood—but we see God by not seeing. Just as the eye does not see the sun [directly without being blinded], but sees it as an object; and this "seeing" is called "not seeing," insofar as that which we see is above us.

---

A certain nature as it could be received; but now we see as through a mirror and in a riddle <note>original: "in speculo et in enigmate"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12, describing the imperfect nature of human knowledge of God on earth.</note>; and this is the darkness. And then it is said that the soul, elevated in such a way, is as if in a certain darkness; as Dionysius says in *Mystical Theology*, chapter 1, where he says: "But you, O Timothy, leave behind the sensible and the intelligible, and all things that are not and those that are; and toward the unity of God, as far as is possible, rise up unknowingly." And then in that darkness, the intellect sees all things; hence it is called "luminous darkness." And then the soul is said to be united with God. In this way, Dionysius says in *Mystical Theology*, chapter 2: "It behooves us to come to be in this luminous darkness, so that through that which we do not see, we may see; and through this very thing, we may know." And this is to know God Himself through ignorance; and through this ignorance, we know Him better than through any science. This is clear from what he says: "For God is not known through science, but through ignorance." Hence he says in *Mystical Theology*, chapter 3, that then the soul is said to be "obscured by darkness." But that light is "luminous darkness"; it is called darkness insofar as our intellect does not perceive it, just as the eye does not see the sun in itself; but it is called luminous insofar as it is light in itself, and insofar as it sees all things through that light.

Hence it appears clearly that the object of our intellect in this life is God; and we have this mode of knowing here, namely through the Divine light which is in us. But because this light is not the essence of God itself as it is in itself, we are therefore said to see God "in a mirror and in a riddle." And this is what Paul says to the Corinthians, chapter 13: "We see now through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face." Hence it is clear that in the **homeland** <term>homeland: original *patria*, the standard Scholastic term for Heaven, where the soul is no longer a "wayfarer" (*viator*) but has reached its destination.</term>, we shall see God Himself through His essence, and then this darkness shall cease. But now we see Him through this light, which, although it is divine, is nevertheless below our intellect [in its current state], and thus the first question is clear.

<column-break/>

The blessed Dionysius says that it is our intellect that wishes to become thus; namely, through this mode, as light is a nature that relates to our intellect. But then it does not wish to become in this mode [only], but it wishes to become this: so that our intellect may have a certain light, and through it, God may be seen. And then it is said that from these remedies—that is, through **affirmations and negations** <note>These are the two paths of theology: *cataphatic* (affirming what God is, e.g., "God is good") and *apophatic* (negating what He is not, e.g., "God is not a body").</note>—the soul reaches God. Hence he says in *Mystical Theology*, chapter 2: "It behooves us to become this luminous darkness, and through that which we do not see, for God to be seen." and this is through negation. And he says: "It is necessary through **removal** <term>removal: original *sublatio*, the act of setting aside finite concepts to better understand the infinite.</term> that through this light we see God, and through the same light all created things, etc." And then from this it appears clearly because it is light; and this light makes the thing to be. It is called light, that is, an agent, which makes all things to be. Dionysius calls this mode the "Divine darkness." Hence it is said in *Mystical Theology*, chapter 2, where he says that this light shines in the darkness, and it is called darkness; and this darkness is light. And then the soul is said to be united with God, through this mode by which it is in this darkness. And then it is clear that this darkness is called light; and it is called darkness insofar as the soul is "above itself," and then it is said to be united with God. And this is light; and it is said that nothing prohibits us from being united to God through this mode, insofar as the light is in us, but not insofar as it is the Divine essence itself.

But then it is said that now we see in a mirror and in a riddle; and then it is clear that this light is not the Divine essence itself. And then regarding the object made concerning **Paul** <note>Referring to St. Paul's vision of being caught up to the "third heaven."</note>; it must be said that he sees God through His essence, but it is not possible for anyone [ordinarily] to see God in the homeland through His essence [while still in this life]. And then Dionysius speaks; hence it must be said that in the homeland, we shall see God Himself through His essence, and then there will not be this darkness. But now we see God through this light, and then it is called darkness. Dionysius speaks of this darkness, namely, that the soul is in a certain darkness; and so it is clear that the soul is in this life, as Dionysius says. But in the homeland, there is no darkness; and thus the answer to that question is clear.

<summary>This page explores the concept of the "Divine Darkness," explaining that God appears as darkness to the human intellect not because He lacks light, but because His light is so intense it exceeds human capacity. Drawing on Pseudo-Dionysius and St. Paul, the text distinguishes between our current "mirrored" knowledge of God on earth and the "face to face" essential vision promised in Heaven.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Darkness, Pseudo-Dionysius, mystical theology, apophatic theology, intellect vs mind, luminous darkness, beatific vision, Paul the Apostle</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the repetitive scribal exercises of the previous page to the formal beginning of Albertus Magnus’s "De Mineralibus" (On Minerals). The handwriting shifts into a structured, academic format common in 13th-century scientific texts.</meta>

**Column 1**

Here begins the first book of Albert the Great on minerals, which is about stones, in which there are two treatises; the first of these is about stones in general, and the second is about stones in particular and precious stones. The first treatise, which is about stones in general, contains nine chapters.

## LET US PROCEED
## NINE <note>These large, stylized words likely introduce the nine chapters mentioned above.</note>

We wish to investigate the mixture, the hardening <note>original: "coagulatione"</note>, the imprinting <note>original: "sigillacione" – a term referring to how stones receive their specific forms or "seals" from celestial or natural powers</note>, and other properties of minerals, not only in general but also in particular. For first, it is necessary for us to speak about stones, then about metals, and finally about those things which are intermediate between these, such as Marcasite <term>Marchasita: a term for iron pyrites or other metallic-looking minerals</term>, Magnesia <term>Magnesia: in this context, likely referring to manganese or lodestone rather than the modern element</term>, alum, salt, ink-stone <term>atramentum: a mineral used to make black pigment or ink, often vitriol</term>, and similar substances. In this first treatise, we will speak first about the generation of stones in general. Second, about their efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the force or agent that brings something into being.</note>. Third, about the place where they are generated. Fourth, about the manner of their mixing. Fifth, about their powers <note>original: "virtutibus" – the medicinal or magical properties believed to reside in stones</note>. Sixth, about their colors and differences. Seventh, about their cleavage <note>original: "scissura"</note>. Eighth, about certain stones which do not seem to be made by the power of nature and their causes. Ninth, about the shapes of stones as they are found in them naturally or made by some power. In the second treatise, however, we shall speak specifically about stones by their names and natures, and about the shapes of certain stones which they seem to have naturally and the causes of those shapes. In the third book, which is about metals, we shall speak about the generation of metals in general and their properties. In the fourth, we shall speak about metals in particular according to their species. In the fifth book, we shall speak about the intermediate substances which are neither properly stones nor metals, such as salt, alum, marcasite, and the like.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

It seems to others, however, that a stone is nothing but a kind of hard earth. Aristotle seems to agree with this, saying in the *Book on the Properties of the Elements* <note>A pseudo-Aristotelian text commonly cited in the Middle Ages.</note> that a stone is "hardened earth and not dry." But this seems to be false because clean and pure earth is never hardened into a stone unless a material of moisture and stickiness <note>original: "viscositatis"</note> has been mixed into it, as was proven in the third book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s treatise on natural phenomena.</note>. Furthermore, if a stone were simply earth, it would dissolve in water; yet we see this is false in the case of a stone. Furthermore, pure earth has no transparency, yet many stones are transparent. Moreover, a stone is sometimes burned by fire and converted into lime; earth, however, is never burned by fire but only dried out. From these points, it is clear that a stone is not earth, but earth provides the matter from which it is made. To others, it seems that a stone is made from frozen water, as is apparent in crystal and in ice. But this also appears to be false, because crystal is sometimes found in places where there was never frost. Furthermore, ice melts in water just as water does; crystal, however, does not melt unless it is crushed. Furthermore, pure water does not have the power to harden itself into stone, as is proven in the *Book of Meteorology*. From all of this, it is clear that neither water nor earth alone is the material of stones, but their material is made from a mixture of them both...

<summary>This page introduces Albertus Magnus's comprehensive study of minerals, outlining the structure of the work and debating the elemental composition of stones against classical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Albertus Magnus, Mineralogy, Aristotle, elemental theory, Marcasite, Magnesia, geology, medieval science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alchemical discussion of the "Philosopher's Stone," shifting from the general classification of minerals to the specific composition and transmutation properties of the Stone, traditionally attributed to authors like Albertus Magnus or pseudo-Geber.</meta>

Otherwise it is said that this is such material, namely stone, water, and fire. In another way it is said that in it are all things: spirit, soul, and body. Hence it is said that our stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> is not one of the elements, but is made from the elements and harmonized from the four elements. Thus it is called water and stone, and yet it is not a stone. It is earth, fire, and air. Specifically, it is water because it is moist and cold; earth because it is cold and dry; air because it is moist and hot; and fire because it is hot and dry.

Also, it should be noted that our stone is called "water" according to the philosophers. This is not because it is natural water, but rather <term>mercurial water</term>, water of life <note>original: "aqua vite"</note>, vegetable water, divine water, <unclear>perpetual</unclear> water, burning water, salt water, alum water, honey water, water of life, marvelous water, mineral water, celestial water, sea water, sharp water <note>original: "aqua acuta" — likely referring to a corrosive acid or "strong water"</note>. The philosophers have called our water by such names because of the power it possesses within itself. It is called water not because of its outward form, but because of its matter. It is called water because it is the source material of all liquids, just as natural water is the material of all liquids. Thus the matter of the stone is water and yet not water—namely <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "mercurius"</note>, which is water and not water. This is because it is a "clean water" that is yet not clean, for it is a water that does not wet the hands <note>A classic alchemical description of quicksilver (mercury).</note>. It is the matter of the stone. Therefore, it is called water because it is moist and cold; and it is called fire because it is hot and dry; and it is called earth because it is cold and dry; and it is called air because it is moist and hot. And so it is said that the stone is harmonized from the four elements.

<column-break/>

Namely, concerning the matter of the stone, it is said that our stone is from one thing: the matter of mercury. Although many philosophers have spoken of many things, they all agree on one point: our stone is from one thing, namely the matter of mercury. Therefore it is said that <term>mercury</term> is the matter of the stone. It is nothing other than mercury by itself; however, mercury requires the help of fire so that it may become the stone. Thus mercury is called the matter of the stone. It is called water because it is moist and cold; it is called stone because it is cold and dry; it is called air because it is moist and hot; and it is called fire because it is hot and dry. For this reason, the stone is said to be harmonized from the four elements.

It should be known that our stone is nothing other than mercury purified by fire. Therefore it is said that mercury is the matter of the stone. It is called water because it is moist and cold; it is called stone because it is cold and dry; it is called air because it is moist and hot; and it is called fire because it is hot and dry. Thus the stone is said to be harmonized from the four elements. <note>The scribe repeats these elemental associations multiple times, a common feature of medieval teaching manuscripts to reinforce the "balance" of the elements in the Great Work.</note>

Also, one should know the manner of joining the stone to the fire. For our stone must remain upon the fire for a long time so that it may be well <unclear>purified</unclear> and become clean and bright. Then our stone is said to be perfect and complete.

---

One must know about the manner of the projection of the stone. It is called "projection" <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the Stone is thrown onto molten metal to transform it.</note> because our stone must be cast upon metallic bodies so that it may transmute them into gold or silver.

Also, it should be known that our stone is composed of three things: namely spirit, soul, and body. The spirit is called <term>mercury</term>. The soul is called <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphur"</note>. The body is called <term>elixir</term> <note>The "elixir" here refers to the physical base or "medicine" of the stone.</note> or the medicine. These three must be joined together through art and skill so that they become one stone, one thing, and one matter.

One should also know about the distilled water which is the matter of the stone. For the distilled water must be clear, clean, and without dregs. It is called the water of life because it gives life to "dead" bodies <note>In alchemy, base metals like lead were considered "dead" or "leprose" until transformed.</note>. It is called the marvelous water <note>original: "aqua mirabilis"</note> because it performs wonders in the arts.

<column-break/>

In <term>mercury</term> are water; our stone is not [one thing but] spirit and soul, earth, fire, air—harmonized from the four elements.

Also, one should know the manner of the multiplication of the stone. For our stone must be multiplied by <term>mercury</term>. It is called "multiplication" because from a small amount, much is made. Therefore it is said our stone has no end in its multiplication. Then our stone is said to be perfect unto infinity. Whence the philosopher says: "if the sea were made of mercury, the stone would convert the whole into gold." <note>A hyperbolic statement common in alchemical texts to illustrate the infinite power of a perfected Stone.</note>

<summary>This text describes the alchemical nature of the Philosopher's Stone as a harmony of the four elements derived from mercury. it details the processes of purification by fire, the "projection" onto metals for transmutation, and the "multiplication" of the stone's power.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, mercury, sulfur, four elements, transmutation, aqua vitae, elixir, multiplication, projection</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the abstract theological and legal discussions of the previous folio to a "Lapidary"—a medieval encyclopedia of stones. While the previous page examined the laws of God and nature, this text explores how God's power is physically manifested in the "hidden virtues" of the natural world, specifically within gems and minerals.</meta>

... hence it is that if you ever set this stone on fire by placing it in a flame, it is never extinguished; from this it also has the name <unclear>indelible</unclear>.

<margin>Asbestos</margin>
Asbestos is a stone of Arcadia with the color of iron, which once ignited is never extinguished. It is said that this stone was once used in the <unclear>temples</unclear> of the <unclear>pagans</unclear> <note>original: "gentilium"; refers to non-Christian, often Roman or Greek, religious sites</note> for <unclear>ever-burning</unclear> lamps; for this reason it is called *abesto* in <unclear>Greek</unclear>, which means "inextinguishable."

<margin>Diamond, the royal gem</margin>
The Diamond <note>original: "Adamas"</note> is the most precious of all gems, which by its own nature is white and bright, and so hard that it cannot be mastered by iron or fire. It is said that this stone <unclear>resists</unclear> the rays of the sun and hinders the power of a magnet, unless it is softened in goat's blood <note>A common medieval belief that the nearly indestructible diamond could only be broken after being soaked in the blood of a goat</note>. It is found in India and Arabia.

<column-break/>

<margin>Agate, the Royal gem</margin>
The Agate was once considered a royal gem found in Sicily near the river of the same name, though it is now found in many places. Its types are many:
<margin>Black</margin>
one is black, with white veins mixed in;
<margin>Cyprian</margin>
another is similar to <unclear>wax</unclear> which is called Cyprian;
<margin>Indian</margin>
another is the Indian type which has a fiery <unclear>color</unclear>.
<margin>Agate by the grace of God</margin>
It is said that this stone is effective against poisons and the bites of serpents, and it <unclear>makes</unclear> a person eloquent and agreeable.

<margin>The Cock-stone</margin>
The Alectorius <note>original: "Alectorius galli"</note> is the stone of a white rooster, which is found in the stomachs of <unclear>old</unclear> roosters after they have been castrated. In size it is like a bean, with the color of crystal or clear water. This stone is said to provide constancy and victory in wars, and to <unclear>foster</unclear> love between spouses.

<column-break/>

<margin>Amethyst, named for drunkenness</margin>
The Amethyst is so named because it does not allow the heads of those drinking wine to become drunk; thus its name is translated from the <unclear>Greek</unclear> as "not drunk" <note>original: "non ebrius"; the name comes from the Greek *a-* (not) and *methystos* (intoxicated)</note>. It is a stone of purple color, similar to a violet, and sometimes a fiery glow is seen in it. It is found in India and Arabia. This stone is said to be effective against drunkenness, to drive away evil thoughts, and to provide good understanding.

<margin>Adromas</margin>
The Adromas is a stone that appears pure in color, similar to crystal, but in hardness it imitates the diamond. It is found in many places, but especially on the sea <unclear>shores</unclear>.

<margin>Borax</margin>
The Borax gem <note>This likely refers to the "Toadstone" or *Crapaudina*, which was frequently called Borax in medieval lapidaries</note> is found in the heads of toads; it is said to have great power against poisons, for if poison is nearby, this stone begins to <unclear>sweat</unclear> and changes color.

<margin>Beryl</margin>
Beryl is a pale green gem, similar to sea water, which is found in India. There are eight types, but the best are those of a pale color. This stone is said to preserve marital love and to heal the ailments of the <unclear>eyes</unclear>.

<column-break/>

... a <unclear>great</unclear> and precious stone, which is found in many places. It is <unclear>said</unclear> that this stone has a marvelous power, for if anyone carries it on their person, they will be honored and <unclear>loved</unclear> by everyone. It is also said that this stone is effective against fevers and headaches.

Furthermore, it should be noted that all these stones are to be held in great value, not only for their beauty but also for the hidden virtues they received from God. For just as herbs and plants have their own properties, so too do precious stones contain within themselves the marvelous effects of nature.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation from the previous folio. While the previous page focused on the theological "Word" as the source of creation, this page applies that logic to Alchemical philosophy. It transitions from the divine essence to the "Stone of the Philosophers," arguing that just as God is one, the work of nature and alchemy must be unified through a single material—Mercury—and governed by the celestial principles of the Sun and Moon.</meta>

### Folio 290r

This sign follows the reasoning where the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>often referring to Aristotle, though here used generally for masters of natural logic</note> and the <term>Alchemist</term> <note>practitioners of the "Art" of transformation</note> agree upon a single opinion. This opinion, which is seen in this art, is that nature creates only one thing from one thing, through one thing, and according to one species. Hence it is said that nature does nothing among the reality of things unless she does it according to her own self. Therefore, it is necessary for there to be a perfect <unclear>eternal gift</unclear> so that it may be the **Stone**; that is, so that it may be perfect, as it is said that nature makes it truly perfect according to its own species. And it is said that there is but one **Alchemy**, one virtue, one matter, one nature, and a unique Stone, which is received not through, but in, overcoming all other "smoke" <note>likely referring to the "vapors" or "fumes" produced during alchemical heating</note>. It is linked to the lunar path, for according to the wise philosophers, whatever is made according to nature by the light of the sun and the light of the moon is the power of the Stone. It is filled with the light of the sun and moon, and the Stone is not made except from these two: namely, from the **Sun** and **Moon**. This is because when this Stone is perfected, it is done through the spirit of the Sun and Moon. This is according to <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy</note>, who said that this power is above every power of the world, since it overcomes every matter, both subtle and gross. It shall penetrate; the **Sun is the father and the Moon is the mother** <note>original: "sol est pater et luna est mater"; a famous axiom from the Emerald Tablet</note>. It is true that the Sun is the perfect Stone, standing uniquely from itself. From the hope of the Sun and Moon, I would bring back perfection; it has matter, for nature is matter. The virtue was perfected through nature, and it is true since the Stone must be made from a "regeneration" of matter. Since the Sun is the son of nature—that is, when the Stone is perfected through nature—this is the perfect Stone. It is seen to have two matters, just as in human generation. Nature is the matter, and the virtue was such that it would break the stone and bring forth the **Mercurial gift**. It was a perfect stone through nature, for we can do nothing [without] this. But the perfect Stone does this according to itself, according to the matter of the spirit of the Sun and Moon, since there were two matters; for one is nothing without the other. I would bring back the offering when it perfected the human element in the realm of the Sun and Moon according to a perfected nature. Therefore, the Stone of nature is great; since the Stone is the perfect Stone of the alchemical Sun, namely from **Mercury**. For it is said the Stone is Mercury, and the matter of the Stone is Mercurial, according to the species of the matter and according to a perfected human nature. And so they arrived at the perfect Sun and the Moon according to their perfected species and according to nature: namely Mercury, or a perfected Mercurial nature. This is the true matter of things according to this opinion.

->**Chapter**<-

<column-break/>

**Concerning the Honey of the Philosophers**, and by what license it exists. **Alchemy** is an art named after **Alchimus** <note>a legendary figure sometimes cited as the inventor of alchemy, though his historical existence is debated</note>, who was of our science and discovered this art. It appears that our science concerns natural things. Mercury, for our part, is the science—that is, so that it may be perfect, for which it is said nature made it according to itself. This is Alchemy: one nature, and one truth of the nature of things. Namely, that **Mercury** <note>often called "Quicksilver" or "Argentum Vivum"</note> is not made except through Mercury. This is what the philosophers mean when they say: **Nature rejoices in nature** <note>original: "natura gaudet natura"; a fundamental alchemical principle suggesting that like affects like</note>. This means that Mercury, according to nature, rejoices in a Mercurial nature. Specifically, for its part, nature only acts according to itself. And it is because Mercury is the truth of the nature of things; Mercury is the matter of the things of metals—namely, of the Sun and Moon. And our science is called the truth of nature; and this is what the philosophers say, namely that nature does nothing in the reality of things except according to itself. However, there is one nature and one matter: namely Mercury, which is the truth of the nature of things and the **fountain of alchemy**. It holds within itself the entire matter of metals. For Mercury is the matter of metals through nature. Mercury is called one virtue, one matter, and one nature, possessing within itself the entire matter of metals. Indeed, Mercury is said to be the fountain of all alchemy. For Alchemy is the science teaching how to produce bodies through their parts; and Mercury makes bodies, namely the **Sun** <note>representing Gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>representing Silver</note>, because Mercury is their source. Mercury is that which discovered the matter of the Stone for the philosopher. For the philosophers call Mercury "the Stone," because nothing is found in the nature of things as perfect as Mercury. For Mercury holds in itself the spirit of the Sun and Moon. Mercury holds in itself the **living spirit** <note>original: "spiritum vivum"</note>. It is true that the Sun and Moon are [derived from it]; it is true that quicksilver is the fountain of all alchemy. And Mercury, according to the saying of the wise, is called **Our Stone**. Mercury is called the fountain of science and the fountain of the art.

<summary>This page discusses the singular nature of alchemy, arguing that all metals and the Philosopher's Stone originate from Mercury (quicksilver). It cites the authority of Hermes Trismegistus and the principle that "nature rejoices in nature" to explain how the Sun and Moon (gold and silver) are perfected through a single unified material.</summary>
<keywords>Alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Mercury, Sun and Moon, Hermes Trismegistus, Argentum Vivum, Natural Philosophy, Alchimus, Transmutation</keywords>

<meta>The previous page established a correspondence between the planets and various metals (Saturn/Lead, Sun/Gold, etc.). This page continues that alchemical investigation by exploring the physical origins of those metals, moving from celestial influences to the terrestrial theories of Plato and Aristotle regarding how matter is formed in the earth.</meta>

<margin>The heat of nature in alchemy.</margin>
<margin>Plato in the Timaeus.</margin>
<margin>The matter of the generation of metals.</margin>

...they are formed, a part of it being almost through fire, <unclear>which</unclear> <unclear>ought</unclear> <unclear>to</unclear> <unclear>happen</unclear> <unclear>naturally</unclear>. But in alchemy it does not seem to be so, because nature produces metals over a long period of time and not so quickly. Thus, **Plato says in the Timaeus** <note>Plato’s Timaeus was a foundational text for medieval science, explaining the creation of the universe and the elements.</note> that the generation of metals is from a dense and oily water that forms in the earth. This is called <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum." In alchemy, mercury/quicksilver represents the feminine, passive, and metallic principle.</note>, and the other part is <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the masculine, active, and combustible principle.</note>, from which metals are formed.

<column-break/>

Whence it appears even to the sun, which, when it generates natural things, does not do so primarily through the art of alchemy, because the art is [merely an imitation]. However, it must have another method; and thus it must be that metals are naturally generated over a long period within the bowels of the earth. Here we find that a certain purity of <term>quicksilver</term> and <term>sulfur</term> is required in them.

---

By comparing them in almost the same order in which nature works in generating metals, so too must art <note>In this context, "art" refers to the human skill of alchemy attempting to replicate or accelerate natural processes.</note> imitate nature. This is so that what is produced in the earth through natural heat might be achieved through fire. Thus the alchemist does not truly generate metals [from nothing], as is said...

<column-break/>

And he also says that almost anything from a perfect form [is made] not rather than that which is done by fire through art. <margin>Aristotle. <note>Aristotle's "Meteorology" was the primary source for the theory that metals form from "exhalations" in the earth.</note></margin> And it is established by nature, but it must have the right matter, such as <term>quicksilver</term> and <term>sulfur</term>. <margin>O, what a good comparison!</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the "Sulfur-Mercury theory" of mineral formation, citing Plato's Timaeus and Aristotle to argue that alchemy must imitate nature's slow process in the earth by using fire and pure materials.</summary>

--- Page 301 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the hidden processes of nature. While the previous page discussed the physical components of metals—mercury and sulfur—this section shifts to the invisible, spiritual force (the "spirit of the world") that animates matter and gives it form through a "vibrating heat" or internal fire.</meta>

<margin>i</margin>
Its roots in the soil soon seem to dry up and <unclear>wither away</unclear>, but they <unclear>remain</unclear> by a certain power <unclear>deeper</unclear> there, where I also am <unclear>among the nations</unclear>, as if drawing from the thinnest earth that which is its own. Its height and depth lie open to itself, which is invisible; and we see nothing except the vibrating fire itself and the heat which goes out toward that which is the form. But because it cannot withdraw from its own center, then through that vibrating fire within its form, its shape exists. For the form is the matter of the fire <note>The author suggests that physical "form" acts as the fuel or container that allows the internal fire to become visible to human eyes.</note>, which could not be seen in its center except through this. But when it goes forth, it brings an increase, a vibrating degree of fire through which all things—

<margin>ii</margin>
—in its center, every power acts and preserves. And from this it follows that the very principles which act for themselves in some invisible place bring forth their own vibrating fire, which is the medium itself, or, as I might say, its form. In this form is that power of its own which is not the form itself, but resides in its center—which is not perceived except in its fire, which is the increase and the burning of its nature within that vibrating form which produces all created things and their shapes.

<margin>iii</margin>
Moreover, the nature of that which you see here is within itself; it is not the form, but it is the principle and the source of the fire and heat from which all things proceed, and through which those very forms are preserved in their being. For if this force and this burning were to withdraw, the form itself would soon fail and seem to be reduced to nothing; yet the power itself <unclear>always</unclear> remains.

<column-break/>

<margin>i</margin>
For as it is evident in all things that we see and feel, there is a <unclear>power</unclear> itself which is not perceived through itself, but through its form. This form is of a certain fiery nature which we call the <term>spirit of the world</term> <note>original: "spiritus mundi." A vitalist concept in alchemy and Neoplatonism referring to a subtle essence that permeates the universe and connects soul to body.</note> or the <term>vibrating heat</term> <note>original: "calorem vibrantem." This suggests a pulsing, active energy rather than static warmth.</note>, through which all things live and are moved. But because the principle itself, which is the source of this heat, is not visible, we therefore do not perceive it except in its effect and in the vibrating form which is diffused through the whole <term>machine of the world</term> <note>original: "mundi machinam." A common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, divinely-ordered system.</note>, and through which all things are preserved in their being. And from this we know that it is the spirit which is life-giving and which contains all things in their vigor.

<margin>ii</margin>
For just as our fire cannot be seen without its matter, but unfolds itself through it, so that universal spirit—which is the principle of life and heat in all things—does not manifest itself to us except through its forms, which it creates and in which it dwells. From this it appears that those forms are like certain garments of the spirit itself, which is in the center of all things and which is the source and origin of all motion and life in this visible world. For if that spirit, which is the source of all life and heat, were to withdraw itself, soon all things would be resolved into dust; for the forms themselves do not subsist by themselves, but only in the power of the principle itself, upon which they depend and from which they draw their entire essence, <unclear>until</unclear> they <unclear>are led</unclear> to <unclear>their end</unclear>.

<summary>This page discusses the "Spiritus Mundi" (World Spirit) and internal "vibrating fire" as the invisible forces that sustain all physical forms. It argues that while we only see the outward shape or "garment" of things, their true existence depends on a central, hidden heat that prevents them from dissolving into dust.</summary>

...and although it possesses something of a fiery and airy nature within itself, nevertheless its greatest and most principal part is earthy and cold; this is the stone of our perfection. And therefore it is said that in this matter there is fire and air, water and earth, and thus it is composed of elements and is elemental, and from it all metals are produced. This is evident from the same author, who says: **Earth is the mother of metals**, and just as a woman does not give birth without a man, so the earth does not produce metals without sulfur. For sulfur is the dross <note>The "fex" or dross refers to the sediment or concentrated essence of the earth.</note> of the earth; it is the active matter, while earth is the passive. When the sulfur is purified and clean, then the metals are coagulated; and thus it is clear that in the matter there is both sulfur and earth.

# THE BRIDGE <note>PONT: likely an abbreviation for Pontanus, an alchemist famous for his "Epistle on the Secret Fire," which serves as a "bridge" to understanding the work.</note>

In these things it is also to be seen, and known, that this matter is most vile, and yet of itself is produced by every creature. Furthermore, it is most noble, because there is no other substance from which our stone may be perfected. We must ask what that thing is, where it is to be sought, and at what time it is to be found. *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: know for certain that the thing of which we speak here is not a rare thing, nor difficult to find. Instead, it is found wherever you wish; it is possessed by everyone and is findable everywhere. For it is in the earth, in the sea, in the waters, and in all men; it is even in all animals, herbs, fruits, stones, and metals, and in all other things. This is why the philosophers said: **our thing is everywhere**...

<column-break/>

...and because the thing is so humble, it is therefore not recognized by the foolish and the ignorant, but is by them spurned and despised. It is even called a "vile thing" by the philosophers, and is given lowly names specifically so that it may not be recognized by the wicked and by sinners. And therefore *Hermes* says: Our son appears so vile and despised that if anyone were to throw him in the mud, no one would pick him up or lift him. And why is it so vile? It is said that this is because it is produced by itself from every creature. Therefore the matter of the stone is called "vile" because it is findable everywhere and possessed by all; but it is most noble, because from it our stone is perfected. Thus it is said: O most vile thing, and yet most noble! For without you nothing is perfected. Therefore, know that this matter is one single thing; it is not two things, nor many, for our stone is perfected from a single thing. And so *Hermes* says: Our stone is from one thing, and is one thing, and there are not many things; for if there were many things, it would not be our stone...

---

<margin>

</margin>

...[It is said] to be sweeter than honey, yet there is something in it that is more bitter; and thus it is one thing. There is no other thing in the world from which our stone may be perfected except from this matter. This matter has within itself something that is very subtle <note>refined or spirit-like</note> and something that is very gross <note>dense or physical</note>; and that which is subtle is that which we seek. Therefore it is said: **separate the subtle from the gross** <note>original Latin: "separa subtile a grosso"</note>... for the humidity in it is twofold: one is accidental, and the other is essential. That accidental humidity is what ought to be removed, and the essential is what ought to be preserved; for it is the soul and life of the stone. Therefore it is said: cleanse the matter of its filth and its superfluities, and then it will remain clean and pure... for heat is the fire that cleanses the matter and removes from it all accidental humidity, and all filth and superfluity...

<column-break/>

...once it is finally clean and pure, let it afterwards be boiled with its own fire until it becomes red and fixed; and then you will have our stone, which transmutes all imperfect metals into pure and excellent gold. And therefore it is said that our stone is the medicine of all imperfect metals...

Hermes Trismegistus: prince of philosophers <note>Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy and the hermetic sciences.</note>

By the student, there shall not be a digestion of <unclear>that</unclear> which they bring as the composition of the matter of its <unclear>body</unclear>. The artisan labors for his own, and what he ought to do he cannot apply, except that which is granted in its own time and by the course of nature, and in its own time is sent back with firmness and <unclear>misery</unclear>. Let there be skill in you so that you may observe how nature touches its own members and virtues, where and how it chooses ends for itself; whether with one matter placed in the nature of one thing, it is produced through itself into diverse things and virtues, or whether it grants to others through forms and properties, so that when its matter has chosen a condition for itself, it may happen. Just as the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: "materia prima"; the formless primordial substance from which all things are created</note> is here similar to nature, the art must serve it while it labors. Consider, you who are not unwise, the virtue of this nature, and there, so that he may overcome that nature, but through it and not beyond it shall you place anything. And the matter is indeed one, which is more of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui"</note> and was acquiring certain additions which, if nature has made them and known their perfection, it achieves. He who has found and made that thing is similar to it, for he understood that perfection itself is the truth and not the false thing which the deceptive <term>sophists</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "sophists" refers to false alchemists or "puffers" who use deceptive methods rather than true natural philosophy.</note> make. Because of this, if anyone should wish to find the true sun and moon <note>original: "solem et lunam"; alchemical metaphors for gold and silver</note> with the helplessness of nature, he would wander, because nature sometimes errs in its works; wherefore, that which nature made defective or in which it sinned, ought to be amended through art. That which nature made admirable in its art is not to be overcome, but is to be helped, and thus nature is to be repaired. Nature ought to overcome nature, because otherwise the thing is frustrated and empty. Without nature nothing is done; therefore, you should know nature with its powers, and thus the understanding of the scriptures, of things, and of practices helps the philosophers to achieve the invention of this work, so that through them that most precious stone may be known, which lies hidden in each of the metals, so that each one may have its form with the perfection which is to be made. And this he seems to do rightfully through nature, because its matter is miserable <note>The word "miserable" (miserabilis) in alchemy often refers to the humble, overlooked, or "vile" starting material of the work.</note> from which it seems to be made, which is miserable matter from things that are not miserable; wherefore the philosopher said: I saw a man surpassing nature, but not being able to pass it unless he passed through it, so that he might achieve the perfection which is to be found in the art. Where nature ends, there art begins; and where art ends, there the grace of God perfects. And this shall be the subject of this present treatise. And they help the philosophers both with the knowledge which he has in it and the understanding of this art and its perfection, to which the philosophers arrive, to whom nature also gives understanding; from which art has its strengths and the matter which the philosopher understood, from which the grace of God may make and perfect it, which in its exercises <unclear>shames</unclear> God the creator.

To labor.

Upon its own matter, from which it seems to be made and grasped, which the philosopher understood equally in the investigation of this art, where nature fails and in what it is perfected; and what he understood with its nature, which cannot be concluded from elsewhere except through the matter itself which is to be found. From which it shall be digested and found, which he understands and perfects by knowledge, which seems to be in vileness, and found through this by which no other thing could be found from elsewhere except through nature itself; so that what it may be from the inventor, and that it may be pursued by his grace and honor. From which, by the knowledge which is in nature itself, it seems to be found; wherefore the philosophers said and prove its divinity to be that which through it made each one so that he might understand the misery itself which made each one divine from nothing; that he might find from it and know it as found, from which it ought to become presumptuous, from which he placed foreign things for his own nature, and that which is from it is to be uprooted, and by merits is the praise of Him who made it, to whom He also gives understanding, from which grace itself may arrive. When grace itself has arrived, and the knowledge of this, from which our treatise finds its beginning; and this from which the philosopher holds something which is to be found, which no other thing seems to be made from elsewhere, that which is given into the hands, which shall have what is the end, the stone. Two of that, each shall be for the Lord, two stones, each one, so that each may be one; and it may have what each one shall be, the discovery of this, from which the opinion here seems to be that since each is what the manner shall be, each is one stone, except that for one it is ignoble, for the other it shall be lightness; each is found as one, each one which has its fruit, so that each of them shall be one, so that it would make one and a multitude of souls; each is one and let it be one through itself. Each of them has a beginning from which each one shall be found to be; from which it is probable in kinds and use each one shall be found which the philosopher understood, from which it seems to be and worthily honored; from which, venerable in merits and use, he did whatever he understood of it, among those where it has virtue from elsewhere, in which he found its nature itself. From which it is offered in need and utility, and understanding to the discovery, so that it may be the end of this discovered work, from which is the truth in perfection itself, from which it was a miserable discovery which the philosopher understood; and his discovery which has many virtues in which they are preferred infinitely, from which they ought to be found, and venerable, from which grace by that dignity, from which by that knowledge they seem to be; from which he considered its merits, it was honorable which he made, and by his benefits which he knew how to find; so that by his benefits what God made, to whom honor and glory are seen to be, to God himself.

### TO A FRIEND

<column-break/>

Therefore there was truth in which is the matter itself, let it be the end of the discovered work where there is truth; for when he began to work and felt himself to enjoy, it was compared and increased toward its perfection, so that finally in the discovery and that which it had from which it ought to be made, so that by its benefits all that is digested shall be discovered, which he understands by knowledge and perfects, which seems to be in vileness and found through this, by which no other thing could be found from elsewhere except through nature itself, so that it may be what it is by the inventor and that he may follow it with grace and honor.

-> TO A FRIEND <-

You write to me, my friend: and you propose by asking: whether one can find the most determined science of this Art from the writings of the philosophers, whether ancient or recent? And if there be any foundation in which the philosophers agree: to which, as if to a rule, whatever pertains to the operation of this art is to be applied: or whether it is to be sought elsewhere: which regards this manner: and to which, as to an end, one must adhere? Answering this question, I say: this venerable art is not found except by divine grace and the intellect which God gives to man, so that through them the secrets of nature and the causes of hidden things may be known, and so that through the same, one can come to the invention of this work, which is most useful to men. Wherefore God grants this art only to his friends, whom he wills, and those whom it pleases him, so that by its benefits they may help the poor and the needy: and so that those laboring in the same art may offer honor and glory to God himself, who is the author of all: so that by the same art men may be instructed, so that they may know God their creator and lord, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. But since you yourself are now worthy to arrive at this art, and to labor happily in it, and to proceed in it: know, my friend, that in this art there is a double way: one, namely, according to nature, the other indeed according to art: and we say both are one, and one alone: because art ought to follow nature, and imitate it, and work in it: because nature is of itself good and perfect: and from which it has grace and honor, as it seems to be made through nature itself.

<margin>
Note this:
</margin>

<margin>
The poverty of the thing
</margin>

Namely, being of one mind: and that this is the principal end of this art, in which all agree, and that the same is the end of all works: namely, one stone and one thing, which they call the Stone of the Philosophers: which is one stone and one thing: wherefore it proceeds from one root and in the same one root it is consummated and perfected. Wherefore the philosophers call this stone "one," because it is made from one matter only, and that which is fashioned from it is one alone: so that there is in it one essence, and one form, and one matter: so that it is the same thing which is fashioned from it. And from this the philosophers have said this stone is in all things, and in every place, and in every time, and in every man: so that all things can be made from it: and from this it seems to happen rightfully: because nature is one, and the matter is one: from which all things are produced: and from which the end of this work may be, so that in it may be found what is sought: and this is that which all philosophers agree upon, and this is the foundation of this art, in which all agree.

And to your other question: namely, whether one can find it from the writings of the philosophers, whether ancient or recent? I respond: that the writings of the philosophers are exceedingly obscure: and in them are many things which seem contrary: wherefore it is difficult to understand them, unless one has an intellect given by God, so that he can know them. And from this the philosophers have hidden many things in them, lest they should arrive at this art, except those whom God has willed, and to whom He himself has given by His grace, so that they might be able to understand them. Wherefore know, my friend: that there is no way to this art, except through the intellect of God and through His grace. And from this know: that the writings of the philosophers are like a mirror, in which the truth is seen, but not the truth itself: wherefore through them one cannot arrive at the art, unless God has given it.

To your third question: namely, if there be any foundation in which the philosophers agree: I respond, as was said above: that the foundation of this art is one matter and one thing, from which all things are made, and in which all things are perfected: and this is that in which all philosophers agree: and from this know, my friend: that this foundation is most certain, and in it there is no error.

The author uses familial metaphors (Mother, Father, Daughter, Son) and planetary associations to explain their properties.</meta>

<page-num>23</page-num>

<column-break/>

<margin>Quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti vivus"</note> left the metallic matrix</margin>
<margin>Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum Vivum"</note></margin>
<margin>Poisonous, or as it is the flatterer of stones.</margin>
<margin>Mercury <note>original: "M-uranus," likely a scribal shorthand for Mercurius</note></margin>
<margin>Too much friction, as I may have done.</margin>

...as they say: Silver born from nature and collected from the mines.

**A** **Quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note>, so called from its lively motion and agility, because it never rests until it is bound by some metal or fixed to some metal. It is called "Silver" <note>original: "Argentum"</note> because it has the color of silver, but "Living" <note>original: "Vivum"</note> because of its continuous motion and restlessness; if anyone touches it, they do not truly touch it, for it soon flees from his hands and fingers. This Quicksilver, therefore, is among the metals like the soul in the body. For just as the soul animates and gives life to the body, so Quicksilver animates and gives life to all metals. Wherefore many philosophers have said: Quicksilver is the **mother of all metals**, because from its substance all metals are created and procreated, just as in the generation of humans from the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>; hence all metals have Quicksilver within them. 

Now, if someone should ask: "If metals have Quicksilver in them, why then do they not melt in the fire like Quicksilver, and why do they not flee from the fire like Quicksilver?" To this I answer that metals have Quicksilver in them not as it is in its free state, but as it is **fixed** and **coagulated** within the metals; and therefore they do not melt nor flee from the fire. For just as water, which is fluid and liquid, does not flow or melt if it is frozen or congealed unless it is first dissolved, so Quicksilver congealed in metals does not flow or melt as Quicksilver flows in itself. In itself, it is liquid and fluid; in metals, however, it is coagulated and fixed. 

This Quicksilver is also called the **water of metals**, because just as water cleanses all bodies, so Quicksilver cleanses and purges all metals. And as water moistens all bodies, so Quicksilver moistens and softens all metals; and as water washes all bodies, so Quicksilver washes and whitens all metals; and as water liquefies all bodies, so Quicksilver liquefies and dissolves all metals; and as water receives all bodies into itself, so Quicksilver receives all metals into itself and is united with them. This Quicksilver is also called **virgin's milk** <note>original: "lac virginis"</note>, because just as milk nourishes a child, so Quicksilver nourishes the metals; and as milk is white and pure, so Quicksilver is white and pure. This Quicksilver is also called the **sperm of metals**, because just as a human is procreated from human sperm, so metals are procreated from Quicksilver.

<column-break/>

<margin>This is called *cassiteros* <note>Greek for tin</note> in the second book of the *Tract on the Failure of Wisdom*, but it is not the end.</margin>
<margin>Lead.</margin>
<margin>Gold?</margin>

...in its own procreation where it may be of the vein, or flowing from a vein of Silver.

**B** **Lead** <note>original: "Plumbum"</note> is a dark and heavy body; just as it is the lowliest among all metals, so it is the heaviest among them all. And just as Quicksilver is the mother of all metals, so Lead is the **father of all metals**; for as a son is procreated from a mother and a father, so the remaining metals are procreated from Quicksilver and Lead. As the father is stronger than the mother, so Lead is stronger than Quicksilver; as the father rules the mother, so Lead rules Quicksilver; and as the father chastises the son, so Lead chastises the remaining metals. 

This Lead is also called **Saturn**, because just as Saturn is the highest and slowest among the planets, so Lead is the highest and slowest in the fire among metals. As Saturn is cold and dry, so Lead is cold and dry; and as Saturn is called the "old man," so Lead is called the **old man of the metals**. This Lead is also called the **lead of the philosophers**, because from it philosophers elicit Quicksilver, gold, and silver; and just as common lead is vile and contemptible, so the lead of the philosophers is precious and honorable. 

This Lead is also called **black lead** <note>original: "plumbum nigrum"</note>, to distinguish it from "white lead," which is tin. This Lead is also called **red lead**, because from it is made <term>minium</term> <note>red lead or cinnabar-colored pigment</note>, which is red. This Lead is also called **yellow lead**, because from it is made <term>ceruse</term> <note>white lead pigment</note>, which is white, but through fire it becomes yellow. This Lead is also called **blue lead**, because it has a bluish color. This Lead is also called **malleable lead**, because it is easily extended under the hammer. This Lead is also called **fusible lead**, because it is quickly melted in the fire. This Lead is also called **heavy lead**, because it is the heaviest among the metals.

<insert>
I saw a gift in the natural manuscripts... regarding a famous branch... most beautiful books of alchemy and they shall be perfected.
</insert>

---

...in whatever things there may be a compulsive fire for the movement of fire, and just as fire is hot and dry, so fire strongly cleanses and removes filth. For just as gold and silver are cleansed by fire, so all metals are cleansed by Lead; and as fire is not touched without burning, so Lead is not touched without staining. This Lead is also called **fixed lead**, because it does not change its color in the fire; whereas Quicksilver changes its color in the fire and escapes. And as common lead is not malleable in itself but becomes malleable through fire, so the lead of the philosophers is not malleable in itself but becomes malleable through fire; and as common lead has a dark and obscure color, so the lead of the philosophers has a dark and obscure color; and as common lead is quickly melted in the fire, so the lead of the philosophers is quickly melted in the fire.

**C** **Silver** <note>original: "Argentum"</note> is a white, clear, bright, and ductile body; it is called *Argentum* as if it were "white earth," because among all metals it is the whitest and the cleanest. And just as Quicksilver is the mother of all metals, so Silver is the **daughter of all metals**; for as a daughter is like her mother, so Silver is like Quicksilver. As a daughter is clean and pure, so Silver is clean and pure; as a daughter is white and bright, so Silver is white and bright; as a daughter is flexible and obedient, so Silver is flexible and obedient; and as a daughter is precious and dear, so Silver is precious and dear. This Silver is also called the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"</note>, because as the Moon is white and bright among the planets and receives light from the Sun, so Silver is white and bright among metals and receives its value from Gold. As the Moon has a bluish color, so Silver has a bluish color; as the Moon is cold and moist, so Silver is cold and moist; and as the Moon is called **Diana**, so Silver is called the Diana of the metals.

<column-break/>

...and just as lead is the father of all metals, so tin is their **son**. As tin is like the father in weight and in melting, so tin is like the father in weight and in melting; as tin is like the mother in color and in cleanliness, so tin is like the mother in color and in cleanliness; and as tin is like the sister—namely, Silver—in brightness and ductility, so tin is like the sister in brightness and ductility; and as tin is like the brother—namely, Gold—in hardness and in value, so tin is like the brother in hardness and in value.

<margin>Tin <note>original: "Stannum"</note></margin>

**D** **Tin** <note>original: "Stannum"</note> is a white body, not pure but mixed. It is called *Stannum* from "standing" <note>original: "stante"</note>, because it cannot stand in the fire except with the help of lead or another metal; if it is alone in the fire, it quickly fails, but if it is with another metal, it is strengthened. This tin is also called **white lead**, to distinguish it from black lead. Just as black lead has a dark and obscure color, so tin has a white and bright color; and as black lead is heavy, so tin is light; and as black lead does not **creak** <note>original: "stridet"; referring to the "cry of tin," a crackling sound made when bending the metal</note> under the teeth or under the hammer, so tin creaks under the teeth and the hammer. As black lead has no sound, so tin has a clear and bright sound; as black lead is malleable, so tin is less malleable; as black lead is fusible, so tin is more quickly fusible; and as black lead is cheaper, so tin is dearer. This tin is also called **Jupiter**, because as Jupiter is white and shining among the planets and has a great voice, so tin is white and shining among metals and has a great sound.

It details their physical properties, planetary associations (Saturn, Moon, Jupiter), and their roles in the transmutation process.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion from folio 304 regarding the primary metallic principles. While the previous page focused on the "family" of metals and the restless nature of Quicksilver, this page shifts toward the internal "spirit" and "marrow" of metals, emphasizing how fire and the elixir animate the "living" metallic body.</meta>

If anyone be noble, ingenious, and just, they ought to seek this most noble art. For here our Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says he has perfected the highest end. Sulfur is living and red with fire, like a serpent that always hastens toward perfection. This is the element of water and matter, and it always has a desire for the other; it possesses the humility of water, the fire, and the dryness of earth. Its perfection is the red color. And it is a "dry water" containing all things preserved; indeed, it is called "white water like milk," and truly perpetual water, which does not perish like other water that comes from the "water of the fish" <note>original: "aqua piscis"; an alchemical metaphor for the mercurial fluid</note>. This is the first and proper water by which he made the living perfectly. Every just person can know this art.

And this Stone has three names, just as there are three elements <note>the text lists three states/colors rather than the four classical elements</note>. It is white, red, and black. The white is called the Moon <note>silver</note>, the red is called the Sun <note>gold</note>, and the black is called Saturn <note>lead</note>. # It Surpasses

<margin>In the faces <note>or "masks"</note> of our gods are enclosed those who are kindled by the heats...</margin>

There are certain bodies that are very hard and cannot be perfected by fire, such as gold and silver. For gold is a perfect body and silver is a perfect body. But other bodies are imperfect, such as iron and lead. For iron is as hard as stone and cannot be softened by fire. Lead, however, is very soft and quickly loses its life through fire. And in these two is the red matter that does not wish to endure the fire.
