--- Page 311 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion of the physical world and the elements (attributed to Almansor) into a deep metaphysical inquiry into the nature of Unity (Unitas) and Multitude (Multitudo). While the previous page focused on the "fountain" of elements and the structure of the universe, this folio applies scholastic logic to define how "One" and "Being" relate to one another, drawing heavily on Aristotle, Augustine, and Boethius.</meta>

### Unity is

Each thing, he says, of those which are singular by themselves in their own kind <note>original: "in proprio genere"</note> is one. However, it rightly seems that division cannot exist, nor can a multitude be defined in such a way, because just as a multitude is formally constituted through unity, it is likewise said in the third book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's "Metaphysics." Although the text says "third," the discussion of unity and being is famously found in Book Gamma (Book 4).</note> that it is not in the "whatness" <term>quidditas; the "what-it-is" or essential nature of a thing</term> of the being of an entity in individuals in its formal institution. For in individuals, that which is said to be "one" through itself or through an accident is "unity"; nor is it said that "one" signifies something above the being of an entity, nor is it properly said. "One" is that which is said in the substance of an entity, because that which is "one" is that which is not divided, though it is nevertheless divided within itself—one in a multitude. For as Augustine says in the sixth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6: there is nothing in a multitude that is not one. But the reason is that a multitude is defined through the "one," but not the other way around. In the third book of the *Metaphysics*, the reasoning is that just as a prior thing is defined through a posterior thing, so "one" is defined through "multitude" as a sign is defined by the thing signified; and likewise, unity is defined through multitude as a prior thing by a posterior thing. It is said in the third book of the *Metaphysics* that "one" is that which is not divided in itself by a posterior thing. Likewise, unity cannot have the aforementioned reasoning because a multitude is formally constituted through unity. Likewise, it is seen that unity is properly said to "be one," and multitude "not to be one," because a multitude is a multitude from the things mentioned before. Likewise, it is said in the third book of the *Metaphysics* that "one" belongs to the essence of an entity under the aspect of being <note>original: "sub esse"</note>. That which is one and not one cannot be anything through itself or through an accident. And "one" does not signify anything over and above "being," because as it is said in the third book of the *Metaphysics*, "one" and "being" are the same in reason and differ only in that "one" signifies nothing except "being undivided." For as Boethius says in the book *On Unity and the One*, "to be" and "one" are interchangeable <note>original: "esse et unum convertuntur." This is a fundamental scholastic principle meaning that everything that exists is, by the very fact of existing, a single thing.</note>. Likewise, by "one" is understood "being undivided." Likewise, "one" does not place anything in reality above the being of an entity, but only posits a privation <term>privatio; the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like darkness being the absence of light</term>. For it is called "one" as if it were "not divided." However, this does not seem to be sufficient, as in its own reasoning in the third book of the *Metaphysics*.

<column-break/>

For it is said that if it is "one," division is absent; just as "being one" is a privation in substance. Because in reality, "privation" is said in the substance of an entity so that the "one" may be an entity through itself. But it does not seem that "being the highest good" and "being one" are formally the same. Just as a multitude is formally constituted through unity, a privation cannot be the constitutive form of something positive, such as a multitude is. Likewise, the reasoning above does not seem to show that "one" is only a privation, just as it is not for a "measure" <term>mensura; a standard of measurement</term> which is metaphysical. It is said that "one" is the first measure and the principle of number; that "one" is the first measure. Likewise, a number, which is a multitude, is formally constituted through unity; a privation cannot be a constitutive form, as said above. Likewise, it is properly said that "one" is in the genus of multitude, just as in the book *On the One and Unity*, it is said that "one" is the principle of number and "one" is the first form of number in which there are "one" and "multitude." Likewise, "one" does not place a thing above being. Likewise, in the third book of the *Metaphysics*, it is said that "one" by reason of measure is the first measure in any genus. Likewise, as it is said in the book *On Unity and the One*, "one" is the principle of number. Likewise, "one" and "multitude" are the same in reality <note>original: "in re"</note> but different in reason <note>original: "ratione"</note>. Just as it is said in the book *On Unity and the One* that "one" and "multitude" are the same being, though the reasoning is not the same. It is seen that to "be one" in reality is properly said not to "be a multitude." Likewise, by "one" is understood "being undivided." Likewise, a multitude in the substance of an entity cannot exist except as "one," just as it is said in the third book of the *Metaphysics* that "one" is a substance that is not divided in itself, yet it is one. Likewise, it is a sign of not being something through itself or through an accident except as "being one." And "one" properly, by reason of "being one," does not signify anything above the being of an entity except only a privation. Because, as Boethius says in the book *On the One and Unity*, "to be" and "one" are interchangeable...

<summary>A dense scholastic defense of the principle that "being" and "unity" are interchangeable, arguing that everything that exists is fundamentally "one." It explores the paradox of how a multitude (many things) can be defined by unity and whether "oneness" is simply the absence of division.</summary>
<keywords>Metaphysics, Unity, Multitude, Being, Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Privation, Principle of Number, Scholasticism</keywords>

This is because in <unclear>one</unclear> it exists as the sensible object in a <unclear>perceptible</unclear> subject, and in the other as a <unclear>formal</unatical> <note>Likely "formali" (formal); relating to the "form" or essence of the thing perceived.</note> subject. 

Just as points relate to a line, so the senses relate to the soul. Just as these two <unclear>formal</unclear> points meet in one point, and this point is one insofar as it is a subject, but two insofar as it is the boundary of two lines, so also the common sense <term>sensus communis; the faculty that integrates data from the five individual senses into a single experience</term>, insofar as it is one <unclear>act</unclear> of the soul, perceives diverse sensible things according to which the particular senses are distinguished. Thus, it is clear that the soul perceives diverse sensible things as one, and they are perceived by it at one time, because its act is one.

<column-break/>

...according to that line which reaches and terminates in the common point. Through this, it is clear that the soul is that which perceives the things sensed, existing as one according to substance, but differing according to being <note>original: "secundum esse"; meaning its functional existence or the way it manifests.</note> because it is the boundary of diverse senses. 

Thus the soul, like a point, is the middle of two, just as the point of a line is the middle of two boundaries, each of which is one, but it is the middle of both of them. Wherefore the soul is one and is, as it were, a middle in which all sensed things converge. Therefore, it is not necessary that in reality <note>original: "secundum rem"</note> it be different things, but only according to reason <note>original: "secundum rationem"; a common distinction meaning something is one thing in physical reality but can be thought of as multiple things based on its functions.</note>, just as there are [multiple] boundaries of lines in a point. 

And just as in a point there are many things according to reason and one according to reality, so also the soul is many according to the diversity of objects, but one according to essence. Therefore, it can judge diverse things simultaneously. Wherefore at the end of this chapter he says that just as it is said of a point, which can be called one and two, so also the soul is called one and many insofar as the particular senses converge in it. Thus it is clear what the common sense is and how it perceives sensible things and their diversity according to <unclear>certain</unclear> linear and punctual similarities which Aristotle poses in the text, as is more clearly seen in the <unclear>previously written</unclear> figure. 

From this, it is clear how the soul judges diverse sensible things, since the soul is indivisible and judges in an indivisible time. What, however, that thing is which is the subject of the common sense, and how it relates to the organ [of the body], shall be discussed in the book *On the Sense and the Sensible* <note>Aristotle's "De Sensu et Sensato," part of the Parva Naturalia.</note>.

# [Folio 312 Recto]

<columns>2</columns>

...[the question is] whether there is one appetite in us which exists in many, or several. It must be said, according to the aforementioned, that if there are several souls, they are either one by aggregation or they are one by essential union. If in the first way, since every act is from one soul or from many insofar as they are one, it follows that there is only one act of the appetite itself. Then, if there are many [appetites], the plurality is only according to reason and not according to reality. 

If, however, there is an essential union such that one soul is the subject of many powers, even then, regarding the act of judging, there can be only one act of appetite. This is because, as was said concerning the common sense: the soul is one, and therefore in one time it judges diverse things. So also the appetitive soul, existing as one, judges diverse desirable things <note>original: "appetibilibus"; things that can be moved toward or desired.</note>. And therefore, although there are diverse senses and diverse particular appetites, nevertheless in the soul there is one universal appetite which operates through all of them. Let these things, which were determined in the second book, suffice.

->The second book ends.<-

### Here Begins [Book III]

Since in the preceding [sections] we prepared for those things which are to be determined in this third book, [the author] has determined the parts of the soul which exist according to themselves and not by accident, but only according to reason—such as the sensitive and nutritive parts, according to which man is seen to differ from beasts and plants <note>original: "vegetabilibus"; referring to the "vegetative soul" common to all living things.</note>. 

And because the sensitive part is not perfected except through motion and the transformation made by sensible things, therefore in this third book he determines those things which pertain to the intellective part <term>pars intellectiva; the faculty of rational thought, unique to humans</term>. First, he determines the intellective part itself according to itself; second, concerning the motion which comes from it. 

Regarding the first, he does two things:
First, he determines the intellective power itself. Second, its act. 
Regarding the first again, two things: first, he raises certain doubts that seem to occur concerning the intellect. Second, he determines the truth. 
The doubts are two. The first is concerning the difference between the intellect and the sense. The second is concerning the organ of the intellect itself <note>Aristotle famously debated whether the intellect had a physical organ like the eyes or ears; he concluded it did not.</note>.

It then introduces Book III, shifting the focus from the animal-like functions of the soul (sensing and eating) to the uniquely human function: the intellect.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from folio 313v, the text shifts from the abstract nature of the soul’s faculties discussed on the previous pages to practical applications of moral and logical reasoning. The author first addresses the ethics of commerce (buying and selling) before transitioning into a technical discussion of Aristotelian logic and self-evident truths.</meta>

# [Folio 313v]
<columns>2</columns>

If someone sells an object to another, it is seen that any seller is bound by their own nature to reveal the defect of their goods, primarily because the <term>Ecclesiasticus</term> <note>original: "ecclius"; likely referring to the Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus in the Bible, often cited in medieval trade ethics</note> says that every buyer wants to buy a thing without vice <note>original: "vicio"; meaning a flaw, defect, or hidden problem</note> and because of this, every seller ought to point out the defects of their goods. But on the opposite side, it is said that every seller wants to sell a thing for as much as they can. And therefore it does not seem that they ought to speak of the defects of their goods unless they are asked.

I say to this that someone can sell their property in two ways: either by themselves or through another. If by themselves, then I say that every seller is bound to show the defect of their goods because if they did not show it, they would then act against that <term>rule of law</term> which says that "one should not wish to be done to another what they do not wish to be done to themselves." Since everyone wants the defects of a thing they are buying to be shown to them, they themselves ought to show them to others.

Second, I say that everyone is bound to tell the defects of their goods unless they are of such a kind that they do not make the thing worth less, or if they are such that the buyer could easily recognize them by themselves.

Third, I say that if a seller sells their property through another person, then I say that the one who sells is bound to tell the defects of that thing which belongs to the owner if they know them. If, however, they do not know them, they are not bound. Nevertheless, if they later learn of the defects of the thing they sold, they are bound to restore a part of the price to the buyer according to the estimated value of that defect.

To this, however, it must be said that ...

<column-break/>

and thus it is clear that although a seller can sell their property for as much as they want, they nevertheless ought to make the defects of their goods manifest to the buyer. And the reason for this is because every buyer ought to know what they are buying, and therefore the seller ought to reveal it to them. To the counter-argument, it is said that although a seller wants to sell a thing for as much as they can, this nevertheless ought to be understood within the bounds of justice and without fraud. Hence, as it is said in the book of <term>Ethics</term> <note>referring to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</note>, an exchange ought to be made according to equality. Therefore, if a seller knows a defect of a thing and does not reveal it to the buyer, they would not be making an exchange according to equality. Therefore, etc.

---

Likewise, it is asked concerning someone who wants to buy something from another, whether they are bound to tell that person the "defects" of their property <note>In this context, this likely refers to a buyer knowing an item is actually more valuable than the seller realizes</note> if they know them and the owner of the thing is ignorant of them. It seems not, because every buyer wants to buy a thing for the lowest price they can. But if they spoke of the "defects" (the hidden value) of the thing, the owner would not sell it for as small a price as they would if they were ignorant of them. Therefore, etc.

# [Folio 314r]

I say therefore that the aforementioned proposition is <term>self-evident</term> <note>original: "per se nota"; a technical term in logic for a statement that is known to be true by its own terms without external proof</note>. For as it is said by Aristotle, that which is through another is not "by itself." But it is manifest that something is "through another" by the way it is understood, and a proposition is self-evident when it is understood that the intellect by itself moves the intellect to assent to the proposition, such that it does not have assent through any other thing except through the proper parts of the proposition itself—just as the proposition is that "every whole is greater than its part," etc.

However, that some people do not assent to self-evident propositions happens because of ignorance of the terms; hence, as it is said in the first book of the <term>Posterior Analytics</term>, self-evident propositions are known only to the wise who know what the terms signify. Hence, those ignorant of what this name "whole" signifies or what this name "part" signifies would not be able to know this proposition to be true: "every whole is greater than its part," etc. From this it is clear that a proposition is called self-evident from the fact that the intellect, as soon as the terms are known, assents to it. And this is clear through Aristotle in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics* where he says that a self-evident proposition is one whose knowledge is immediately had once the terms are known. And from this it follows that a proposition is not called self-evident through anything other than itself, such as an argument or a demonstration, but only through itself. And so it is clear concerning the first, etc.

<column-break/>

To the second, it must be said that it seems, as is said by Aristotle in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, that every definition is a formula signifying "what it is for a thing to be" <note>original: "quid est esse rei"; essentially the essence or core nature of a thing</note>. But it is manifest that a definition is not a proposition, but is a term. For as it is said there, a definition is a term that signifies what it is for a thing to be. And therefore, just as a term is not said to be self-evident or unknown, but only a proposition is, so it seems that a definition ought not to be called self-evident or unknown.

But to this it is said that although a definition by itself is not a proposition, it nevertheless virtually contains a proposition. For as it is said there, a definition is a formula whose parts are self-evident, and therefore a definition is called self-evident insofar as it is a principle of demonstration. For from definitions, as if from principles, demonstration proceeds. And thus it is clear that just as a proposition is called self-evident because it does not need another thing for its manifestation, so a definition is called self-evident because it does not need another thing for its manifestation, but it is manifest of itself once the terms that constitute it are known. Hence, as it is said there, a definition manifests what a thing is. And it does this by itself and not through another. Therefore it is called self-evident, etc.

<summary>This page discusses the moral obligations of disclosure in sales, arguing that sellers must reveal defects based on the Golden Rule and Aristotelian equality. It then shifts to logic, explaining that self-evident propositions and definitions are understood immediately by anyone who knows the meaning of the terms involved.</summary>
<keywords>ethics of sale, disclosure of defects, Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, self-evident propositions, Posterior Analytics, definitions, logic, scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 317 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the scholastic exploration of the soul's faculties. While the previous page was heavily damaged, the text here clarifies the relationship between the soul, the mind, and the spirit using the metaphor of a marriage.</meta>

Whatever the soul may now appear to be,
it is in no way seen as separate from the body so long as
the soul possesses a mind,
nor can it lack reason and its rational
mind, which is its lord and husband <note>original: "dominus et uir"</note>. For this reason,
namely, that reason and mind are the soul's lord: it appears
as though the rational power, to which the Lord has not come,
nor has He come to the mind for the judgment of the mind
which is called the "spirit of reason" <note>original: "spiritum rationis"</note>. And thus the soul
possesses its reason and mind as its husband and lord,
through which reason and mind the Lord comes
to the mind of the soul. And through this mind, as
it has been said, the wife is sanctified through her husband—
that is, the soul—just as it is said that through a holy mind the husband
is enlightened, so the wife is; likewise, through this mind as her husband
and lord, the soul is sanctified and enlightened
through the Holy Spirit and through the grace of the Lord. Thus,
from this it appears that the soul can
do nothing without its reason and mind,
for the reason and mind are called the "husband" of the soul.

---
-> - <-

The soul is truly called
a woman <note>original: "mulier"</note> by its nature. For just as
through a woman a woman produces
children without a man <note>The text here seems to imply the necessity of the male principle for reproduction as a metaphor for the intellect's role in producing virtues</note>: so the soul,
as a human being possessing a mind, does not produce good
works without its reason and mind.
Hence, as it is said in the book *On the Woman of the Lord* <note>original: "liber de muliere domini"</note>:
the mind of the husband enlightens the wife and thus causes
the wife to produce children, and so the woman produces children
by the power of the husband. Likewise, the soul produces good
works by the power of reason and the mind. And through this spirit of reason which
every person has by nature, insofar as they have a holy
mind, a person is called "rational" and "spiritual."
However, this spiritual and rational person, insofar
as they are called so of themselves, is so through this holy mind. Hence,
the holy mind, which is called the "spirit of reason," through this
mind and reason the Lord enlightens the mind
of the soul. And through this mind and reason of the soul,
the wife—that is, the soul—is said to be sanctified by her mind.
For the mind of the mind, the soul, is called the "wife,"
because she looks toward her husband, namely, toward
her reason, and by that holy mind
and reason she is illustrated and enlightened.
And it is said, as it were, that the husband is sanctified through the woman—
that is, the soul is sanctified through the mind.
<meta>catchword: monstrat (shows)</meta>

<column-break/>

it shows the soul as the husband and the
holy mind as the wife enlightening the mind.
Hence, just as the mind enlightens the soul as
a husband does a woman: so the mind is sanctified and enlightened
by the grace of the Lord, sanctified through the mind
and reason of the human being. Through the holy mind, the
soul is sanctified. And as it is said in the book *On the Spirit and the Soul* <note>original: "liber de spiritu et anima," a popular 12th-century treatise often attributed to Augustine</note>:
the spirit is called the "husband," the soul indeed
is the "woman." Hence, the spirit enlightens the mind
of the soul as a husband does a woman. And it is seen
that the spirit enlightens and illuminates the mind;
and every human being possesses this spirit of the mind
by nature in regard to the mind's reason.
However, this spirit through which the soul is sanctified
is called the "Holy of Holies" <note>original: "sanctus sanctorum"</note>, and only
the saints possess this spirit through the grace of the Lord.
Hence, as it has been said, the soul can
do nothing without reason and a holy mind,
except as it is said: "as the husband wills." Hence,
if the husband wills that the soul's mind be sanctified,
it shall be enlightened; and through this spirit,
the mind of the soul is enlightened by the grace of God.
This "spirit of reason," which both sinners
and the just have by nature, he calls "reason."
However, this sanctified spirit he calls
the "Holy Spirit." Only the
just and the holy have this spirit through the grace of the Lord. Hence, it is said
here that the soul does nothing by itself without its husband—
that is, reason. Therefore, just as the soul is said to be
sanctified through the mind, so the soul is
enlightened and sanctified through the mind of the Lord. Hence,
Dionysius <note>referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian</note> says regarding this spirit of reason which
a person has by nature: through this spirit,
 the rational person judges all things. And this is what
he wants to say: through this spirit of the mind which
every person has by nature, through this spirit,
a person judges all things through reason. However, this
spirit of the human mind does not sanctify the mind
of a person by itself without the grace of the Lord. Hence, the soul
without its husband—that is, reason—has no good
works and does not produce them; likewise, the mind of the soul is not enlightened
without the holy mind. Hence,
the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says in 1 Corinthians 7: "the unbelieving husband
is sanctified through the faithful wife." Likewise,
here the unbelieving mind of the soul is sanctified
through the holy mind of reason. Hence, the holy soul
sanctifies its mind through the grace of the Lord and
enlightens the reason of its mind. Hence, it is said
here that the soul does nothing without its husband—
that is, reason—just as it is said in 1 Corinthians 7.
The wife is named through her mind where they call
upon the reason of the husband; hence the husband is called "reason" through the mind.
<meta>catchword: quid (what)</meta>

<column-break/>

what it may take, nor does it breathe just so,
as if it were permitted to it to be able to do something by
itself without the help of the husband, as is seen in these matters;
nor does it seem likely in its order, unless it has
pleased its husband, who shall have it wherever
he wills; the soul or spirit itself cannot do
anything without the help of its husband, namely, reason.
For the "head of the woman is the man" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:3</note>: the soul is reason,
the <unclear>faculties</unclear> of the husband's virtue through which the spirit...

---

However, this is the spirit which
gives vital power and connection
to the soul and the body. Hence, just as the limbs are moved
by the animal spirit <note>term: "animal spirit" (spiritus animalis): in medieval physiology, a subtle substance that carries signals from the brain to the muscles</note>, so through this spirit
and virtue which the husband—namely, reason—gives it,
the vital powers are moved as he wills, both
sensible and interior and exterior powers.
For the Spirit, as it is said in 2 Corinthians 3: "where the Spirit
of the Lord is, there is liberty." And so, for the soul to become free,
it is necessary that it be moved by the Spirit of the Lord.
For the spiritual life in us is the "spirit of reason,"
that is, of the intelligence. Regarding this
spirit in terms of the intellect, Job says in chapter 32:
"it is the spirit of God that teaches intelligence."
It is called the spirit of reason, namely, that spark <term>scintilla: often called the "scintilla conscientiae" (spark of conscience), the highest, uncorrupted part of the human soul</term>
which resides in the mind of a person, through which the Lord
enlightens the reason and the mind to understand the truth.
As Dionysius says: through this spirit,
the Lord makes an "inspiring voice" through which the mind
is illuminated toward the truth. Not only the just
have this spirit, but also sinners, in regard
to the judgment of reason, in which there remains some
rectitude, as Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> says. This spirit
moves the mind toward the right, and through this spirit,
the soul can do nothing of itself
except as its husband—reason—wills, according to whose
will the soul is moved and governed.
For just as it is said of the woman in 1 Corinthians 7:
"the mind of the husband sanctifies the unbelieving wife," so
here the mind of the husband—that is, of rational reason—illustrates
and enlightens the mind of the sinning soul
and illuminates it so that it may become good through the spirit
of reason and through the grace of God. Hence, through this spirit,
in regard to the virtue of the person, the soul becomes free,
vital, and good. For through reason and its mind,
and through the spirit of reason in itself, as
has been said, the soul is moved, and through this it produces
good works; and they call this the "spirit of reason,"
as it is said through reason.
<meta>catchword: spiritualis (spiritual)</meta>

<column-break/>

it is called "spiritual" through the grace of the Lord, as if
through the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies the person and
enlightens them and makes them do the things that are of the Lord.
The just and holy possess this spirit, through which
spirit the mind of the person is enlightened to do good
things. And through this, the person is called "spiritual," through
which spirit the reason of the person is enlightened toward the Lord
and toward spiritual things; and sinners do not have this spirit.
For the Holy Spirit of the Lord,
who is seen in the intelligence of reason,
was that by which a person might understand. And only the
just and holy possess this. Hence, Dionysius says this spirit
enlightens the minds of the saints. And this is what
he wants to say through this spirit of reason which he mentions
here. This is the spirit which judges all things,
which the saints possess through the grace of the Lord.
For the spirit of reason, which every person has through reason
and through the mind, is that by which a person is called "rational."
But the Holy Spirit, which the saints possess through grace,
is that by which a person is called "spiritual," through which a person
does the things that are of the Lord. And each spirit
enlightens the mind of the soul—that is, the reason of the rational person—
and illustrates the reason of the soul so that it becomes good.
And through this spirit of reason, which every person
possesses by nature through reason: through this spirit,
a person judges all things through reason, as it is said
in 2 Corinthians 2: "the spiritual person judges all things, and he
is judged by no one." But this is said concerning the Holy Spirit.
However, in regard to the spirit of reason, the mind
of a person judges all things that pertain to reason.
Now, this spirit through which the soul
becomes spiritual is the reason of the saints, enlightened
by the grace of the Lord. This spirit sanctifies
the mind of a person and makes that reason holy.
And the Lord dwells in it; hence it is said in 1 Corinthians 3:
"do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit
of God dwells in you?" It is as if he were saying, "it is so."
Hence, the saints possess this spirit of reason and grace,
through which their rational mind becomes holy.
Through this spirit, the soul judges all things
and possesses a sanctified reason. Moreover, this
spirit through which the mind is sanctified and enlightened
is that through which a person understands the things that are of the Lord.
Hence it is said in 1 Corinthians 2: "the animal man <note>original: "animalis homo," meaning the person led by natural instincts rather than the spirit</note> does not
perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is
foolishness to him, and he cannot understand
because it is examined spiritually. But the spiritual person
judges all things, and he is judged by no one."
This spirit is the holy reason of the saints,
which they possess through the grace of God. Hence, this spirit
is called the "mind of the saints," sanctified through grace
and reason. Hence, the Lord dwells in this spirit, just as
it is said: "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty."

<summary>This page explores the medieval theological concept of the soul's hierarchy, using the marriage metaphor to describe how reason (the husband) must govern and enlighten the soul (the wife) to produce virtuous works. It distinguishes between the natural "spirit of reason" found in all humans and the "Holy Spirit" granted to the just through grace.</summary>
<keywords>soul, reason, mind, Holy Spirit, marriage metaphor, scholastic psychology, grace, free will, enlightenment, Dionysius the Areopagite, Gregory the Great, Saint Paul</keywords>
